Orientation and ReferenceHow to Read This Book

This reference section of the book contains a summary of its six central claims, a diagram connecting them, and a glossary for reference.

First time here? Begin with the Author’s Note and the Preface, then continue into Chapter 1.

Looking for a refresher? Use What This Book Argues for the six central claims and their relationships, and the Glossary for definitions.

The book asks how we can safely grant autonomy to commodity intelligence. Chapter 1 frames the engineering problem. Chapters 2–5 develop MAGE through software engineering, explaining its mechanisms and examining the evidence. Chapter 6 develops the theory, Chapter 7 considers its broader implications, and the Conclusion asks what engineers remain responsible for when they delegate the work. Figure 0.1-1 traces the progression.

The book's argument in three movements — the engineering question, the nested software-engineering case, and the engineering argument it substantiates, from the Preface's question to the Conclusion's answer A single descent through the book's argument, in three movements. The Preface poses the opening question: how do we safely grant autonomy to commodity intelligence? It leads to Chapter 1, The New Engineering Problem — changed economics. A subtly shaded region then nests the software-engineering case — the chapters that develop the mechanisms and supply the evidence. Inside it: Chapter 2, Modeling — make knowledge and intent explicit. Then Chapter 3, Alignment — enforce selected obligations. Then Chapter 4, MAGE in Motion — the mechanisms put in motion on a worked problem: model, align, work, convert. Then Chapter 5, Agentic Software Factories — the production system that supplies the evidence: a deep case, industrial variation, and what the factories show. The descent leaves the case region at Chapter 6, The Theory — the abstraction from those factories: dynamics, economics, predictions, and scope conditions. Then Chapter 7, The Profession — how software work reorganizes, agentic engineering beyond software, and the responsibility that remains the engineer's. The descent ends at the Conclusion, which returns to the Preface's question and asks its converse: what cannot be delegated? Responsibility. question → worked case → theory → implications → answer Preface “How do we safely grant autonomy to commodity intelligence?” Chapter 1 · The New Engineering Problem changed economics THE SOFTWARE ENGINEERING CASE mechanisms · practice · evidence Chapter 2 · Modeling make knowledge + intent explicit Chapter 3 · Alignment enforce selected obligations Chapter 4 · MAGE in Motion model · align · work · convert Chapter 5 · Agentic Software Factories deep case · industrial variation · production systems abstract from the factories Chapter 6 · The Theory dynamics · economics · predictions · scope Chapter 7 · The Profession software work · broader engineering · responsibility Conclusion returns to the question, and asks its converse: “What cannot be delegated?” — RESPONSIBILITY Figure 0.1-1. The book’s argument. The software-engineering case leads to theory, broader implications, and responsibility.

Readers can also take shorter routes:

  • Try it Monday: Chapter 1 → Chapter 4 → Appendix B.
  • Adopt it in an organization: Chapter 1 → §5.4 → Appendix B.
  • The theory: Preface → Chapter 1 → Chapter 6.

docs.title: What This Book Argues
docs.text:
Orientation and ReferenceWhat This Book Argues

This section is a compact statement of the book's argument, intended for orientation and later reference. This book makes six central claims. Together they explain how commodity intelligence changes the economics of engineering, why scale remains a problem, and how MAGE responds.

MAGE is a framework for governing agentic engineering work. This book develops that framework through software engineering, its first worked domain and the source of its evidence. The six claims below are therefore stated primarily in software-engineering terms; Chapter 6 abstracts their mechanisms, and Chapter 7 asks what transfers beyond software.

  1. Commodity intelligence changes the economics of software engineering. You can now purchase a kind of intelligence. The resulting implementation capacity is becoming abundant relative to engineering judgment. As implementation gets cheaper, engineering effort shifts toward what remains scarce: deciding what to build, representing the system clearly enough to reason about it, producing evidence, and making requirements enforceable by the engineering environment.
  1. Scale creates a reasoning problem. Large software systems exceed the reasoning horizon of humans; agents have the same problem. Software engineering has always answered scale with abstraction. Commodity intelligence does not remove that need. It makes the representations that guide the work more important.
  1. Purposeful models can reduce the cost of engineering reasoning. Engineering models capture the knowledge and intent needed for decisions. Software engineers have always used such abstractions to reason about architecture and other system properties. As commodity intelligence lowers the cost of deriving, maintaining, and using such representations, more engineering knowledge can be carried forward rather than held implicit or reconstructed from implementation.
  1. Enforcing obligations makes autonomous implementation governable. When agents perform more of the implementation, deciding what the system must do becomes increasingly separate from writing the code that does it. Important engineering decisions therefore cannot live only in instructions to an agent or in a person's head. Engineers can enforce these obligations through checks and controls that constrain work, distinguishing choices an agent is free to make from decisions engineers have already made. Engineers can then give agents substantial freedom in how they build the system while retaining control over the properties that matter.
  1. Governance conversion turns recurring judgment into durable engineering structure. When a failure exposes missing knowledge or an unenforced obligation, encode the lesson into a model, procedure, or mechanism that future work can inherit. Durable structure becomes engineering capital when later work keeps benefiting from it.
  1. Engineering work will reorganize around what remains scarce. As implementation becomes cheaper, engineering effort will move toward representation, evidence, governance, coordination, and judgment. Agents may perform increasing portions of that work as well. The enduring boundary will not be a particular task or level of abstraction, but responsibility for deciding what matters, what evidence is sufficient, which obligations should be enforced, and what tradeoffs remain acceptable.

In operation, MAGE has two principles and a conversion loop. Modeling makes consequential knowledge and intent explicit, while Alignment makes selected obligations enforceable. As engineering work progresses, gaps are inevitable. Governance conversion turns recurring human judgment into explicit engineering structure that future work can inherit. Figure 0.2-1 connects these responses to the economic change, the reasoning problem, and the predicted reorganization of engineering work.

The six claims, connected Claims one and two motivate two parallel principles: Modeling and Alignment. Both guide and govern engineering work. Recurring failures and judgment lead to governance conversion; feedback adapts models and controls for future work. Engineering capital depends on later benefit. Claim six is a separate prediction about the reorganization of engineering work. 1 · Commodity intelligence changes the economics of software engineering Implementation capacity becomes abundant relative to engineering judgment. 2 · Scale creates a reasoning problem Large software systems exceed the reasoning horizon of humans and agents. 3 · Modeling Purposeful models can reduce the cost of engineering reasoning. Capture consequential knowledge and intent while leaving irrelevant choices open. 4 · Alignment Explicit obligations can make autonomous implementation governable. Constraints restrict; sensors observe; gates control admission. Governed engineering work Substantial implementation freedom; control over the properties that matter. 5 · Governance conversion Recurring judgment becomes durable structure. Future work inherits models and controls. Engineering capital when later work keeps benefiting. 6 · Predicted reorganization of engineering work Engineering work will reorganize around what remains scarce. docs.title: Author’s Note
docs.text:
Orientation and ReferenceAuthor’s Note

As a professor, I direct a research lab by identifying promising directions and delegating their detailed investigation to my assistants. I can give those students a broad sense of my goals through meetings and whiteboard drawings, and they carry them out.

When I began working with GenAI, I treated it much the same way. The agent confidently translated my strategic orders into local implementation and tactical choices. But after about 200,000 lines, I found that although my ability to issue orders was unchanged (if anything, my ambition had grown!), the agents’ ability to carry them out appeared to be decaying. The good vibes had turned bad: how could an agent implement a complicated request one day, yet struggle to correct a simple defect the next? As I examined the software more carefully, I found that it looked and sounded like my vision, but was not. It was a facsimile of my goals, akin to a child’s finger-painted version of the Mona Lisa or a first-year engineering student’s popsicle-stick bridge. My sense of progress had been a mirage. Claude had not fully understood all my intentions, and had not perfectly implemented those it had.

This book describes what I did next. Firm in the belief that there must be some way to get agents to build reliable systems, I turned to my Professor’s Bookshelf. I revisited the engineering ideas that had shaped my own practice: abstraction, modularity, specifications, and the separation of design from implementation. I began experimenting with different ways of conveying my intentions to agents and different ways of checking that the resulting software honored them. Eventually, it worked.

I share what I learned in the tradition of books on software engineering methodologies. My own understanding of how to engineer was shaped by Dijkstra, Ousterhout, McConnell, Meyer, Uncle Bob, Martin Fowler, Kent Beck, the Gang of Four, and others. Their books taught me how to reason about software, organize its construction, and recognize good engineering. But none of them trained me to delegate implementation to an eager and capable subordinate who could produce extraordinary amounts of code without necessarily understanding what I wanted. This book is my account of learning how to do that.

James C. DavisWest Lafayette, IN2026

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Orientation and ReferenceGlossary

This glossary groups the book’s vocabulary under Engineering, Software Agents, and MAGE.

docs.title: Engineering
docs.text:
Authority. Who is entitled to exercise engineering judgment: to decide what a system must do, permit or refuse an action, and answer for the result? Authority is a matter of decision rights and responsibility, held by a person or institution and delegated deliberately. It is distinct from enforcement—the mechanisms through which the environment holds work to an obligation—and from an authoritative source, the canonical origin of a fact.

Engineering. The discipline of exercising informed control over consequential systems and accepting responsibility for their outcomes. Control means retaining sufficient command of a system to understand and direct it, evaluate the evidence for its consequential properties, recognize when its assumptions fail, and intervene when necessary. Responsibility means remaining answerable for the consequential decisions made under one's authority and for the resulting system. Engineering does not require personally performing every act of implementation, and work may be delegated to other humans or to machine intelligence. Engineering is defined by the control, evidence, expertise, and responsibility exercised, regardless of whether the work belongs to a conventionally named engineering discipline. Software engineering applies this discipline to software systems.

Engineering judgment. The use of technical knowledge, evidence, and experience to decide what matters in an engineering situation and what action is justified. It includes choosing appropriate models and assumptions, assessing whether evidence is sufficient, and weighing the consequences for people affected by the system 12.1. Henry Petroski, “Failure as a Source of Engineering Judgment: John Roebling as a Paradigmatic Designer,” chap. 8 in Design Paradigms: Case Histories of Error and Judgment in Engineering (Cambridge University Press, 1994), https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511805073.009.2. Jessica Swenson et al., “A Taxonomy of Emerging Engineering Modeling Judgment in Undergraduate Engineering Courses,” Journal of Engineering Education 114, no. 4 (2025): e70011, https://doi.org/10.1002/jee.70011. Competence in making these decisions, together with accountability for their consequences, helps justify society entrusting engineers with authority over consequential systems 3.3. Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering, “Statement of Ethical Principles,” 2026, https://www.engc.org.uk/resources-and-guidance/guidance-for-the-profession/ethical-principles.

Engineering obligation. A requirement or engineering decision that the responsible engineering authority has determined a system or its development must satisfy. Obligations may arise externally—from users, regulations, standards, contracts, or operating environments—or internally, from decisions about architecture, behavior, quality, or process. An obligation is evaluable when the environment can obtain evidence about whether it holds. It is enforceable when that evidence can be connected to a mechanism that prevents or refuses violations within a declared scope. Enforcement is the application of that mechanism.

Model. A purposeful simplification of a system that preserves what matters for a particular engineering question. By leaving other details out, a model makes the relevant properties easier to understand and reason about than the system itself.

Software engineering. The engineering discipline associated with the creation and modification of software systems. Due to the flexibility of the engineering medium, software engineering is unusual in the rate of change of the engineered system.

Tolerance and degree of freedom. Engineering obligations need not determine a single acceptable implementation. Tolerances describe the bounds of acceptable variation; degrees of freedom describe the choices remaining within those bounds. Note that an unmodeled choice may not truly be free. If some alternatives would violate an unwritten engineering obligation, the choice remains constrained even if the model does not express that constraint.

Traceability. Explicit, machine-readable links from model elements to the artifacts, evidence, obligations, or other model elements they represent, constrain, or correspond to. A link can remain intact while its meaning has gone stale: a test may still carry a requirement’s identifier after it has stopped testing that requirement.

docs.title: Software Agents
docs.text:
Agent. An AI system that pursues an open-ended or underspecified task through multiple steps, exercising judgment about what to do next and using tools in response to intermediate results. This book is focused specifically on the use of “coding agents” in a software development context.

Agentic harness. The runtime that turns a foundation model’s reasoning into action by managing context, invoking tools, and returning results to the model. It may expose hooks at which additional code can run. How those facilities are configured and used is part of the engineered environment.

Churn. Work spent rediscovering context, undoing recent changes, repairing regressions, or reconciling inconsistencies instead of advancing the system.

Commodity intelligence. General-purpose machine intelligence available cheaply and at enough scale that implementation becomes less scarce relative to engineering judgment. The term describes an economic change, not a claim that such intelligence is free, unlimited, excellent, or sufficient for engineering.

Foundation model. The trained model at the bottom of the agent stack. Its capabilities and context capacity shape the harness and engineered environment around it.

Reasoning horizon. Reasoning is the use of available information to draw inferences, evaluate alternatives, and work toward a solution. A reasoning horizon is the practical limit of the work a reasoner and its supporting machinery can carry through reliably, given the available representations and resources. For an agent, this depends on the foundation model together with the harness and engineered environment.

Skills and tools. Capabilities exposed through an agentic harness that extend what an agent can do. A skill provides reusable guidance for a recurring class of work; a tool provides a capability the agent can invoke rather than approximate through reasoning.

docs.title: MAGE
docs.text:
Agentic engineering. The engineering of systems and environments in which autonomous agents perform consequential work. MAGE develops one approach, using software engineering as its principal example.

Alignment Principle. Make selected engineering obligations enforceable through constraints that restrict actions or states, sensors that produce evidence, and gates that evaluate evidence and control whether work may proceed. Some obligations can be enforced directly on actions or artifacts; explicit models let the environment state and check richer properties, including acceptable bounds on variation.

Engineering capital. Durable engineering structure—models, packaged procedures, mechanisms, canonical documentation, and other reusable assets—that makes later work cheaper or less uncertain. Governance conversion creates such structure; it becomes capital when later work benefits from it, and depreciates when it no longer fits the system or costs more to maintain than it returns.

Governance. Deciding what autonomous work must know, what it may do, what evidence it must produce, and what mechanisms will hold those decisions over time.

Governance conversion. Turning a lesson from a recurring failure, repeated judgment, or observed gap into durable engineering structure that future work inherits. The structure may be an engineering model, packaged procedure, or mechanism that enforces an obligation. The conversion lets later work use the resulting structure without reconstructing the original judgment.

Governance mechanisms. Repeatable structures in the engineered environment that constrain agentic work, produce evidence about it, or control whether it may proceed. This book distinguishes three kinds of mechanisms.

  • Constraint. Restricts available actions or states.
  • Sensor. Observes the work or system and produces evidence about artifacts, proposed actions, or executions.
  • Gate. Evaluates whether an action or result may proceed and enforces the decision.

Governed Engineering Environment. The engineered environment surrounding autonomous work, comprising the existing system and the representations, tools, processes, permissions, and controls through which engineers direct and govern its development. Repeatable mechanisms enforce selected engineering obligations, allowing consequential decisions to persist across successive agents and changes.

Model drift. Disagreement between a model and the system, evidence, or other representation to which it is meant to correspond. The disagreement identifies a correspondence problem whose resolution may require engineering judgment, especially if it is unclear which view is authoritative. Reconciliation often requires aligning the system with the engineering intent captured in the model. See also: Ratcheteering.

Modeling Principle. Externalize knowledge and intent into engineering models that both engineers and agents can reason through. Appropriate representations make otherwise intractable engineering questions manageable and make additional properties available for Alignment.

Ratcheteering. The practice of introducing an authoritative engineering model that deliberately disagrees with an existing system, then directing agents to change the implementation until it conforms to the model. Rather than adapting the model to describe the existing implementation, the engineer uses the model to establish how the system should be structured or behave. See also: Model drift.

Semantic gap. The distance between where an engineering obligation arises and where the environment has enough meaning and evidence to decide whether the obligation is satisfied. The gap explains why some checks must wait until a later boundary, when enough of the system has been assembled to make the obligation decidable.

docs.title: How do we safely grant autonomy to commodity intelligence?
docs.text:
This is a book about engineering: what engineering becomes when reasoning capacity is abundant. Engineering is the discipline of exercising informed control over consequential systems and accepting responsibility for their outcomes. Engineers need not personally perform every act required to realize a system. They must understand and direct the work, evaluate evidence for the properties that matter, and intervene when necessary. They remain answerable for the consequential decisions made under their authority.

Society has long entrusted consequential work to computers. Software tallies tax returns, flies aircraft, and operates power plants. Traditionally, software engineers translated human intent into programs and controls that computers could execute. Now, general-purpose machine intelligence can interpret intent, make judgments, and produce implementation cheaply enough and at enough scale to become an ordinary engineering resource. In this book, I call this increasingly available capability commodity intelligence 11. John Nosta, “Intelligence as a Commodity,” Psychology Today, March 12, 2026, https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-digital-self/202603/intelligence-as-a-commodity. 22. Darwin Ling, “The $0.50 Barrel of Intelligence,” GoodAI, July 20, 2026, https://goodai.substack.com/p/the-050-barrel-of-intelligence., and the tools that supply it, agents.

Agents can be used to produce and modify software at rates far exceeding what human engineers can review. Engineers need ways to preserve control, because engineers remain responsible for ensuring that the resulting systems satisfy their requirements. Important decisions must survive successive changes, and engineers need evidence for properties that may be difficult to see in any one change. How should we engineer the environment in which that autonomous work takes place?

docs.title: MAGE: Model-Based Agentic Engineering
docs.text:
Agentic engineering is the engineering of systems and environments in which autonomous agents perform consequential work. Model-Based Agentic Engineering (MAGE) is the approach this book develops. It rests on two principles. Modeling makes consequential engineering knowledge and intent explicit in purposeful representations. Alignment makes selected engineering obligations enforceable, so those obligations can hold independently of an agent’s judgment.

The MAGE method combines these principles through four recurring engineering activities:

  1. Model consequential knowledge. Choose the engineering question, then represent the facts, relationships, and decisions needed to answer it without carrying unnecessary detail.
  1. Enforce important obligations. Use constraints to restrict actions or states, or gates to admit work only when required conditions hold.
  1. Do the governed work. Let agents operate within the resulting environment, using its models and mechanisms while exercising the implementation freedom engineers have left open.
  1. Convert recurring judgment. Identify engineering decisions that require repeated human intervention, then encode them in models, procedures, or mechanisms that subsequent work can inherit.

Together, these activities develop a governed engineering environment: representations help humans and agents reason about the system, while mechanisms enforce selected obligations. The activities need not occur in a fixed order, and the environment can change as experience reveals what needs better understanding or control. Useful structure becomes engineering capital when later work benefits from it.

docs.title: Why MAGE? Why Models?
docs.text:
One way to understand MAGE is as a classical software-engineering move: add a level of indirection.** In software engineering, adding a level of indirection is so commonly a solution that it is jokingly called the Fundamental Theorem of Software Engineering. Conventional engineering has long separated the engineering of an artifact from its physical realization. The familiar inscription “Designed by Apple in California, Made in China” is an everyday example: the people who establish a product’s architecture, requirements, and tolerances need not be the people—or machines—that realize it. Drawings, specifications, and other representations preserve consequential decisions across that separation.

When software engineers wrote most of the code themselves, they could make design decisions and implement them directly. Much of their knowledge remained implicit in the implementation and in their minds. That arrangement of work is less effective with agents. An agent needs to know which dependencies are permitted, who owns a resource, and what behaviors must survive changes. Engineering models give that knowledge an explicit form that engineers and agents can inspect and reason through, without repeatedly reconstructing it from the code.

The purpose of this indirection is to preserve important engineering decisions while leaving other implementation choices open. Agents can search, implement, revise, and improve solutions within that freedom. Engineers can impose additional constraints, but more structure is not automatically valuable. The engineer must decide what matters enough to make explicit and whether the resulting understanding, assurance, or efficiency justifies the cost.

docs.title: The origins of MAGE
docs.text:
MAGE grew out of an engineering problem I encountered while building DocAble, a service for making documents accessible to people with disabilities. I built DocAble by myself—just me and Claude, which produces software far faster than I can inspect. Yet DocAble has to satisfy legal accessibility requirements. I could not solve that problem by supervising the agents more closely; human attention was precisely the resource I did not have.

As I watched the collapse of my weekly Apple Watch sleep score, I realized I had to make the requirements and other consequential properties explicit enough that Claude could preserve and evaluate them without requiring me to inspect every step. I needed to capture my engineering judgment in order to reduce how often I had to supply it.

DocAble provides the book’s deepest worked example: a system developed over several months and used in production at Purdue. I also reconstruct published industrial accounts to examine related mechanisms in other organizations. DocAble provides depth about engineering decisions and their consequences; the industrial accounts provide breadth across production environments. Chapter 5 presents both sources of evidence and their limitations. Chapter 6 develops the theoretical account, and Chapter 7 asks what may transfer beyond software.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
This book is for software engineers who want to understand what changes when implementation can be delegated to capable agents. It is also for architects, technical leads, and engineering managers responsible for the environment around that work.

The book is also intended for advanced undergraduate and graduate students. It assumes familiarity with ordinary software-development practice: source control, testing, APIs, build and deployment workflows, and basic software architecture. No prior experience with coding agents, formal methods, model-based engineering, or machine learning is required. Concepts from those areas are introduced where the argument needs them.

MAGE draws on established engineering disciplines without attempting to replace their textbooks. The machinery described here is a repertoire, not a required architecture. Different problems call for different representations and controls, and some need very little of either. Your task is to judge what structure is worth building, which choices can remain with the agents, and what evidence is sufficient to accept their work.

docs.title: §1.1 · The Printer
docs.text:
Chapter 1 — The New Engineering Problem  ::  §1.1§1.1 The Printer

Coding agents make software implementation cheap enough to change the engineering problem. Describe a change and an agent can often implement it quickly. The opportunity is substantial, but what should we do with this new capacity?

For an analogy, let us begin with office supplies. A stapler joins sheets of paper and a hole punch makes holes in them. Their purposes and limitations are in their names. A printer leaves more for us to decide. The same 2D printer can produce a newspaper, a poster, or a map, each with its own conventions for layout and legibility. A 3D printer can turn a description of a shape into a mounting bracket, a protective enclosure, or an adapter, each with different requirements for strength, clearance, and fit. As people discover what the machinery can usefully make, they develop templates, reusable designs, and production practices that give the next person a place to start.

Software agents are printers, not staplers. Like printers, agents supply broad productive capacity. Like printers, agents can follow instructions. But agents can infer much more from an incomplete description than a physical printer can: an algorithm, a data structure, or a decomposition may never have been specified, and yet an agent can choose them and produce an implementation. That inferential capacity is precisely what makes the machinery powerful.

Working with agents therefore means delegating judgment as well as implementation. The engineering challenge is deciding how much judgment to delegate.

docs.text: Chapter 1 — The New Engineering Problem  ::  §1.2§1.2 The Engineering Object

docs.title: 1.2.1 Consequential Choices and Degrees of Freedom
docs.text:
Delegating implementation is useful only if we can avoid doing much of the implementation work ourselves. Imagine asking an agent to build a feature. The first attempt fails, so we specify the data structures. The next attempt performs poorly, so we prescribe the indexes and queries. Then come the transaction boundaries, the function signatures, and eventually the variable names. Should we just write the code ourselves? How much direction, and of what kind, does an agent need to produce an acceptable result? We want to specify the decisions that matter without having to make all the decisions that implementation requires.

When implementation is delegated, engineers must decide which choices to make and which to leave open. A function could be implemented in ten lines or ten thousand. A service could be built as a monolith or decomposed into microservices. Different algorithms, data structures, and architectures might all satisfy the same requirements. Some choices are better than others, but engineers need not make every choice in advance. They can specify the properties that matter and leave other decisions to the intelligence performing the work. Which choices can safely remain open is itself an engineering decision.

Commodity intelligence can also change why an engineering choice matters. Consider the choice of a programming language. A human team might favor Java because its developers know it well. If agents can implement competently in several languages, that consideration weakens, while the ability to review their output may become more important. Meanwhile, a safety requirement may favor a language that provides a needed property, such as automatic garbage collection to reduce memory leaks caused by missing deallocation. A deployment target may also require a particular toolchain. These latter considerations persist regardless of who writes the code. The relevant question is what made the choice matter, and how those reasons change when agents perform the implementation.

The same distinction applies at larger scales. Suppose a service needs persistent storage. If either a relational or nonrelational database can satisfy every property that matters, choosing between them may simply be a degree of freedom left to implementation. But if the system requires transactions across related records, a particular consistency model, or another property that distinguishes the alternatives, the choice becomes consequential. MAGE does not supply the database theory needed to make that judgment. It asks that the consequential property be represented—and, where necessary, enforced—rather than relying on each implementing agent to rediscover why the choice mattered.

Notice the distinction between unmodeled and free. A choice is unmodeled when the engineering representations do not state it; it is free only when engineers permit the alternatives. Suppose the model says nothing about which database to use. If either database really can satisfy every consequential property, the omission represents a genuine degree of freedom. But if one alternative would violate a security, consistency, or performance obligation, the choice was never free. The engineering model simply failed to make the relevant obligation explicit.

docs.title: 1.2.2 Engineering the Environment
docs.text:
Engineers can externalize those decisions by shaping the environment in which agents work. As with printers, making productive machinery useful requires developing forms and ways of working around it. An engineering environment includes the representations, tools, processes, permissions, evidence, and mechanisms surrounding the agents’ work. In MAGE, a Governed Engineering Environment (GEE) deliberately carries engineering decisions forward by making consequential knowledge available, enforcing selected obligations, and preserving evidence needed for engineering control. Figure 1.2-1 shows how engineering leverage shifts from implementation toward this environment.

Where engineering leverage acts Two pipelines are stacked for contrast. In the classical pipeline the engineer builds the implementation directly, so the implementation is the primary point of engineering control: Engineer, then Implementation, then Product. In the agentic pipeline agents build the implementation inside an engineered environment the engineer constructs, so the environment becomes the primary point of engineering control: Engineer, then Engineered Environment, then Agents, then Implementation, then Product. A rust badge marks the primary node in each row; it moves upstream from the implementation to the environment. A footer strip unpacks the environment into models, obligations, evidence, controls, and infrastructure. WHERE ENGINEERING LEVERAGE ACTS CLASSICAL engineer writes the implementation Engineer Implementation Primary point of engineering control Product AGENTIC agents write the implementation Engineer Engineered Environment Agents Implementation Product Primary point of engineering control Governed Engineering Environment the engineered instructions around autonomous realization models · obligations · evidence · controls · infrastructure Figure 1.2-1. Where engineering leverage acts. When engineers implement systems directly, much of their control acts through the code. With agentic implementation, more of that control acts through the governed engineering environment, which represents consequential intent, constrains work, and evaluates results.

Such an environment serves two different purposes: establishing consequential properties and reducing the cost of repeated engineering work. For assurance, models and checks can provide a manageable basis for evaluating a system even when an agent needs little help understanding its implementation. For efficiency, reusable representations can reduce the work agents spend recovering system knowledge. The two benefits may arise at different scales. Their value must justify the cost of building and maintaining the supporting structure.

An engineering environment intended for agents need not mirror the one we have traditionally built for human developers. Agents can consume and maintain representations at scales that would be impractical for people. These representations also support analyses at a scale and level of detail previously impractical — and perhaps now necessary, given agents’ predilection for shortcuts. The design question is therefore two-sided: what existing engineering machinery should agents inherit, and what stronger machinery becomes practical because some of the workers are now machines?

docs.title: 1.2.3 When Agents Produce the Wrong Result
docs.text:
“’Tis a poor craftsman who blames his tools.” A 3D-printed bracket may fail because the printer lacks the required accuracy, but also because its design or fabrication instructions were unsuitable. Software agents blur this distinction because they can infer missing structure. A capable agent may produce an impressive result from a screenshot, prose request, or incomplete specification, filling in decisions that an engineer might otherwise have had to make explicit. That inferential capacity makes delegation useful, but it can also make omissions in the engineer’s work harder to notice. A completed artifact does not establish that the inferred choices satisfy the intended properties or reflect acceptable tradeoffs.

When an agent produces the wrong result, start with what the engineer controlled: the instructions, representations, task boundaries, available tools, and required evidence. Were important properties missing? Did an instruction leave a decision open that should have been settled? Could the checks detect the error? Sometimes the foundation model simply lacks the necessary capability. Failed output alone does not establish that diagnosis.

Abundant implementation raises the stakes. Capable agents can execute a bad direction with extraordinary speed. Velocity amplifies sound engineering and bad engineering alike.** My field notes on this point were less measured: “Claude is the fastest road to hell.”

docs.title: §1.3 · MAGE by Example: DocAble
docs.text:
Chapter 1 — The New Engineering Problem  ::  §1.3§1.3 MAGE by Example: DocAble

The engineering methodology described in this book emerged from six months of developing and studying a production document-accessibility system called DocAble. I directed the development, but coding agents wrote every line of its implementation. My role was to exercise engineering judgment, direct the agents, and develop the models and controls governing their work. Chapter 5 examines the system and its development in detail. For now, a few facts about DocAble are in order.

docs.title: 1.3.1 The Accessibility Problem
docs.text:
In 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) adopted a rule under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). This rule required covered state and local government entities, including public universities, to make their digital content accessible, whether delivered through the web or mobile applications. The rule sets the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.1 Level AA) as the technical standard. The DOJ later extended the compliance deadline for larger public entities by one year, from April 2026 to April 2027 1.1. U.S. Department of Justice, “Extension of Compliance Dates for Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities,” Federal Register 91 (2026): 20902–12, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/20/2026-07663/extension-of-compliance-dates-for-nondiscrimination-on-the-basis-of-disability-accessibility-of-web. The educational purpose is straightforward: students using assistive technologies, such as screen readers, should be able to obtain and use the information their classmates can access. The rule describes access in terms of “substantially equivalent timeliness, privacy, independence, and ease of use” 2.2. U.S. Department of Justice, Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities, 89 Fed. Reg. 31,320, 2024.

A university’s digital content extends well beyond its public website. Faculty distribute lecture slides, readings, assignments, laboratory instructions, spreadsheets, and other materials through personal websites and learning-management systems. These documents come in many formats, including Microsoft Office (PowerPoint, Word, Excel), their LibreOffice equivalents, HTML, PDF, and LaTeX. Accessibility requires more than making their text machine-readable. A screen reader needs a meaningful reading order, figures need descriptions that convey their educational purpose, and tables and headings need structure that supports navigation 3.3. World Wide Web Consortium, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, 2018, https://www.w3.org/TR/2018/REC-WCAG21-20180605/. One way to eliminate the problem would be to stop distributing documents to students altogether, but the students might take this amiss.** Of course, the U.S. Department of Justice might have taken an even dimmer view of inaccessible course documents. UC Berkeley removed thousands of publicly available lecture recordings in 2017 following a DOJ accessibility investigation.

The scale makes manual remediation difficult. A single course may distribute dozens of slide decks and readings, amounting to hundreds or thousands of pages and slides. Multiply that workload by the thousands of courses offered by many universities, with materials revised each semester, and accessibility becomes a substantial continuing obligation. DocAble would need to improve accessibility without damaging the original documents, interpret their content accurately, explain its changes, and operate economically at institutional scale. Table 1.3-1 groups these requirements.

Table 1.3-1. What DocAble had to accomplish, grouped into four kinds of obligation. Chapter 5 states the complete requirements this grouping summarizes.Kind of obligationDocAble must…Genuine accessibilityRepair problems that require understanding document content, judged against the governing standard (WCAG 2.1 AA) rather than proxy checker scores.PreservationRetain the document's content, appearance, and behavior except where remediation requires a change.AccountabilityRecord what motivated each change and what evidence supports the result, keeping consequential changes inspectable and, where appropriate, reversible.Practical operation at scaleHandle the formats people actually use, at practical sizes, costs, and latency, as a deployed service for thousands of faculty.

docs.title: 1.3.2 The Challenge of Automated Accessibility
docs.text:
Purdue had licensed tools that could identify accessibility problems in course materials, but they did not fix them. I personally maintain two courses containing hundreds of pages and slides, and had no desire to spend a semester remediating them manually. I could delegate some of that work to other people, but delegation would not make me any less responsible for the result. As a lazy software engineer, however, I was perfectly willing to spend six months attempting to automate the work to my own standard.

In early 2026, coding agents had also become capable enough to make a different experiment possible. I wanted to discover what software engineering would look like if I delegated implementation to agents. Accessibility remediation provided a real problem on which to find out. From the user’s perspective, the intended service was simple: upload an inaccessible document; receive a remediated document and a changelog. DocAble would support Word, PowerPoint, Excel, their LibreOffice equivalents, PDF, and text-based formats including LaTeX and Typst. Where possible, it would describe figures, repair reading order, and restore structural accessibility while preserving the original content and presentation. Figure 1.3-1 shows the intended result.

A running glimpse of DocAble — one object in, one object back A single input-to-output panel with no internal structure. On the left, an inaccessible document: a page with unlabeled images, no reading order, and no tags, marked not accessible. An arrow labelled the upload leads into DocAble, drawn as one closed box — the production system at scholaccess.com — with a note that this shows what it does, not yet how. An arrow labelled the file, remediated leads out to the right, to an accessible document with described images, reading order, and tags, carrying an evidence record in which every fix is explained. The caption reads: here is the kind of production system these ideas govern — what it does, not yet how. A running glimpse of DocAble One object in, one object back. image — no alt text not accessible ! inaccessible document unlabeled images · untagged · no reading order DocAble the production system scholaccess.com upload remediated file image — described ✓ evidence record accessible document + evidence tagged · reading order · every fix explained Figure 1.3-1. DocAble from the user's view. An inaccessible document goes in; a remediated document and evidence of consequential changes come back. Internal structure is omitted because it is not yet relevant.

Deciding what to change requires understanding what the content contributes to the lesson. A blue square might decorate a restaurant menu but be the subject of a lecture on modern art. The same visual object calls for different treatment because its purpose differs. Foreign-language materials pose another problem. Language tagging can help a screen reader pronounce a French passage correctly, but supplying a translation that students are supposed to produce themselves would undermine the assignment. A scanned page of handwritten mathematics presents yet another challenge: making it accessible may require recovering notation in a form assistive technology can interpret, while preserving its mathematical meaning.

These examples illustrate why accessibility remediation requires interpreting content in context. Generative AI can help with that interpretation, but building a reliable remediation system requires more. It must handle document formats correctly, preserve the author’s content and presentation, and provide evidence of what changed and what remains uncertain.

docs.title: §1.4 · Agentic Machinery and Its Properties
docs.text:
Chapter 1 — The New Engineering Problem  ::  §1.4§1.4 Agentic Machinery and Its Properties

Engineering methods must fit the machinery they govern. Figure 1.4-1 distinguishes three components of an agentic engineering system: the foundation model that supplies general capabilities, the harness that turns those capabilities into actions, and the engineered environment in which agents work. Understanding their respective roles helps explain where engineers can exercise control.

Commodity intelligence in a governed engineering environmentTraining supplies the foundation model. The model sends outputs to the harness and receives context. The harness acts on the governed engineering environment and receives evidence. Engineers maintain the environment, which supplies project knowledge and controls which actions are permitted. Model development Training data and training Engineer Develops and maintains GEE Foundation model General-purpose reasoning Agentic harness Context management Tools and hooks Action execution Governed engineering environment (GEE) Existing system Project knowledge and controls Outputs Context Actions Evidence Figure 1.4-1. Commodity intelligence in a governed engineering environment. General capabilities from a foundation model become useful engineering machinery when connected to an agentic harness and a governed engineering environment. The environment contains both the existing system and the engineering structure used to guide and govern work. Engineers develop and maintain this environment.

docs.title: 1.4.1 Foundation Models: The Source of Commodity Intelligence
docs.text:
The coding agents available in 2026 are built primarily around large language models (LLMs), which serve as their foundation models. These models acquire general capabilities through training on large collections of text, software, and other data.** Engineering predates machine learning in its use of models as purposeful representations of systems. Machine learning later adopted the same word for a learned approximation of a function—also reasonably a model, but a different kind. This book gives the engineering usage precedence: unqualified model means a purposeful representation of an engineered system or some property of it. I therefore use foundation model for the trained machine-learning system and agent for the acting system built around one through a harness, tools, and working state. Where the distinction matters, I will not ask the reader to infer which “model” I mean. Publicly available source code, including open-source repositories, has been an important source of training material for coding models 1.1. Mark Chen et al., Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code, arXiv preprint arXiv:2107.03374, 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374. Training mixtures can also include licensed material, and their full composition is not always disclosed 2.2. OpenAI, GPT-4 Technical Report, arXiv preprint arXiv:2303.08774, 2023, https://cdn.openai.com/papers/gpt-4.pdf.

The goal of training is to develop a model that can make useful predictions and generalize beyond its training examples. Training typically begins with a prediction objective: given a sequence of tokens, predict the next one. Tokens are units of representation, often words, parts of words, or punctuation. Training adjusts numerical parameters, or weights, to improve these predictions. Additional training can improve how a foundation model follows instructions and responds to human requests 3.3. Long Ouyang et al., “Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback,” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (2022): 27730–44, https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/b1efde53be364a73914f58805a001731-Abstract-Conference.html. At inference time, the trained model processes the context supplied to it and generates a response. An agentic harness turns some of those responses into actions, such as searching a repository, modifying files, running tests, or invoking development tools. Tool results can then be returned as context for further reasoning 4.4. Shunyu Yao et al., “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models,” International Conference on Learning Representations, 2023.

A foundation model trained on public software may know programming languages, libraries, common architectures, and established engineering practices. It ordinarily will not know the current state of the particular system an engineer asks it to modify. That system may be proprietary, may have changed since training, or may contain local design decisions that general programming knowledge cannot supply. Even a seemingly local change may depend on an architectural boundary established years earlier, a configuration convention shared across services, or an operational constraint that appears nowhere near the code being edited. Agents must recover relevant knowledge from the codebase, documentation, configuration, and other available evidence. General programming knowledge must be connected to the particular system and the obligations its changes must preserve.

Engineers can influence a language-based agent in two broad ways. They can modify the foundation model through training or fine-tuning, changing its weights. Alternatively, they can change what the agent receives and the environment in which it operates: instructions, system knowledge, tools, permissions, and feedback. The agentic harness provides some of the machinery for exercising this control, including context management, tool access, and hooks through which engineers can observe or constrain actions. Training a frontier foundation model requires resources far beyond those of an ordinary software engineering project. Fine-tuning is more accessible, particularly through techniques that update only a fraction of the model’s parameters 55. Edward J. Hu et al., “LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models,” International Conference on Learning Representations, 2022, https://openreview.net/forum?id=nZeVKeeFYf9., but still requires suitable training data, evaluation, and maintenance. It may also be unavailable for a particular foundation model. By contrast, engineers can often configure the harness and establish project-specific controls without modifying the model’s weights.

MAGE concentrates on this second approach. The engineer acquires general-purpose intelligence as a service or software component, then engineers the environment in which that intelligence performs consequential work. The foundation model supplies general capabilities, the harness turns its outputs into actions and exposes points of control, and the governed engineering environment supplies the knowledge, obligations, and mechanisms governing those actions.

REASONING

Inset — Do LLMs Reason?

Whether LLMs genuinely reason remains a subject of scientific debate. Bender and colleagues challenged the identification of linguistic fluency with understanding 66. Emily M. Bender et al., “On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big?” Proceedings of the 2021 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, 2021, 610–23, https://doi.org/10.1145/3442188.3445922., while Bubeck and colleagues demonstrated broad problem-solving behavior in an early GPT-4 7.7. Sébastien Bubeck et al., Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early Experiments with GPT-4, arXiv preprint arXiv:2303.12712, 2023, https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12712. More controlled experiments have found evidence of learned internal representations: studies of Othello-playing models recovered representations of board state and demonstrated their influence on predictions 898. Kenneth Li et al., “Emergent World Representations: Exploring a Sequence Model Trained on a Synthetic Task,” International Conference on Learning Representations, 2023, https://openreview.net/forum?id=DeG07_TcZvT.9. Neel Nanda et al., “Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models,” Proceedings of the 6th BlackboxNLP Workshop: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP (Singapore), 2023, 16–30, https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2023.blackboxnlp-1.2., while Jin and Rinard found evidence that models trained on programs had learned aspects of program semantics 10.10. Charles Jin and Martin Rinard, “Emergent Representations of Program Semantics in Language Models Trained on Programs,” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, vol. 235 (2024): 22160–84, https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/jin24e.html. These studies establish different things: observable problem-solving behavior, learned structure, and evidence connecting internal representations to computation. None establishes that an agent will reason reliably about arbitrary production software. For this book, reasoning is a functional capability: using available information to draw inferences, evaluate alternatives, and work toward a solution. LLM-based systems can supply enough of that capability to undertake substantial engineering work. The question for engineering is how to put it to work under informed control.

docs.title: 1.4.2 Four Properties of Commodity Intelligence
docs.text:
Four properties of contemporary foundation models matter to the engineering argument.

Broad semantic reasoning. A foundation model can interpret instructions, synthesize information, draw inferences, and search for solutions across open-ended domains. Give it an abstraction—a schema, state table, architectural model, or policy—and it can work with that abstraction rather than merely execute a fixed script. This makes it possible to delegate implementation decisions that engineers have not specified in advance. A plausible decision may nevertheless be inappropriate for the system at hand. An agent may select a familiar architecture or design pattern that works well elsewhere but violates a local constraint, introduces unnecessary complexity, or conflicts with an established design decision.

Probabilistic output. Repeated invocations may produce different implementations or judgments. A foundation model’s confidence in its own result supplies no independent evidence of correctness. An agent may also fail consistently when its attempts share an incorrect assumption. Asking another foundation model to review the work can improve reliability, but the errors of the producer and evaluator may be correlated. Engineering assurance therefore cannot rest solely on the judgment that produced the result.

Bounded working state. The information available to a foundation model during an invocation is finite. An agentic harness can extend its effective working state through retrieval, external memory, compaction, and repeated tool use, but information needed for a particular decision must be available when that decision is made. A long-horizon task requires carrying earlier decisions or commitments into later steps. Large software systems exceed what can be presented in a single reasoning episode, so agents must select and reconstruct relevant system knowledge. The reasoning horizon is the practical limit of the work a reasoner and its supporting machinery can carry through reliably, given the available representations and resources.

Inexpensive repeated reasoning. Agents can explore alternatives at a speed and cost that human engineers cannot match. An agent can propose an implementation, run checks, revise its work, and try again, often many times in the time a human engineer would need for one attempt. This is particularly valuable when the engineer can state what constitutes an acceptable result. Human engineers are fallible reasoners too: they misunderstand requirements, overlook interactions, make incorrect assumptions, and introduce defects. Software engineering has long responded with specifications, types, tests, reviews, and other means of checking work independently of its author. Artificial reasoners introduce a new source of implementation capacity, not a new need for engineering assurance.

These capabilities make natural language a remarkably productive interface for programming. In the practice known as vibe coding, a developer describes what an application should do, tries the generated software, and asks for changes in light of what happens. Some developers work almost entirely through that conversation. Others inspect or edit the code when a result surprises them 1112.11. Advait Sarkar and Ian Drosos, “Vibe Coding: Programming Through Conversation with Artificial Intelligence,” Proceedings of the 36th Annual Workshop of the Psychology of Programming Interest Group, 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.23253.12. Yi-Hung Chou et al., “Building Software by Rolling the Dice: A Qualitative Study of Vibe Coding,” Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering 3, no. FSE (2026), https://doi.org/10.1145/3797105. Either way, a developer can go from an idea to a working application with little code written by hand. For prototypes, this may be enough.

On more complex systems, a change must also preserve requirements that nobody thought to repeat in the latest request. In experiments at Columbia University, applications that appeared to work mishandled business rules or lost track of state as users moved between components 13.13. Reya Vir, 9 Critical Failure Patterns of Coding Agents, DAPLab, Columbia University, 2026, https://daplab.cs.columbia.edu/general/2026/01/08/9-critical-failure-patterns-of-coding-agents.html. The FlowCheck study gives a particularly clear example. Three coding systems were asked to let several speakers share a time slot. All three also allowed a speaker to occupy several slots, violating an earlier rule 14.14. Reya Vir et al., “FlowCheck: Helping End-Users Specify and Verify Intent in Vibe-Coded Web Apps,” Proceedings of the 2nd ACM SIGPLAN International Workshop on Language Models and Programming Languages (Oakland, CA, USA), 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3843750.3843844. A developer who tried only the newly requested feature could easily miss what the change had undone.

AGENT HARNESS

Inset — Context Windows, Compaction, and the Reasoning Horizon

A long-running engineering task can fail even when an agent has enough information for each step in isolation. An earlier decision or test result may be missing when the next step depends on it. In seqBench, reasoning horizon describes the length of a sequence a model can reliably complete 1515. Mohammad Ramezanali et al., “seqBench: A Tunable Benchmark to Quantify Sequential Reasoning Limits of LLMs,” Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2025, 33771–92, https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.1714.; here it includes what the harness and external resources make possible.

A context window limits how much information a foundation model can process in one invocation. Instructions, conversation history, files, and tool results compete for space measured in tokens. A harness can carry work beyond one window by storing records for retrieval or using compaction: replacing accumulated context with a shorter account. Pages of investigation and test output might become a handoff recording the plan, decisions, checks, and remaining work. If the handoff says only “the tests passed,” the next agent cannot tell which tests ran or which version they exercised. Keeping the original results helps only if the agent retrieves them when needed 16.16. Prithvi Rajasekaran et al., “Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents,” Anthropic, September 29, 2025, https://www.anthropic.com/research/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents.

The generation of commodity intelligence that motivated this book is built around language models with bounded context windows. The reasoning horizon is broader than a context-window limit and is intended to remain useful as new kinds of intelligence bring different capabilities and constraints.

docs.title: 1.4.3 Steering Agents
docs.text:
A foundation model supplies general reasoning capabilities, but the effectiveness of an agent also depends on how its harness organizes the work. A harness manages the context supplied to the foundation model, invokes tools in response to its outputs, and returns their results for further reasoning. It may also provide memory, task management, parallel execution, and hooks at which additional code can run. Engineers can use these facilities to influence both the information available to an agent and the sequence of actions through which it pursues a task.

One approach, often called context engineering, concerns selecting and organizing the information available to an agent when it makes decisions 16. A foundation model’s context window is finite, so supplying irrelevant material consumes limited capacity and processing resources. Instructions, repository files, documentation, earlier decisions, and tool results must be selected and presented so that the agent can recover the knowledge it needs. Research on external representations has long shown that how information is organized affects the effort needed to reason with it 1718.17. Jill H. Larkin and Herbert A. Simon, “Why a Diagram Is (Sometimes) Worth Ten Thousand Words,” Cognitive Science 11, no. 1 (1987): 65–100, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1551-6708.1987.tb00863.x.18. Jiajie Zhang and Donald A. Norman, “Representations in Distributed Cognitive Tasks,” Cognitive Science 18, no. 1 (1994): 87–122, https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1801_3. A useful representation preserves relationships that would otherwise have to be reconstructed from implementation. Better representations can reduce that work without changing the underlying foundation model.

Another approach is to structure agent behavior through feedback loops. Rather than asking an agent to produce a complete implementation in one attempt, the harness can organize repeated cycles of proposing changes, running tools, observing results, and revising the work 4. Tests, static analyses, and other checks can provide feedback that helps the agent improve successive attempts. The effectiveness of these loops depends on the evidence they produce: an agent may repeatedly pursue an incorrect assumption, optimize for an inadequate test, or satisfy a new request while losing an earlier requirement. Repeated attempts can improve a result, but they do not establish that the result is correct. Figure 1.4-2 illustrates these two approaches.

Two ways to steer an agentTwo ways to steer an agent. Panel (a) compares reconstructing relevant structure from raw code at higher cost with retrieving it from a purposeful representation at lower cost. Panel (b) shows a loop from proposing a change through running tools, observing results, and revising. It repeats until acceptance criteria are met or work stops. (a) Context engineering: make the right information available (b) Feedback loops: improve results through iteration Raw code Purposeful representation Reconstruct relevant structure Higher cost (more work) Retrieve relevant structure Lower cost (less work) Propose change Run tools (check, test, etc.) Observe results Revise and try again Repeat until acceptance criteria are met or work stops Figure 1.4-2. Two ways to steer an agent. (a) Purposeful representations can reduce the effort needed to recover relevant system knowledge. (b) Feedback loops let agents revise their work using observations from tools and checks. Both can improve performance without changing the foundation model, but neither guarantees an acceptable result.

docs.title: 1.4.4 A Simple Probabilistic Model of Success with Agents
docs.text:
Commodity intelligence is probabilistic. This book focuses on the implications for engineering. A foundation model’s answer does not ordinarily come with a guarantee that its engineering judgments are correct. Generation can vary between runs, a request may admit several interpretations, and the model may choose different reasoning steps or tools. A task can depend on many such judgments before it produces a result. The reliability of the complete process also depends on how the harness and engineered environment organize the work.

A simple model illustrates why reliability on individual features does not guarantee reliability across a product. Suppose an agent implements n features, with pi denoting the probability that feature i is implemented correctly. Under the simplifying assumption that these outcomes are independent, the probability that all features are correct is

P(all features correct)=∏i=1npi

When probabilities between zero and one are multiplied, their product decreases as more factors are added. If an agent implements each feature correctly with probability 99%, the probability that all three features are correct is 0.993≈97%. For ten features it is approximately 90%, and for one hundred it falls to approximately 37%. At 95% reliability per feature, the probability of implementing all ten correctly is approximately 60%. An agent that usually gets individual features right can therefore have a much lower probability of getting every feature in a product right.

The independence assumption is deliberately simple; real implementation failures may be correlated, and a product’s features are not necessarily equally difficult. The calculation is not a prediction of agent performance. It illustrates why the reliability of the whole system cannot be inferred from success on individual tasks. Human review, automated checks, iterative repair, and more capable models can improve the final result, but their costs and limitations belong in the evaluation of the complete engineering process.

The decisions that depend on agentic inference form the system’s probabilistic surface. Other parts may be deterministic, such as a tool that applies a fixed transformation or a test suite that evaluates explicit conditions. Better models and iterative loops can improve the reliability of inferred judgments. Engineers can also establish mechanisms that enforce selected requirements even when an agent makes a mistake. The engineering objective is not to eliminate probabilistic reasoning, but to decide where its uncertainty is acceptable and where stronger controls are needed.

docs.title: §1.5 · Two Engineering Problems, One Method
docs.text:
Chapter 1 — The New Engineering Problem  ::  §1.5§1.5 Two Engineering Problems, One Method

Commodity intelligence changes the cost of implementation, but it does not remove the engineer’s responsibility for deciding what the system must do or establishing that it does so. The properties discussed in §1.4 suggest two complementary engineering problems. Bounded working state makes it costly to recover and maintain system knowledge across tasks, while probabilistic judgment makes an agent’s own assessment insufficient evidence that important obligations have been met.

MAGE

Inset — Two Engineering Problems

The Representation Problem. How should a large, evolving system be represented so that the properties relevant to an engineering question can be reasoned about without continually reconstructing them from implementation?

The Enforcement Problem. How should engineering intent be enforced over autonomous work, so that satisfying important obligations does not depend on the agent remembering, agreeing, or self-certifying each time?

MAGE addresses these problems through two complementary activities: Modeling makes consequential knowledge explicit, while Alignment makes selected obligations enforceable. Modeling preserves relationships that people and agents would otherwise have to reconstruct during each task. Providing a model, however, does not ensure that its obligations will be respected. An agent may overlook a constraint, interpret it incorrectly, or violate it while satisfying another requirement. Alignment connects selected obligations to mechanisms outside that producing judgment: constraints restrict actions or states, sensors produce evidence, and gates evaluate evidence and control whether work may proceed. Figure 1.5-1 summarizes the primary relationships. The activities are complementary rather than inseparable: a model can make system knowledge available without enforcing it, while a gate can enforce a permission without requiring an elaborate system model.

From agentic machinery to MAGE Two rows connect substrate properties to engineering problems and MAGE responses: finite working state to the Representation Problem and Modeling; probabilistic agentic work to the Enforcement Problem and Alignment. Finite working state Representation Problem Modeling Probabilistic agentic work Enforcement Problem Alignment SUBSTRATE PROBLEM RESPONSE Figure 1.5-1. From agentic machinery to MAGE. Finite working state motivates Modeling; probabilistic autonomous work motivates Alignment. The two principles address different engineering problems and operate together.

The two activities extend the techniques for steering agents described in §1.4. Context engineering supplies information relevant to an agent’s work; Modeling supplies information about consequential system properties through explicit engineering representations. Feedback loops help agents revise their work in response to observations; Alignment supplies feedback about whether selected engineering obligations have been satisfied, together with mechanisms that prevent violations from being accepted.

Both activities can increase the probability of successful engineering work. Better information helps agents make appropriate decisions, while better feedback helps them identify and correct mistakes. Alignment goes further: where an obligation can be enforced by a sufficiently complete and correct mechanism, violating it can be made impossible within the mechanism’s scope. The resulting assurance need not depend on the probability that an agent will make the right decision.

The engineer must still decide which properties deserve explicit representation, which obligations require independent enforcement, and which implementation choices can remain open. These decisions depend on the system’s purpose and the consequences of getting them wrong. A model that records every implementation detail may be expensive to maintain and unnecessarily restrict the agent. A check over an inadequate representation may reliably establish the wrong property. Conversely, leaving a consequential requirement implicit forces each new agent or engineering episode to reconstruct it. MAGE asks engineers to make these choices deliberately: preserve the distinctions and obligations that justify durable structure, provide evidence suited to their consequences, and leave genuinely acceptable alternatives open to the implementer.

The same questions arise beyond software, although the representations and evidence differ. Chapters 2 and 3 develop Modeling and Alignment separately, Chapter 4 shows how they work together as systems evolve, and Chapter 5 examines DocAble and other software factories. Chapter 6 develops the theoretical argument, while Chapter 7 considers its implications beyond software.
