docs.title: §2.5 · Decision Models: What Should Happen Next?
docs.text:
Chapter 2 — Modeling  ::  §2.5§2.5 Decision Models: What Should Happen Next?

A behavioral model can tell us that a failed job may be retried, escalated, or stopped. A decision model addresses the next question: given what we know about this failure, which alternative should we choose? A transient error may justify another attempt, while an exhausted retry budget may call for escalation. What makes this a decision model is that it represents the criteria for choosing among alternatives. The most useful form depends on the choice we face and the information available when we must make it.

docs.title: Constructing a Decision Model
docs.text:
Begin with one request. A service sells prepaid credits and also offers unlimited subscriptions. A customer requests work costing five credits. Should the service admit the request, and if so, should it charge five credits? To answer, we need to know which entitlement applies. For a prepaid customer we also need the balance. For an unlimited subscriber we need to know whether the work is covered.

A decision table makes the cases easy to inspect when there are only a few. In Table 2.5-1, assume the request falls under exactly one entitlement. Read across the row whose conditions hold. A prepaid customer with five credits can proceed and spends the five; with four credits, the same request is rejected. For an unlimited subscription covering the work, the service admits the request without drawing on a balance.

Table 2.5-1. Admission under one entitlement. Unlimited entitlement admits covered work without drawing down finite credit; a finite balance must cover the requested work.EntitlementRequested workDecisionUnlimitedAny amount covered by the subscriptionAdmit without drawing down finite creditFinite balanceEnough credit for the requestAdmit and charge the required creditFinite balanceInsufficient credit for the requestReject for insufficient credit

The input to the decision must preserve every distinction that can change its outcome. Suppose a caller supplies only the number of prepaid credits. A customer who has spent the last credit and an unlimited subscriber who never bought credits can both have a balance of zero. The table gives them different answers. No revision to a rule that sees only the balance can recover the missing entitlement.

A decision tree arranges the same choice as a sequence of tests: first determine the entitlement, then consult the balance only on the prepaid branch. Rules can express exceptions and their precedence; constraints can describe which combinations of features may be selected together. For permissions, an access-control matrix records which operations a subject may perform on an object 1.1. Butler W. Lampson, “Protection,” ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 8, no. 1 (1974): 18–24, https://doi.org/10.1145/775265.775268. When the alternatives differ in cost or performance, a quantitative model may help choose among them. Predicting a deployment’s latency supplies one input; selecting the least expensive deployment that meets a latency target uses that input to make a decision.

A permission graph is useful when the decision concerns a relationship. In Figure 2.5-1, a web interface may call a report service, and the report service may call a renderer. To decide whether Web may call Renderer directly, look for that particular edge in the declared policy. The two-hop route through the report service grants no such permission. The observed graph records a direct Web-to-Renderer call. Comparing the two identifies a violation. If the observation had missed the call, its absence from the trace would tell us only what was recorded.

Illustrative observed calls compared with declared permissionsObserved callsDeclared permissionswebreportservicerendererwebreportservicerendererFigure 2.5-1. Observation compared with declared permission. The observed web-to-renderer call violates the declared policy.

Some decisions cannot be made from the object alone. Accessibility standards distinguish informative images, which need a text alternative, from decorative images, which assistive technology can ignore 2.2. World Wide Web Consortium, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, 2018, https://www.w3.org/TR/2018/REC-WCAG21-20180605/. A blue square might decorate a restaurant menu but be the subject of a lecture on modern art.** For a real example, consider Yves Klein’s Blue Monochrome (1961), in the Museum of Modern Art’s collection 3.3. Museum of Modern Art, Yves Klein. Blue Monochrome. 1961, n.d., https://www.moma.org/collection/works/80103. What matters is the image’s contribution to the document, not merely what it depicts. A classifier can supply evidence about that role. The decision rule must say when the evidence warrants omitting a description and what to do when the role is uncertain.

docs.title: Properties and Analyses
docs.text:
A decision table is complete if it prescribes an outcome for every case in its declared scope. To check Table 2.5-1, examine the balance below, exactly at, and above the requested amount. If the finite rows used only strict inequalities, a customer with exactly five credits requesting five credits would match neither row. Consistency asks whether applicable rules can prescribe incompatible outcomes. If both rows included equality, that customer would match both the admitting and rejecting rows unless a precedence rule settled the conflict. A request covered by several entitlements presents a different issue: the table assumes one. Extending the policy to such requests requires deciding how the entitlements combine.

For a quantitative decision, first check admissibility: does an alternative satisfy every applicable constraint? Suppose a deployment must fit in 8 GB of memory and respond within 200 ms. A candidate requiring 9 GB is out, however fast or inexpensive it may be. Of the candidates that meet both limits, which costs least? That is an optimality question. A constraint solver can search for a feasible assignment; ranking feasible candidates by cost also requires an objective and comparable cost estimates. The least expensive candidate among those examined is an optimum over that set. A claim about all possible deployments needs a correspondingly wider analysis.

Checking conformance asks whether a particular decision or observed action agrees with the declared policy. For the service graph, compare the observed edges with the permitted set. For the entitlement table, use the inputs to select a row and compare its verdict with the service’s actual response. Neither comparison settles whether the policy expresses the right judgment. A consistent policy could permit the very call the architect meant to exclude, just as an optimizer could minimize cost while omitting a requirement users care about. Engineers must examine the choice of inputs and criteria as well as the decisions made from them.

docs.title: 2.5.2 DocAble: Policies and Decisions
docs.text:
DocAble uses decision models for several purposes: deciding whether an image needs a description, declaring which services may communicate, and determining whether a user may upload a document. The representations differ because the decisions depend on different information. Each must preserve the distinctions that can change its answer.

When is an image decorative?

Accessibility remediation must distinguish images that convey information from those that are merely decorative. As the worked example illustrated, the same image can serve either purpose depending on its context. DocAble supplies a rendered slide to a vision-language model (VLM), which classifies each image or shape as clearly decorative, uncertain, or informational. The classification supplies evidence; the decision policy determines what to do with it. Only a clearly decorative verdict permits suppressing a description. An uncertain or missing verdict preserves the image’s informational role. This asymmetry is deliberate: an unnecessary description is audible, while wrongly hiding information can leave a screen-reader user unaware that anything was omitted.

The need for an explicit uncertainty policy emerged from evaluation. Earlier classifiers had marked content-bearing images as decorative, particularly in visualization-heavy documents. We tightened the policy by representing uncertainty explicitly and making its conservative interpretation common to the classification paths. The decision model now states how uncertain evidence affects remediation without prescribing which VLM must supply that evidence. A different VLM can make the semantic judgment; it does not redefine the policy for acting on it.

The remaining two DocAble examples concern permission. The system accepts documents for accessibility remediation, sends work among internal services, and returns corrected artifacts. Two decisions arise at different boundaries: which service may call another, and whether a user's entitlement permits a requested upload. Both can be modeled as permission, but they need different representations.

Which services may communicate?

DocAble distributes document remediation across several services. The public web tier receives requests, while internal services perform document editing, generation, rendering, OCR, and other work. Rather than specifying the permitted connections independently in deployment configuration, DocAble records them in a service-flow model. Each directed edge declares that one service may invoke another; an absent edge excludes that relationship from the declared policy.

Service-flow model · Decision

  • Engineering question — Which service may call which, and what may be reached from outside?
  • Model — a declared graph of services and the permitted edges between them; the deployment is wired from the graph rather than the graph inferred from the deployment.
  • Property — internal communication is permitted only along a declared edge; one declared node is the public entry.
  • Quality attribute — least privilege; architectural integrity; security.

Figure 2.5-2 shows a reduced view of the service-invocation policy. The web tier is the only publicly reachable service. Its declared outgoing edges permit calls to selected internal services. Separately, the worker may invoke generation, rendering, and OCR services. The arrows express permissions, not observed traffic or a requirement that every permitted call occur. Asynchronous job dispatch is omitted from this selected view; absence here does not imply prohibition by the full policy.

The declared graph answers whether a proposed service invocation is permitted: look for the corresponding directed edge. It also supports reachability questions, such as which services the public web tier can reach through permitted calls. DocAble treats this graph as the source of truth for service-flow relationships and generates deployment configuration from its declared edges. A completeness check requires each gated edge to contain the information needed for deployment. These checks establish properties of the declaration and its generated configuration, not whether runtime traffic follows the intended policy.

Selected declared service invocations in DocAbleInternetwebworkerdocumenteditorothersgenerationrenderOCRFigure 2.5-2. DocAble’s service-flow model. Arrows show selected permitted service invocations; asynchronous job dispatch is omitted. The web tier is the sole public entry point. Deployment configuration is generated from the full model, while runtime conformance requires separate enforcement.

The declared graph can also serve as the policy against which observed service calls are checked. DocAble does not currently reconcile runtime traffic against that declaration. Whether to add such a check, and what consequences a violation should have, are Alignment decisions taken up in Chapter 3.

Which entitlement authorizes an upload?

The service-flow model determines which calls are permitted. Upload admission presents a different decision: whether a user’s entitlements authorize a particular document. This became a modeling problem when DocAble added unlimited-use groups to a system originally designed around finite credits.

Table 2.5-1 assumed that exactly one entitlement applied to a request. DocAble’s domain is more complex: a user may belong to several groups, each with its own entitlement. The upload decision must account for the available finite credits and whether any applicable group grants unlimited use (Figure 2.5-3). The production failure arose when these facts traveled separately through the system.

The upload-entitlement domain: users, groups, finite and unlimited entitlement, and the admission decision A user belongs to one or more groups. A group is either a finite-credit group, carrying remaining credits, or an unlimited group, carrying no credit limit. Both kinds feed the upload decision, which must preserve both facts and ends in admit or reject. Upload entitlement — the domain the decision must preserve User belongs to one or more Groups Finite-credit group a remaining credit balance Unlimited group no credit limit how many credits remain? is any entitlement unlimited? Upload decision ADMIT REJECT Figure 2.5-3. The upload-entitlement domain. A finite balance alone cannot determine admission: the model must also preserve whether any applicable group grants unlimited use.

The original client upload rule was easy to understand from the code: if the user’s credits covered the upload cost, allow the upload; otherwise, reject it. Box (1) in Figure 2.5-4 shows this balance-based check. A separate decision model would have added little to understanding that simple rule.

Unlimited groups changed what the upload decision had to account for. As box (2) shows, a group could authorize an upload without contributing finite credits to the balance. The server’s balance calculation, the client’s check before sending an upload, and the server admission gate represented entitlement in different ways. Understanding and updating the intended policy now required checking how each part of the implementation handled both finite and unlimited entitlement.

Box (3) traces the production failure. In August 2026, a user whose personal group provided unlimited use was blocked from uploading a thirty-eight-page presentation: the upload needs 38 credits, and you have 0. The legacy server function read each group’s unlimited flag twice: once to exclude unlimited groups from the credit sum, and once to compute a display class. For this user it returned zero credits and the class individual. The login response omitted the detailed group records but carried a separate unlimited-status flag. The client upload check ignored that flag, compared the zero balance with the required 38 credits, and rejected the upload before sending the file. The server’s admission logic, which handled this entitlement correctly, was never reached. The failure came from using the finite-credit total as an admission decision even though other system representations retained the unlimited entitlement.

The immediate fix made the client consult the unlimited-status flag it had been ignoring. That repaired the observed failure, but left the admission policy represented separately across the client and server. We therefore introduced the entitlement decision model shown in box (4): given the user’s group entitlements and the requested work, should the upload be admitted, and under which entitlement? Property tests checked the model, a cross-runtime parity corpus checked shared policy cases in the server and client, and another check validated the model’s shape. The display code derived its values from the model, while server admission delegated the policy decision to it.

Entitlement decision model · Decision

  • Engineering question — May this user upload this document, and under which entitlement?
  • Model — per-group entitlements that keep finite and unlimited as distinct cases; the output is a structured admission decision: admitted or not, the group that authorizes it, and the ordered plan by which the verdict was reached.
  • Property — an uncapped unlimited group can authorize an upload with zero finite credits; the display projection does not decide admission.
  • Quality attribute — decision correctness; fidelity between the domain and its representations.

The repaired model preserves the distinction that the earlier admission check lost. For the same uncapped unlimited group and 38-page request, it admits the upload and records the authorizing group and an admit_unlimited plan step, even though the finite credit balance remains zero. The display projection answers a different question: it returns a special numeric value for unlimited use, or a finite credit sum when all groups are finite. That display value cannot determine admission. The model can therefore be tested against cases involving finite credits, unlimited entitlement, and their combinations without treating a display value as the decision itself.

From a credit balance to an explicit upload-admission decision Four numbered panels explain a legacy balance check, the addition of unlimited entitlement, the actual client upload-check failure, and the later model. There are no arrows between panels. In panel 3, the server excludes the unlimited group from a finite-credit sum; the client compares zero with thirty-eight while ignoring a separate unlimited signal, then rejects before POST. In panel 4, the same uncapped group feeds an admission decision that admits and a separate display projection that returns an unlimited sentinel. The display value is not an admission input. (1) Legacy balance-based check Only finite credit is represented (2) Unlimited groups are added Entitlement now has two cases A finite balance does not identify unlimited use. (3) Client rejects the upload 38-page Office upload Server admission code is never reached. (4) Separate admission and display Same group and request; no cap Admission uses the decision. The display value does not decide permission. Finite group balances Sum of balances Client compares balance with request cost Group entitlement Finite balance Unlimited mode One unlimited personal group finite balance = 0 Server sums finite balances and excludes unlimited groups credit_balance = 0 Client upload check: 0 < 38 ignores separate unlimited signal REJECT before POST Per-group entitlement unlimited mode; finite balance = 0 Admission rules + upload request Display projection admit = True selected group admit_unlimited Unlimited sentinel (display-only) Figure 2.5-4. The admission check must preserve unlimited entitlement. Panels (1)–(4) explain the old representation, domain change, failure, and repair; they are not one runtime pipeline. In (3), the client uses the finite-credit total and ignores a separate unlimited signal. In (4), the same uncapped entitlement produces an admitting decision and a separate display value for unlimited use.

A note in the first person: I changed the domain in one place — groups could now be unlimited — and did not carry the change into every representation of the same decision. An explicit model would not have made the change automatically correct; it would have made the inconsistency visible as an engineering obligation. When the domain contains a consequential distinction, every representation used to reason about that decision must be capable of expressing it. Chapter 3 gives the recurring pattern here — a failure converted into explicit structure that later work inherits — a name.

The three decision models preserve different kinds of information: evidence about an image’s role, permitted relationships between services, and the entitlements that authorize an upload. Each makes a decision inspectable by separating the information used to make it from the criteria governing the outcome. That separation also makes it possible to revise a classifier, service topology, or entitlement scheme without silently redefining the decision policy.

Decision models make the criteria for a choice explicit, whether the choice concerns permission or what to do next. The final section steps back from one representation to ask how a family of models can answer questions together.

docs.title: §2.6 · System Knowledge: Connecting the Models
docs.text:
Chapter 2 — Modeling  ::  §2.6§2.6 System Knowledge: Connecting the Models

Different questions require different views of the same system. Following Fairbanks, we understand software architecture as the structures needed to reason about a system, including the software elements, the relations among them, and properties of both 1.1. George Fairbanks, Just Enough Software Architecture: A Risk-Driven Approach (Marshall & Brainerd, 2010). A component view exposes decomposition, a behavioral view shows legal transitions, a deployment view records allocation, and a quantitative view can supply a resource bound. An architectural decision can draw on several of these views. To decide whether two workers can share a host within its memory budget, for example, an engineer needs to know which workers may run together, how much memory each needs, and how much the host provides.

The views need to agree on the identities and relationships that their questions cross. A deployment record and a memory budget can each serve its own purpose if the engineer can identify the workers and host in both. MBSE methods likewise connect requirements, design models, analyses, and verification results so that engineers can follow a decision across representations 22. Jeff A. Estefan, Survey of Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Methodologies, INCOSE-TD-2007-003-02 (International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE), 2008). 3.3. Azad M. Madni and Michael Sievers, “Model-Based Systems Engineering: Motivation, Current Status, and Research Opportunities,” Systems Engineering 21, no. 3 (2018): 172–90, https://doi.org/10.1002/sys.21438. When these views are cheap to derive, maintain, and query, more of that knowledge can remain explicit between tasks.

docs.title: 2.6.1 Connecting Models to Answer Engineering Questions
docs.text:
Models can be connected across different concerns or across levels of abstraction. A service catalog, deployment model, and measurement record provide different views of the same service; joining them connects information that no individual view contains. A service-level architecture and a module-level dependency graph instead describe related structure at different levels of detail. The latter introduces classes, interfaces, and dependencies omitted from the former, but must preserve any architectural boundaries established by the higher-level model.

The relationship between abstraction levels recalls the classical technique of stepwise refinement 44. Niklaus Wirth, “Program Development by Stepwise Refinement,” Communications of the ACM 14, no. 4 (1971): 221–27, https://doi.org/10.1145/362575.362577.: progressively transforming an abstract description into a more detailed realization while preserving its required properties. In agentic engineering, an agent can perform much of this refinement, choosing algorithms, data structures, and internal organization within the freedom left by the higher-level model. The engineer remains responsible for deciding which properties must survive that translation. Explicit relationships between abstraction levels make those obligations available for analysis and checking rather than relying on the agent to infer them correctly.

A shared service identifier can connect a catalog entry to a deployment and its measurements without requiring those records to share a file format.

Suppose an agent is investigating a slow report service. The service catalog identifies its owner, the deployment model records its resource allocation, and a measurement record supplies recent response times. Shared service identities let the agent connect these representations and obtain the relevant facts without reconstructing their relationships from source code or directory names.

The deployment model describes where the service runs and what resources it has been assigned; an execution history records what happened during particular requests. Joining measurements from that history to the service identity can reveal a performance problem without turning the deployment model into a log. Why not combine all these representations into one comprehensive description? Taken to its extreme, that description would read like the implementation itself, with all the detail that modeling was intended to suppress. Separate models preserve the distinctions needed for different questions; their connections let engineers reason across those distinctions without carrying every detail into every analysis.

Some answers require a join. Suppose the policy allows a report service to invoke a renderer. The policy names the two services, while the deployment model records the runtime identity under which the report service runs. Joining the permitted call to that identity determines which principal needs permission to invoke the renderer. Neither model contains that complete answer by itself: the policy does not name the environment's principal, and the deployment record does not decide which calls should be permitted.

A model can also connect an obligation to its evidence. A latency requirement might identify the workload and response-time bound, while a test catalog identifies the measurement that evaluates them. Linking the requirement to that test makes a missing measurement visible. SysML represents this relationship through verification cases that identify the subject and the requirements to be evaluated 5.5. Object Management Group, OMG Systems Modeling Language (SysML), Version 2.0, OMG Document formal/26-03-02 (Object Management Group, 2026), https://www.omg.org/spec/SysML/2.0. Whether the test supplies adequate evidence, and whether its result should block release, remain further engineering decisions.

A join only works if it preserves the distinctions the decision needs. A record may use the correct user identifier and still reduce an unlimited entitlement to a finite-credit balance. Shared identity makes the connection explicit; it does not guarantee that the information passed across it is adequate.

An engineer or agent can therefore enter through the object named by a task and follow the relations its question requires: from service to owner, from service to deployment, from deployment to measurement. A query interface makes these connections traversable. The agent needs the connected slice that answers the question, rather than every model in the project.

docs.title: 2.6.2 Maintaining Correspondence
docs.text:
Prefer shared identity and derivation over independently maintained copies of the same fact. A deployment record can refer to the service catalog's identifier rather than copying the service's description and owner. A report can join the two records when it needs their combined information. Where a second representation must contain a copy, make its source and correspondence check explicit. Otherwise every copy becomes another fact engineers must remember to update.

Models and implementations can fall out of correspondence as a system changes. Maintaining their relationships requires deciding which representation is authoritative for each property and how correspondence with other representations should be established and checked. Figure 2.6-1 distinguishes three arrangements:

  • Derive from implementation. A dependency graph extracted from call sites describes the connections found in the code. A drift check can repeat the extraction and compare the result with a maintained view. Agreement covers the relationships the extraction observes.
  • Generate from models. An authoritative schema can generate the types used by interface clients. A freshness check compares the checked-in types with the current generator output. The schema determines those types while leaving the client’s algorithms open.
  • Trace and check correspondence. A behavioral model might specify permitted transitions while leaving their implementation to an agent. Traceability links each modeled transition to the functions that implement it. A check can establish that a referenced function still exists; whether it implements the transition correctly requires further evidence.
Three correspondence patterns Derive extracts selected models from implementation. Generate determines a portion of implementation from a model. Trace and check connect separately maintained model and implementation elements using distinct directional relations; other implementation decisions remain open. DERIVE Implementation is authoritative Model(s) State Response Idle Start() Done Stop() … … Implementation Agent creates implementation from prompts (and iteration) GENERATE Model is authoritative Model(s) State Response Idle Start() Done Stop() … … Implementation Generated portion (determined by model) Other implementation decisions remain open TRACE + CHECK Neither fully determines the other Model(s) State Response Idle Start() Done Stop() … … Implementation Corresponding portion (maintained and checked) Other implementation decisions derive (extract model from implementation) generate (produce implementation artifacts from model) trace (bind related elements) check (evaluate where decidable) Figure 2.6-1. Three correspondence patterns. Derivation extracts models from implementation; generation produces implementation artifacts from models; traceability connects representations maintained independently. Each relationship covers selected properties or artifacts rather than necessarily determining the entire implementation.

An authoritative model can also be interpreted directly during execution. Consider the build with two independent compilations and one link task. The runner reads the declared dependencies to start each compilation when it is ready and to delay linking until both object files exist. Nothing has to generate a schedule in advance. An engineer can query those same dependencies to find which task a changed object file could affect.

The third arrangement is particularly useful when agents implement systems whose models specify only selected properties. The models preserve engineering decisions while leaving other implementation choices open. The three arrangements can coexist within one system, and their coverage can change as engineers learn which properties need explicit representation. These correspondence patterns apply between models at different abstraction levels as well as between models and implementation; a refinement relationship identifies which higher-level properties a more detailed representation must preserve.

docs.title: 2.6.3 DocAble: Connecting Engineering Models
docs.text:
DocAble improves document accessibility through passes that analyze or change a document. Workers and services execute those passes, and the product retains evidence about the resulting artifact. Its modeling problem therefore crosses several views: the intended computation, the execution arrangement, and what one run actually changed. The worked question is how those views can share facts without becoming independent accounts that drift apart.

DocAble uses different representations for different engineering questions. Roughly 130 structured model records and several data dialects describe components, deployment, data flow, behavior, and governance. Shared identities let an engineer move among these records as a question requires. Figure 2.6-2 follows the slow service from its registry entry to its deployment and then to performance measurements.

The models are represented as data rather than importing the implementation they describe. Keeping the representations separate lets engineers check their correspondence. Where a model is intended to provide independent evidence about an artifact, the model must remain distinguishable from that artifact. Chapter 5 shows how these models are maintained and used in the governed engineering environment.

Heterogeneous models over shared identities A service performance question follows the service registry into the shared-identity hub, out to deployment topology, back through the hub, then out to measurements. Four other representations have thin connections to the same hub. Traverse via shared identities e.g., investigate a service’s performance Service registry (identify service) Provenance records Computation graph Entitlement policy State machines Deployment topology (where it runs) Measurements (how it performs) 1 2 3 Figure 2.6-2. Heterogeneous models over shared identities. An engineering question selects a path through the available representations. The highlighted traversal follows a service from its registry entry through deployment topology to performance measurements, using shared identities to connect the models. Other models remain available for different questions.

docs.title: One Dependency for Execution and Analysis
docs.text:
Suppose we change a remediation pass. Which later computations depend on its output, and will they still execute in the required order? In [ref:chapter:2.3-structural], we introduced DocAble's remediation-computation graph for investigating dependencies. Connecting those dependencies to the execution declarations lets us examine their scheduling consequences without reconstructing the pipeline from code. For a DOCX job with table-header repair enabled, one pass marks table headers and another checks the table's structure. The registry declares that the repair pass writes table-header information and that the structure check reads it.

Matching that write to that read gives a dependency: repair must precede the check. The scheduler uses the dependency to order the work, so the check examines the table after the header pass has run.

The Office registry also emits its resource dependencies for a separate Python graph view. The edge from table-header repair to the structure check therefore comes from the same read/write metadata used by scheduling. An engineer can inspect which computations depend on table-header information, or join their identities to measurements, without executing the remediation pipeline. The Python graph provides the analytical view; the execution machinery does not schedule from it.

PDF uses a different connection. Its analytical edges are projected from parallel typed declarations of what each pass produces and consumes, including information consulted only to decide whether a pass runs. Blocking checks hold those declared relationships in correspondence with the executable pipeline.

The Office example makes the same dependency available for execution and analysis; it does not derive a new relationship by joining independent models. The execution machinery uses the declared relationships to schedule work; the analytical view exposes the structure needed for queries and checks. The important question is which representation owns each fact and how each consumer remains connected to that source. Where separate declarations are necessary, as in the PDF view, checked correspondence carries that connection.

docs.title: What One Document Run Changed
docs.text:
A static computation graph does not record the mutations performed during a particular run. DocAble records consequential document changes as typed operations: each operation names its target, the mutation made, the responsible remediation pass, and the retained evidence. That history supports audit, debugging, and a changelog. Recording only “document modified” would lose the very distinctions those uses need.

During a PDF remediation session, typed edit values form a per-session log. A replay engine can apply the same sequence deterministically. This record preserves the mutations while omitting the reasoning, analyses, control decisions, and retries that produced them. The computation graph asks what may compose; the edit record asks what happened to this artifact. Figure 2.6-3 contrasts these two reductions.

DocAble’s PDF changeset interface also represents edits before they happen. A changeset is an ordered collection of typed operations, each naming a target and a supported mutation, such as assigning alternative text or changing a structural tag. The proposing computation does not manipulate PDF objects directly. An applier resolves the targets against the current document and returns a result for each operation. The proposal expresses intended mutations; the results and attribution record show what was actually applied.

A specialized remediation pass, a general-purpose agent, or a human editor can propose operations using the same vocabulary. The interface preserves the information needed to apply and inspect the change while leaving its producer’s reasoning unspecified. Chapter 3 examines the constraints on applying such proposals; Chapter 5 returns to the reasoning strategies that can produce them.

Computation structure versus recorded history Two reductions of the same remediation system, side by side. Left: the static computation graph — named passes joined by a typed data edge and a typed control gate, modeling what computations may compose. Right: one session's edit record — a run that emits a sequence of typed PdfEdit operations, recording what mutations did occur. A dashed link between them marks that they are not joined today; a shared computation identity would join them, and the join is added when a question needs it. Computation graph what computations may compose Edit record what mutations one run did emit Analyze pass Remediate pass Route gate DATA_FLOW CONTROL_GATE Session run PdfEdit · SetAltText PdfEdit · TagFigure PdfEdit · SetReadingOrder static structure recorded history not joined today Figure 2.6-3. Computation structure versus recorded history. Declared computations and a run’s actual mutations answer different questions. A shared computation identity can join the recorded edits to the static model when needed, while preserving the distinction between what was declared and what happened.

DocAble joins staged-run latency and cost to stable computation identities, so measurements can be queried alongside the static graph. The per-session edit log remains a separate provenance record; it is not a per-run execution graph over computation nodes. Recording attribution is also distinct from ensuring that every mutation records it. A structural check requires typed mutation operations to emit attribution, but it cannot establish that the semantic explanation inside the record is correct.

docs.title: Joining a Call to Its Deployment Permission
docs.text:
A permitted interservice call requires several models to agree. A typed edge records that one service may call another. Deployment configuration identifies the environment variable carrying the callee's URL. The caller's runtime identity determines which invocation grant the cloud's access-control configuration must contain. Joining the edge to these records determines both how to reach the callee and who is permitted to invoke it; a further comparison checks agreement with the service catalog's documented topology. Twenty-eight modeled call edges produce ten distinct invocation grants once shared runtime identities are accounted for. No single source artifact contains that deployment plan.

DocAble introduced the join after service URLs were wired correctly but the matching invocation grant was absent, taking staging down with authorization errors. The repair made URL wiring and authorization two consequences of the same modeled edge, so a later change could derive them together rather than requiring another bespoke grant.

Connections can create information that no individual model contains. The call model does not contain the environment-specific runtime identity; the deployment environment does not independently state the intended call topology. Joining them determines the permission that should exist.

Each connection has a specific purpose. Resource declarations supply a dependency, computation identities connect measured cost to a pass, an edit record explains a document change, and a call joined to a deployment identity determines a permission. Keeping those relations explicit lets engineers inspect the connection that an analysis depends on, instead of treating membership in a model family as evidence that the models agree.

docs.title: §2.7 · Summary
docs.text:
Chapter 2 — Modeling  ::  §2.7§2.7 Summary

Engineering models make selected properties of a system available for reasoning without requiring engineers or agents to reconstruct them from implementation. The useful representation depends on the question: architecture, behavior, decisions, and quantitative properties call for different reductions. As engineers learn more about a system, they may add newly consequential distinctions to their models or remove details that no longer serve an engineering purpose. Across these forms, the engineering task is to preserve the distinctions that matter, leave other choices open, and maintain the relationships on which subsequent reasoning depends.

  1. Model parsimoniously for an engineering question. Preserve the distinctions needed to answer the question. A model earns its carrying cost while the reasoning it enables justifies the work of keeping it current.
  1. Externalize consequential knowledge and intent. A relationship or obligation recorded in a model is available to the next engineer or agent. Each can use it without having to infer the original decision from the code.
  1. Preserve degrees of freedom deliberately. State the obligations every acceptable implementation must satisfy. Where several choices satisfy those obligations, leave the choice to the implementer.
  1. Maintain the correspondences you depend on. Shared identities connect representations of the same system. Derivation and generation can carry facts from an authoritative source, while checked traceability can expose disagreements between independently maintained artifacts.
  1. Distinguish description from authority. A model may describe the implementation or prescribe properties the implementation must satisfy. When the two disagree, which one should change depends on which is authoritative for the property in question.

Modeling Principle

Externalize knowledge and intent into engineering models that both engineers and agents can reason through.

Appropriate representations make otherwise intractable engineering questions manageable and make additional properties available for Alignment.

A model can make an obligation explicit without ensuring that an implementation satisfies it. An agent may misunderstand the representation, overlook a constraint, or produce a result that violates a property the model states correctly. Chapter 3 takes up the complementary engineering problem: how to make selected obligations enforceable in the environment where agents work.

docs.title: §3.1 · Where Obligations Can Be Enforced
docs.text:
Chapter 3 — Alignment  ::  §3.1§3.1 Where Obligations Can Be Enforced

A foundation model produces probabilistic outputs; a harness turns selected outputs into actions. Once those actions can alter a repository, invoke an API, change infrastructure, or ship an artifact, the engineering question is no longer only how to steer the reasoner. It is where the surrounding environment can intervene between a proposed action and its consequence.

Guidance influences behavior; enforcement determines what the environment will permit or accept. A prompt, brief, example, or playbook can make one action more likely than another. A permission boundary can forbid an action, while a validator and gate can refuse a result. Feedback can return evidence to the reasoner—a failing test, an observed call, a measured latency, or a validator’s explanation—so that subsequent work can respond. The distinction matters when choosing where to intervene: the environment must be able to constrain the relevant action or determine whether the resulting work is accepted, rather than merely advising the reasoner.

Recent agentic-security guidance draws a similar boundary. Once agents act before commit time, the repository is too late to be the security boundary: the tools, permissions, and execution environment that produce a change join the trusted base, so agentic security must secure the process that creates the artifact, not only the artifact 1.1. Snyk, “The Agentic Development Lifecycle,” Snyk, 2026, https://snyk.io/blog/agentic-development-lifecycle/.

A correct result does not excuse an unacceptable process. An agent might produce working software while accessing data it was not authorized to read, modifying dependencies without approval, or deploying before the required checks completed. Testing the resulting artifact cannot establish that those actions were permissible. Some engineering obligations govern the product. Others govern how the product may be produced. The environment must be able to enforce both.

Where the environment intervenes determines what it can examine and control. Figure 3.1-1 distinguishes reasoning input, where guidance ordinarily operates, from three enforcement boundaries: individual actions, composed units of work, and the resulting artifact or runtime state. Moving toward larger units of work can make additional obligations legible because more context and evidence are available. The appropriate boundary is the earliest one where the environment can evaluate and enforce the obligation.

Intervention boundaries: guidance, actions, work, and artifacts Four columns compare intervention boundaries. Reasoning input is guidance: context supplied to the reasoner, with instructions, models and examples. The three enforcement boundaries are action, covering one proposed action with permissions, hooks and tool restrictions; work unit, covering a composed body of work with task-completion checks, merge gates and deployment gates; and artifact or runtime, covering the resulting artifact or running state with API boundaries, schemas and runtime permissions. Rows identify Boundary, Scope and Examples. A rightward arrow indicates increasing scope of work considered and more context for evaluating obligations, not increasing enforcement strength. GUIDANCE ENFORCEMENT BOUNDARIES Reasoning input Context supplied to the reasoner Instructions models examples Action One proposed action Permissions hooks tool restrictions Work unit Composed body of work Task-completion checks merge gates deployment gates Artifact / runtime Resulting artifact or running state API boundaries schemas runtime permissions Boundary Scope Examples Increasing scope of work considered More context for evaluating obligations Figure 3.1-1. Intervention boundaries. Guidance influences reasoning; enforcement constrains actions or determines whether work and artifacts are accepted. Moving from individual actions to larger units of work can make additional obligations legible as evidence accumulates. Later boundaries are not necessarily stronger. Choose the earliest boundary where the obligation can be evaluated and enforced.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Reasoning Input, Action, Work Unit, and Artifact/Runtime
docs.text:
The first location is reasoning input: the context, representations, examples, and instructions put in front of the reasoner. This is where Modeling and context engineering do most of their work: a finite reasoner does better when the relevant system knowledge is already externalized and selected for the task. But placement in context is ordinarily guidance, not enforcement. The model can misread, forget, or disregard what it was shown.

The context supplied to an agent can change as the work becomes better understood. Figure 3.1-2 illustrates dynamic context injection in two stages. At dispatch, anticipated files and components determine an initial selection of relevant engineering knowledge. After planning, the agent's refined understanding of the work determines a second selection, which may add or remove relevant material. Standing instructions remain available throughout. This arrangement limits unnecessary context while allowing newly relevant obligations to be surfaced before implementation.

An agent assigned to change DocAble’s code needs the rules relevant to the files it expects to edit. DocAble is a document-remediation service developed with agents, and its engineering environment selects those rules for each task. Those rules include architectural invariants, ownership declarations, lint requirements, and links to design decisions. The engineering problem is to select that knowledge for a particular task without making every agent reconstruct it from the repository.

DocAble selects context twice. At dispatch, an agent hook matches the work order’s anticipated files against file-scoped constraint declarations and the models’ file-to-component mappings. The resulting knowledge joins the standing instructions in the agent’s initial context. After planning, the agent triggers a second extraction using its refined file set. This selection may surface obligations missed initially or discard material no longer relevant to the proposed change 2.2. James C. Davis, DocAble: Automated Document-Accessibility Remediation, Good Fast and Cheap, SEIP manuscript, October 28, 2026, 2026. This is dynamic context injection: the knowledge supplied to an agent changes as the work becomes better understood. Figure 3.1-2 illustrates both selections and the separate gate that requires evidence of the second.

Dynamic context injection and enforcement Three rows distinguish agent workflow, dynamic context selection, and engineering knowledge as a resource. The workflow is initial agent context, planning to refine scope, refined agent context, a Git precommit gate, then implementation. The gate requires evidence of refined selection for the initial commit that permits implementation to begin. At task dispatch a hook selects initial knowledge from anticipated files and components. Planning passes refined scope to a second selection using refined files and dependencies; that selection may add or remove knowledge. Each selection feeds its corresponding agent context. Both draw from the same engineering knowledge repository of models, rules, procedures and examples. Standing instructions remain available throughout. Context retrieval supplies guidance; the distinct precommit gate enforces completion of the second selection. Agent workflow Context selection Engineering knowledge (actor) (dynamic) (resource) Initial agent context standing + initial Refined agent context standing + refined Planning Refine scope Implementation Gate Git precommit Evidence of refined selection Dispatch hook At start of task Initial selection Anticipated files and components Refined selection After planning Refined files and dependencies May add or remove Refined scope Engineering knowledge repository models · rules · procedures · examples Standing instructions — available throughout mission · compact method · compact policy Figure 3.1-2. Dynamic context injection and enforcement. A dispatch hook selects initial engineering knowledge from anticipated files and components. After planning, the agent selects context again using its refined scope. Standing instructions remain available throughout. A Git precommit gate requires evidence of the second selection for the initial commit that permits implementation to begin.

Before implementation begins, the agent must make an initial commit demonstrating that the required discovery occurred. A separate Git pre-commit gate rejects that commit if the dispatch has no recorded second-extraction event. Its condition is deliberately narrower than “the agent followed the rules.” It does not compare the extraction’s file set with the committed files, or establish that the selected constraints were complete, correct, read, or followed. The gate requires a discovery event; correspondence checks and implementation gates must evaluate the obligations that discovery exposes.

Completion requires a different view of the work. DocAble’s definition-of-done audit recomputes evidence over the completed task instead of relying only on an earlier record. Several intermediate commits may legitimately leave a model and its implementation temporarily inconsistent; the completed task is where their required agreement can be assessed. The two mechanisms therefore answer different questions: did the required discovery occur, and does the finished work carry the evidence needed for acceptance? Neither question is answered merely by placing instructions in context. (Appendix A traces an actual dispatch through model selection, work-order construction, and completion checks.)

Guidance can make an acceptable realization more likely. A sound constraint or admission mechanism can instead rule a represented class of unacceptable realizations out of the surface it governs. Guidance improves the producer's odds; enforcement changes what admission must trust.

guidance: pi↑enforcement: selected Ji need not be trusted for admission

The first of the three enforcement boundaries is the action boundary exposed by the harness and its tools. Here, one attempted side effect is in view: a tool call, an API request, a shell command, or a file mutation.

AGENT HARNESS

Inset — Hooks and Permissions

Many agent harnesses let engineers intervene in an agent’s work through permissions and lifecycle hooks. For example, a deployment tool can be permitted to inspect production state while its credentials deny permission to modify it. A pre-action hook can invoke a check on a proposed command; if the check is configured to block violations, the harness refuses the command. A post-action hook can check the result or collect evidence, but the operation has already occurred. That evidence can inform a later acceptance decision: a CI or deployment gate can reject a larger unit of work when required checks fail.

We can understand these facilities by separating where an intervention occurs from what the configured mechanism does. The boundary determines what evidence is available in time to affect the decision. The mechanism determines how that evidence is used: the same failed check at the same hook might produce a warning or stop execution. If the deployment tool must not modify production state, permissions enforced by the production service can refuse a write before it takes effect. A warning after a write cannot satisfy that obligation: the forbidden effect has already occurred. The engineer therefore starts with what must be prevented or established, then chooses a boundary with sufficient evidence and a mechanism whose response enforces that requirement.

The second enforcement boundary is the work-unit boundary, where many actions compose into a meaningful unit: a completed task, pull request, build, migration step, or deployment candidate. Obligations that no single action can express become legible here: that the model and the implementation agree at task completion, that a change carries all its required evidence, that "done" actually holds. A pre-commit check can reject a local defect; a task-completion audit can weigh the whole body of work; a deployment gate can refuse a candidate whose accumulated evidence is inadequate. The larger scope makes obligations involving several actions available for evaluation, even when no individual action provides enough evidence.

The third enforcement boundary is the artifact or runtime boundary: the resulting system or running state. Types, narrow APIs, architectural seams, schemas, runtime permissions, and admission policies can make a forbidden state impossible to express or impossible to accept. For example, a service account may have permission to read production records but no permission to change them. The permission restricts what the running system can do, regardless of how the agent wrote its code.

docs.title: 3.1.2 Placement and Strength Are Different Decisions
docs.text:
These locations do not form a monotonic scale from weak to strong. A narrowly scoped API permission may enforce its obligation more strictly than a late CI check; a type may rule out one state completely while saying nothing about a system-level obligation a task-completion gate can weigh. Where a mechanism acts and how strongly it enforces an obligation are different design decisions.

Richer models can expand the properties the environment is able to state and govern, but substantial enforcement can exist without them. A bounded execution sandbox, for example, can constrain actions without requiring a rich model of the system it contains.

docs.title: 3.1.3 Return Evidence at the Earliest Useful Boundary
docs.text:
The boundaries also determine what feedback can return and when. An action hook can explain why a call was refused; a CI check can report a violated invariant in the change under review; a deployment validator can identify failed checks or missing required evidence. Placing a check where the obligation can first be evaluated allows useful evidence to return while the relevant work is still in progress. The agent can then revise the change using the reasoning and context already at hand. If feedback arrives after it has moved on, it may have to reconstruct what it changed and why before it can understand the failure and correct the work.

Controls within the GEE can also interact or conflict; §3.5 treats their growing portfolio as a system in its own right.

The Alignment Principle: Make selected engineering obligations enforceable through constraints that restrict actions or states, sensors that produce evidence, and gates that evaluate evidence and control whether work may proceed. Once an obligation is entrusted to the engineering environment, satisfying it should not depend solely on each future agent remembering it.

Worked Examples

Takeaway. Place the enforcing mechanism at a boundary where the obligation is legible and the environment can evaluate or constrain the relevant work. The appropriate boundary depends on the obligation.

The next section asks what must be true before an obligation deserves enforcement.
