docs.title: §3.4 · Growing the Governed Environment
docs.text:
Chapter 3 — Alignment  ::  §3.4§3.4 Growing the Governed Environment

No engineered environment begins with every future obligation already represented and mechanized. Some obligations are known in advance: an API must require authentication, a state transition is forbidden, a format mutation must cross a particular seam. Others become visible only when the work exposes a failure nobody represented or controlled. A governed environment acquires durable structure in two ways: up front, from obligations already known, and in response to failures and surprises.

The second route is governance conversion. A failure exposes a recurring class, engineers identify what was missing, and the environment encodes the lesson as durable structure. Later work inherits the result. The repair fixes this instance. Conversion changes the environment.

This concept rhymes with what you may have learned about software postmortems 1.1. Torgeir Dingsøyr, “Postmortem Reviews: Purpose and Approaches in Software Engineering,” Information and Software Technology 47, no. 5 (2005): 293–303, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2004.08.008. After diagnosing a failure, ask why you were surprised. What did you expect to happen, and which assumption proved wrong? The diagnosis reopens the design space. You might repair the immediate defect, change the design, or introduce a control against a broader class of failures. The consequences and costs of each option help you decide which lesson to carry forward.

Getting a lesson into subsequent work is harder. Dingsøyr and colleagues found few companies that analyzed findings across project postmortems to support organizational learning 2.2. Torgeir Dingsøyr et al., “Organizational Learning Through Project Postmortem Reviews: An Explorative Case Study,” Software Process Improvement, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 4764 (2007): 136–47, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-75381-0_13. In interviews at a national space research center, Anandayuvaraj and colleagues found that engineers often applied lessons only when someone remembered an earlier failure or knew where to look for it 3.3. Dharun Anandayuvaraj et al., “Learning From Software Failures: A Case Study at a National Space Research Center,” Proceedings of the 48th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE 2026), 2026, https://doi.org/10.1145/3744916.3773149. Commodity intelligence changes the economics. Agents can help build the models and controls that carry a lesson forward, and more changes can benefit from the same investment. Governance conversion makes selected lessons part of the environment that subsequent work inherits.

Inset — Failure Modes Before and After Failure

Failure-mode analysis need not wait for a failure. The FMEA approach discussed in §3.3 can identify possible failures before operation and guide decisions about prevention, detection, and mitigation. Known obligations can therefore produce durable engineering structure before experience forces the issue.

Governance conversion works in the complementary direction. A failure or important surprise supplies evidence that something was missing. Engineers identify the failure mode behind the instance and ask what durable structure should address the class: a model, obligation, constraint, sensor, gate, or other durable structure.

docs.title: 3.4.1 Up Front: Encode What You Already Know
docs.text:
Start with obligations you can state before the work begins and that are consequential, recurrent, or reusable enough to make durable. A required output shape may become a schema; a forbidden dependency may become an architectural relation plus a validator; a service boundary may become a permission or narrow API; a legal lifecycle may become a closed transition table. Encode recurring obligations when the environment can carry them more cheaply and reliably than repeated judgment.

Chapter 4 turns this into a method for starting and migrating systems; here the distinction is simply that these obligations are known before failure forces the issue.

docs.title: 3.4.2 As You Learn: Convert What the Work Teaches
docs.text:
The harder half begins when the system surprises you. Do not assume every failure calls for another gate. Diagnose what was missing.

The conversion can land in one of five places:

  • Missing representation / semantics → improve the model. Make the fact or relation durable at the abstraction where the question becomes answerable.
  • Missing obligation or tolerance → state the governing boundary. A failure may show that variation treated as free was not actually acceptable. Make the invariant, policy, bound, or permitted set explicit enough for future work to reason against it.
  • Missing evidence → add a sensor or trace. Make the relevant state observable.
  • Missing evaluation → strengthen the check. Turn evidence into a repeatable judgment, whether advisory or enforced by a gate.
  • Missing enforcement → add or strengthen a constraint or gate. Make the verdict control the relevant action or admission.

These diagnoses are not mutually exclusive. In practice, one failure often exposes several missing pieces at once. A property that was never represented may also lack an explicit invariant and the sensor needed to observe it. The durable repair can therefore add a model, an obligation, and evidence together. The categories identify where engineering structure was missing; they do not require the repair to land in only one place.

Failures and surprises can reveal obligations that were previously implicit, including choices treated as implementation freedoms that turned out to matter. Engineers investigate what was missing and decide whether to revise the model, state a new obligation, collect different evidence, or change enforcement. The revised environment then shapes later work, which may expose further gaps. Figure 3.4-1 shows how this process converts experience into durable engineering structure.

Governance conversion: a failure is diagnosed for what was missing, and the missing piece is encoded as durable structure that future work benefits from inheriting as engineering capital A failure or surprise flows down into one question — what was missing — with five possible answers: missing representation/semantics, obligation, evidence, evaluation, or consequence. Each branch encodes a durable answer: a model, an invariant, a sensor, a validator, or a constraint or gate. The five converge into durable engineering structure, which future work benefits from inheriting, accumulating as engineering capital. The figure's point: a recurring failure is not automatically a request for another gate — you diagnose what the environment lacked and encode that. FAILURE / SURPRISE What was missing? representation model obligation invariant evidence sensor evaluation validator enforcement constraint / gate DURABLE ENGINEERING STRUCTURE Future work benefits from inheriting it ENGINEERING CAPITAL A failure is not a request for another gate — diagnose what was missing, then encode it. Figure 3.4-1. Governance conversion. When a failure exposes a recurring failure mode rooted in missing representation, obligation, evidence, evaluation, or enforcement, encode the missing structure at the appropriate layer. Future work inherits the result as engineering capital when that durable structure continues to lower future cost or uncertainty.

docs.title: 3.4.3 Correct Judgment Without Enforcement
docs.text:
Suppose a deployment pipeline checks that every required configuration value is present. The validator detects a missing value, but the pipeline records only a warning and continues deploying. The evidence and evaluation are adequate for that obligation; acceptance does not depend on the verdict. Adding another check for the same missing value would repeat the judgment without repairing the gap.

The durable change is to make the deployment decision depend on that result, if the configuration really is required. In another case, the safer repair may remove an unsafe operation entirely and require review when it would have been used. Governance conversion should change the part of the environment that permitted the failure. It can add a mechanism, strengthen its consequence, or retire a capability whose risk no longer has a useful justification.

docs.title: 3.4.4 Engineering Capital
docs.text:
Governance conversion motivates a useful concept: engineering capital. You may be familiar with the opposite idea, technical debt: a shortcut today that makes future changes more costly. Where technical debt reduces your ability to make changes, engineering capital increases it. You have durable models, checks, and other engineering structure that lower the cost or uncertainty of future changes. Commodity intelligence can lower the cost of constructing that structure, while increasing the number of engineering episodes over which its cost can be recovered.

The capital must be something future work can actually inherit. A model can eliminate repeated reconstruction; a constraint can prevent a recurring failure; a sensor can expose previously hidden state; a gate can evaluate evidence and control whether work proceeds; a skill or runbook can package judgment for reuse. These assets change the starting conditions of future work. They earn a return when future work requires less reconstruction, repeated judgment, failure, or rework because the structure exists.

Engineering capital can also transfer between projects. A reusable build check or task-completion procedure can give a new project an established starting point. Engineers may adapt the mechanism directly, or reuse the design judgment that led to it while building a different mechanism. The value comes from work the next project no longer has to repeat, after accounting for the cost of adapting and maintaining what it inherits.

Reuse still requires engineering. A deployment check may assume a particular hosting platform; a review procedure may assume a team structure the new project lacks. The receiving project must identify those assumptions, test whether they hold, and adapt or discard the parts that do not fit. Inherited structure improves the starting conditions only where its obligations and mechanisms remain appropriate.

The engineered environment evolves with the system it governs.** Lehman's work on software evolution made the analogous observation about software itself: software used in a changing real-world environment must continually adapt, and its complexity tends to increase unless effort is spent maintaining or reducing it. MAGE extends that caution to the engineered environment surrounding the software. Models, validators, constraints, and procedures evolve too — and can become liabilities when they no longer fit what they govern. See Lehman & Ramil 2003 4.4. M. M. Lehman and J. F. Ramil, “Software Evolution—Background, Theory, Practice,” Information Processing Letters 88 (2003): 33–44. Capital also depreciates. A model can drift from the system it represents. A validator can encode an assumption the architecture has outgrown. A sensor can become noisy; a gate can impose more delay than the failure it prevents; a once-important control can survive long after its obligation disappears. Maintenance preserves useful capital; reconciliation repairs assets that no longer match the system; retirement removes assets whose carrying cost now exceeds their return. This is why accumulation cannot be the objective. A governed environment with more mechanisms is not necessarily richer than one with fewer. What matters is the future engineering value those mechanisms continue to produce.

Debt makes future work pay again for today's expedience; capital lets future work inherit today's judgment. Governance conversion turns lessons from individual engineering efforts into structure that subsequent work can reuse.

docs.title: 3.4.5 Where Enforcement Stops
docs.text:
Not every engineering obligation should be enforced mechanically. An obligation may remain unrepresented, require expert judgment, be evaluated without enforcement, or be governed. Figure 3.4-2 shows these four possible stopping points.

Where enforcement stops: three questions place any obligation in one of four states — residual, judgment required, evaluated only, or governed A staircase of three questions. First: is the obligation explicit in a form the environment can use? No leads to RESIDUAL — a reasoner must reconstruct it. Yes leads to the second question: can it be evaluated adequately? No leads to JUDGMENT REQUIRED. Yes leads to the third: does the environment enforce the result? No leads to EVALUATED ONLY — evidence produced and evaluated, but not enforced. Yes leads to GOVERNED. These classify current dispositions, not equally desirable outcomes. Is the obligation explicit in a form the environment can use? no RESIDUAL a reasoner must reconstruct it yes Can it be evaluated adequately? no JUDGMENT REQUIRED no adequate evaluator available yes Does the environment enforce the result? no EVALUATED ONLY evaluated, not enforced yes GOVERNED mechanically enforced Figure 3.4-2. Where enforcement stops. An obligation may remain unrepresented, require expert judgment, be evaluated without enforcement, or be governed. These are possible dispositions, not equally desirable outcomes.

Residual. The obligation is not explicit in a form the environment can use. An engineer or agent must reconstruct the relevant meaning when the decision arises.

Judgment required. The obligation is explicit, but available mechanisms cannot evaluate it adequately. The decision still requires human judgment.

Evaluated only. The environment can evaluate the obligation, but the result does not control whether work may proceed.

Governed. The environment enforces the obligation through a constraint on available actions or states, or through a gate that makes an action or admission depend on the evaluation.

The same restraint applies to tolerance. Making an acceptable boundary explicit does not require tightening it or enforcing it mechanically. As Figure 3.3-3 illustrated, measurements can reveal how much margin remains within a quantitative tolerance, even when the environment does not use those measurements to block work. A broad tolerance may be the correct engineering decision, and variation within it remains legitimate implementation freedom. Stronger Alignment means more dependable adherence to the obligations engineers actually chose, not progressively narrowing the acceptable realization space.

Different concerns can warrant different stopping points. A team may record service cost while leaving the spending decision to a human, rather than imposing a hard daily ceiling. It may review a trend in incident reports without setting a required number, which would reward the count instead of the improvement. A design decision may require context that the available checks cannot evaluate adequately. In each case, engineers should make the remaining judgment or policy choice explicit instead of treating non-enforcement as an accidental omission.

The mechanism that exposes a problem need not be the one that ultimately enforces the repair. A complexity warning may identify code worth examining without justifying a ban on every similar function. Investigation may instead reveal a missing type or an architectural boundary that a more precise control can enforce. Chapter 4 follows a migration of this kind, from an audit signal to more specific representations and controls.

Governance conversion also creates the next problem: the environment now contains an expanding portfolio of controls, and those controls can themselves become inconsistent, redundant, or orphaned.

docs.title: §3.5 · When Controls Become a System
docs.text:
Chapter 3 — Alignment  ::  §3.5§3.5 When Controls Become a System

As governance mechanisms accumulate, they become control machinery: the constraints, sensors, and gates through which the environment governs agentic work. The machinery can fail even when every individual control is reasonable. Controls may impose incompatible demands, interfere with one another, outlive their purpose, or leave important obligations uncovered.

Figure 3.5-1 shows three ways to examine this machinery. A catalogue identifies the controls and their purposes; an interaction graph relates controls through the resources they access; and a coverage view compares the controls with independently established engineering obligations. The views share control identities but answer different questions. Maintaining them requires recording where each control acts, which resources it accesses, and what justifies its existence.

Three views of the control machinery Control machinery supplies the catalogue, interaction graph, and coverage view. Independently identified obligations also feed coverage. The squash rule and diff-size guard share the commit set. Atomic delivery traces to the squash rule, bounded change scope to the diff-size guard. A cost ceiling lacks coverage, and a legacy export check lacks a recorded justification. Control machinery Controls · Resources Engineering obligations Catalogue What exists? Interaction graph What collides? Coverage What is governed? [A] Squash rule [B] Diff-size guard [C] Legacy export check [A] Squash rule One atomic commit Commit set [B] Diff-size guard Maximum diff size Potentially incompatible obligations Atomic delivery [A] Bounded change scope [B] Cost ceiling [C] Coverage gap Candidate orphan Figure 3.5-1. Three views of the control machinery. A catalogue identifies controls; an interaction graph relates controls through shared resources and exposes potential conflicts; and a coverage view relates controls to independently identified engineering obligations. The same control identities appear across all three views. Coverage analysis can reveal obligations lacking adequate controls (coverage gaps) and controls lacking a current justification (candidate orphans).

docs.title: 3.5.1 Model Interactions Between Controls
docs.text:
The squash rule and diff-size guard in Figure 3.5-1 both act on the commit set. If a task’s changes exceed the size limit for a single commit, neither order of execution can satisfy both requirements.

The interaction graph uses controls as nodes and shared resources as the principal join key. A resource may be ordinary — a lock, a file, a commit-set, a deployment slot — or operational, such as a lifecycle event or a context budget. Controls need not call one another to interact; they only need to make potentially incompatible demands on the same modeled resource.

A shared resource is a conservative signal of interaction, not proof that every conflict has been captured. Within the represented surface, it lets engineers and tools ask useful questions before the controls interact in production work: which controls fire on this event, which touch this resource, which pairs have no declared order, and which known combinations impose incompatible requirements.

Some candidate conflicts can be evaluated mechanically, such as a cycle in declared ordering requirements. Others need judgment. A static check can show that two controls touch the same commit set; a validator or human reviewer must determine whether their requirements conflict. The graph exposes the interaction for evaluation before it disrupts work. Conflicts can arise from incompatible obligations or from mechanisms that interfere while enforcing compatible obligations. The first requires reconsidering the requirements or specification. The second may be resolved by changing the mechanisms or their interaction without weakening either obligation.

DocAble’s implemented interaction analysis covers one class of interaction: potentially conflicting access to a shared resource. I adopted an interaction model borrowed from concurrency control’s read/write conflict test 1.1. Philip A. Bernstein and Nathan Goodman, “Concurrency Control in Distributed Database Systems,” ACM Computing Surveys 13, no. 2 (1981): 185–221, https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~brewer/cs262/concurrency-distributed-databases.pdf. For each governance mechanism, the model records when it executes and which resources it reads or writes. Two mechanisms running at the same event have a potential conflict if they access the same resource and at least one writes it. For example, a post-commit code-style formatter writes a file that a subsequent checker reads. If the checker must inspect the formatted result, it must run afterward. The conflict graph identifies such interactions; the governance model records their resolutions.

Two DocAble hooks share a finite context budget at the end of an agent turn. In Claude Code (as of 2026), lifecycle hooks run configured checks at defined events and can prompt an agent to continue working when it tries to stop 2.2. Anthropic, “Automate Actions with Hooks,” accessed November 8, 2026, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide. The first, recurring failure, prompts Claude to reflect on notable failures or repeated issues in its recent history that might warrant conversion into durable governance mechanisms (§3.4), either through human review or autonomous follow-up. The other, stranded work, prompts the orchestrator to compare the subagent’s completed and landed work against its original brief to identify work that may have been lost. Both consume context, and the stranded-work inspection may exhaust the remaining context window before recurring-failure reflection can complete its analysis. Each hook is useful independently, but their order matters. The governance model therefore requires the recurring-failure hook to run before the stranded-work hook.

The governance graph records conflicts and their resolutions, including ordering, merging mechanisms, separating execution points, or accepting an interaction. Topological sorting computes a sequence from the declared ordering constraints and reports cycles; a separate check compares the governance model with the configured mechanisms.

The hook interaction also illustrates a limit of the simple read/write model I adopted for DocAble. The stranded-work inspection can exhaust the context needed by recurring-failure reflection. This is a resource-consumption dependency rather than an ordinary read/write conflict. DocAble does not model that distinction separately; the required order is recorded directly. Read/write conflicts are one way to discover interactions, not a complete account of them. The broader engineering question is whether one mechanism can interfere with another’s ability to fulfill its obligation. Larger engineering environments may benefit from modeling resource dependencies explicitly, particularly when several mechanisms compete for limited context, time, or execution capacity.

The squash rule and diff-size guard expose a different limit of read/write analysis. Both checks may only read the commit set, so the conflict test can miss incompatible obligations. Resolving that conflict requires revisiting what the checks demand.

docs.title: 3.5.2 Trace Obligations to Mechanisms
docs.text:
To find an uncovered obligation, start from the obligations engineers expect the environment to govern. An inventory assembled from existing controls alone would omit any obligation for which no control was built.

Tracing in both directions yields two findings:

  • Coverage gap. A consequential obligation for which the intended evidence or enforcement is not adequately supplied.
  • Orphan. A mechanism that no longer traces to a current obligation, failure class, or documented purpose. An orphan is a finding to reconcile, not proof that the mechanism should be deleted.

docs.title: 3.5.3 Add, Reconcile, and Retire Controls
docs.text:
Governance conversion and coverage auditing provide complementary pressures. Conversion adds durable structure when experience exposes a recurring gap; coverage auditing finds controls that are missing, redundant, or obsolete. The audit can therefore lead to consolidation or retirement.

The control model must remain connected to the controls it represents. An entry can identify the script or configured permission that implements a control, while a correspondence check reports missing or unrecognized targets. The check should expose a gap in the relation rather than silently treating an unmatched control as covered. This applies the broader rule from Chapter 2: a model of the engineering environment must stay connected to the machinery that engineers and agents use it to reason about.

Do not recursively govern every relation merely because it can be modeled. Extend the control model only when a recurring engineering question or observed failure justifies the added machinery.

The worked control-machinery model is grounded primarily in the originating case. Its broader value is a hypothesis for other engineering environments: the catalogue, interaction, and coverage views provide concrete questions to test when a growing set of controls becomes difficult to manage.

docs.title: Preserve Engineering Freedom
docs.text:
Alignment must preserve two kinds of freedom. The first is freedom of implementation: which acceptable realizations remain available after obligations are enforced. The second is freedom to extend the engineering environment: whether additional controls can coexist with those already installed. The realization-space model in §3.3 addresses the first question; the governance graph addresses the second.

Agents may explore implementation alternatives without being authorized to merge, deploy, or otherwise commit them. The engineer decides which choices remain open and which require stronger control. The same judgment applies to the engineering environment itself: adding a control may prevent one failure while interfering with mechanisms already in place.

docs.title: §3.6 · Summary
docs.text:
Chapter 3 — Alignment  ::  §3.6§3.6 Summary

Modeling establishes what an engineered system should satisfy; Alignment determines how selected obligations will be upheld as agents work. Constraints restrict available actions or states, sensors produce evidence, and gates use evidence to decide what may proceed. Their effectiveness depends on choosing obligations independently of the work being judged, placing mechanisms where those obligations can be evaluated, and understanding the limits of the resulting assurance.

  1. Enforcement makes an obligation more than a request. Guidance tells an agent how it should act. Enforcement determines which actions the environment permits or which results it accepts.
  1. Enforce at the earliest decidable boundary. A constraint can prohibit an action as soon as the relevant facts are available. An obligation about the result may have to wait until a sensor can produce the evidence a gate needs.
  1. Correspondence is not correctness. A model and its implementation can agree and share the same error. To judge correctness, engineers need an independent obligation and evidence capable of revealing a violation.
  1. Convert recurring judgment into durable structure. When a failure or repeated decision reveals something future work should inherit, preserve it in a model, check, or control. That structure becomes engineering capital when subsequent work benefits from it.
  1. Govern the governance machinery. Controls can leave an obligation uncovered, interfere with one another, or become too costly to maintain. Engineers need to know which controls exist, how they interact, and which obligations they govern.

Alignment Principle

Make selected engineering obligations enforceable through constraints that restrict actions or states, sensors that produce evidence, and gates that evaluate evidence and control whether work may proceed.

Modeling and Alignment have been examined separately, but engineering does not proceed in two isolated phases. Implementations expose missing models; analyses reveal obligations worth enforcing; and failures motivate changes to the governed environment. In the next chapter, we follow these interactions as they unfold, showing how engineers introduce, revise, and retain models and controls while a system evolves.

docs.title: §4.1 · The Dynamics of MAGE
docs.text:
Chapter 4 — MAGE in Motion: Engineering Through Models  ::  §4.1§4.1 The Dynamics of MAGE

MAGE can look static when described one principle at a time. Chapter 2 introduced models as projections of consequential properties; Chapter 3 introduced Alignment as the mechanisms that evaluate and enforce selected obligations against a realization. A working engineering system, however, is dynamic. Models are discovered, realizations change, new properties become consequential, and knowledge accumulated during one change constrains the next.

Engineers do not interact with agents through a single interface. On the Modeling side of Figure 4.1-1, natural language, specifications, and models play different roles. Natural language supports inexpensive, fluid interaction: asking questions, expressing intent, exploring alternatives, and requesting changes. A specification makes obligations on an acceptable realization explicit. Models make selected properties and relationships explicit so that they can participate directly in reasoning about the system. These forms complement one another. A model does not eliminate conversation, and neither does a specification.

The return path is similarly varied. On the Alignment side, review, testing, and analysis provide different forms of evidence about the resulting realization. Review permits contextual human judgment. Testing observes selected executions. Analysis reasons about properties that may not be adequately established by sampled executions alone. The engineer interprets this evidence against the relevant specification and models, deciding whether the realization is acceptable, must change, or has exposed something that should change the engineer's understanding.

Engineer–agent interaction through Modeling and Alignment Two panels over one shared implementation node. Left panel, Modeling / Communicating: the engineer fans out through three parallel channels — natural language, specification, and models — which converge on the agent; the agent produces the implementation. Right panel, Alignment / Evaluating: the implementation yields a result, which fans out through three parallel channels — review, testing, and analysis — that converge back on the engineer. The same engineer appears at both upper ends; the single implementation node at the bottom is the hinge between communicating intent and evaluating evidence. MODELING / COMMUNICATING what do I know, intend, and need to make explicit? ALIGNMENT / EVALUATING what does the evidence justify believing or doing? engineer engineer natural language specification models review testing analysis agent result implementation Figure 4.1-1. Engineer–agent interaction through Modeling and Alignment. Engineers communicate intent and knowledge through natural language, specifications, and models; delegated realization returns evidence through review, testing, and analysis. The channels are complementary rather than sequential. Modeling makes selected engineering knowledge available to guide realization, while Alignment provides evidence for evaluating and revising it.

These interactions do not prescribe a fixed sequence of activities. Models make selected knowledge available to guide delegated work; review, testing, and analysis provide evidence for evaluating the result. Alignment uses that evidence to establish or preserve correspondence: an engineer may require a correction, or a gate may reject a change that violates an obligation. An engineer may move among these interactions repeatedly during a single change.

These channels differ in their governing force. Natural language and specifications remain useful throughout engineering, but preserving an obligation as the system changes requires additional machinery. A consequential property should survive beyond the prompt, conversation, or review in which it was first articulated. Once the property is sufficiently understood, Modeling makes it explicit and automated Alignment keeps the realization in correspondence with it. Engineers can therefore leave ordinary exchanges informal while making consequential properties durable.

Three ideas describe the resulting dynamics: alignment can operate actively or passively; models can be brought into governance incrementally around an alignment kernel; and the models themselves can emerge from engineering work rather than being specified completely in advance.

docs.title: 4.1.1 Alignment Changes the System
docs.text:
Alignment can establish correspondence with a model or preserve it as the system changes. These two modes are active and passive alignment, illustrated in Figure 4.1-2.

In active alignment, an engineer may deliberately introduce a mismatch between the models and the implementation. A new model expresses an obligation that the existing system does not yet satisfy. Rather than weakening the model to describe the current implementation, the engineer directs agents to change the system until it conforms. The environment evaluates the resulting work against the obligation, exposing remaining gaps for further correction. This process can also begin when an existing obligation is found to be violated; the essential feature is that the implementation changes to satisfy the model.

Once the system satisfies the obligation, the same models and alignment mechanisms can serve a different purpose. Passive alignment evaluates subsequent changes against the established obligations, constraining or refusing changes that would violate them. The engineer need not prescribe how each change is implemented, provided the result remains acceptable. Models introduced to direct one transformation thus become durable engineering structure that governs later work.

Active and passive alignment Two stacked shaded panels. Active alignment uses models with new obligations to compare and detect gaps, modify the system with agents, and evaluate and check alignment, repeating until correspondence and producing an aligned system. Retain the models and mechanisms after success. Passive alignment evaluates proposed changes against the same models and known obligations, admitting or rejecting changes and continuing to protect correspondence. The retained models, mechanisms, and governance are engineering capital for subsequent changes. Active Alignment (convergence) Use the models to change the system until it satisfies them. Passive Alignment (preservation) The same models and mechanisms keep the system aligned. Models M New obligations Compare and detect gaps Modify the system (with agents) Evaluate and check alignment Aligned system S′ Repeat until correspondence Once active alignment succeeds, retain the models and mechanisms. Models M Known obligations Proposed change ΔS Evaluate the change against the models Updated system S′ Admit or reject Continue protecting correspondence Figure 4.1-2. Active and passive alignment. Active alignment brings an implementation into conformance with modeled obligations, including newly introduced obligations that deliberately differ from the current system. The retained models, mechanisms, and governance become engineering capital when subsequent changes benefit from them. Passive alignment uses them to evaluate subsequent changes and preserve the properties already brought under governance.

The models and checks established through active alignment become engineering capital when later changes benefit from them. Subsequent work inherits both the obligation and the machinery for evaluating it.

This matters because active alignment is not necessarily behavior preserving. Asking an agent to make a state machine explicit, replace an architectural boundary, separate storage from computation, or satisfy a new ownership model may require substantial changes to the realization. Those changes may satisfy the new model while damaging some other property that has not yet been made visible to the environment. That possibility creates an ordering problem.

docs.title: 4.1.2 Establish a Kernel Before Expanding
docs.text:
The first models brought into governance should protect the properties that subsequent transformations must not be allowed to damage. Together, these models form the alignment kernel.

Chapter 2 organized models by the properties they represent. The kernel instead concerns their order of introduction: protect the properties that an upcoming transformation must preserve, then expand the governed surface under those existing constraints (Figure 4.1-3).

Incrementally extending the alignment kernel Left, a numbered four-step procedure: 1 identify the kernel — model the properties that must stay protected while the system changes; 2 actively align — use the models to change the system until it satisfies the kernel; 3 extend — add the next models, subject to the constraints already established; 4 repeat — each new model narrows what later change is allowed to do. Right, a flat concentric diagram: the kernel M1 sits at the centre, with M2, M3, and M4 as successively larger nested rings. An annotation notes that the governed surface grows over time; another that each new model is admitted under the constraints of the models inside it; and a third that active alignment operates within the protected region. 1 Identify the kernel model the properties that must stay protected while the system changes 2 Actively align use the models to change the system until it satisfies the kernel and all prior models 3 Extend add the next models, subject to the constraints already established 4 Repeat each new model narrows what later change is allowed to do kernel M1 M2 M3 M4 the governed surface grows over time … each new model is admitted under the constraints of the models inside it active alignment operates within the protected region Figure 4.1-3. Incrementally extending the alignment kernel. The kernel contains the modeled properties that must already be protected while active alignment changes the system. Additional models extend the governed surface, but each new alignment operates subject to the constraints established by the models already in the kernel. The layers are not different classes of model; they show models such as those introduced in Chapter 2 becoming governing constraints over time.

The order is system-dependent. For a conventional information system, behavioral correctness and state management may belong in the initial kernel: later structural changes must preserve what the system does. For an embedded system, resource properties such as latency, memory, or energy may need to enter first. An implementation may contain unusual structure precisely because it satisfies a timing constraint. Asking an agent first to make an implicit state machine explicit could invite a reasonable-looking refactoring that removes those optimizations. If the timing model is already aligned and enforced, the agent remains free to restructure the implementation—but only within the performance envelope that must survive.

This ordering is a form of risk-driven engineering. Boehm’s spiral model organized development around identifying and resolving risks, while risk-driven software architecture similarly asks engineers to invest in architectural knowledge where uncertainty threatens consequential decisions 12.1. Barry W. Boehm, “A Spiral Model of Software Development and Enhancement,” Computer 21, no. 5 (1988): 61–72, https://doi.org/10.1109/2.59.2. George Fairbanks, Just Enough Software Architecture: A Risk-Driven Approach (Marshall & Brainerd, 2010). The alignment kernel applies that judgment to the properties that must survive an upcoming transformation. An engineer should consider what the transformation might damage, the consequences of that damage, and whether the available evidence would detect it. A property that is expensive to recover, difficult to observe, or capable of invalidating subsequent work may warrant protection before other models are introduced.

Cheap implementation changes this calculation. Agents can rapidly explore alternatives and carry out substantial transformations, but that speed does not make the consequences of an incorrect transformation inexpensive. Nor does every uncertainty justify a model or control. Where failure is cheap and reversible, exploratory implementation may provide better information than modeling in advance. Where a transformation threatens properties on which the system already depends, those obligations should enter the kernel before the transformation proceeds. The objective is not to model everything first, but to protect what the next change cannot safely put at risk.

A newly aligned model can join the protected environment for the next episode. Adoption therefore proceeds incrementally; it does not require a complete model of the system before governance begins.

The kernel should grow only while additional models justify their cost. A model earns its place by making a consequential property cheaper to understand, predict, constrain, or evaluate than leaving that knowledge implicit. The kernel is large enough when the consequential degrees of freedom are under control.

docs.title: 4.1.3 Greenfield and Brownfield MAGE
docs.text:
Incremental adoption is easiest to see in a brownfield system. A realization already exists. Engineers can observe it, identify consequential properties, induce models from the implementation and their own knowledge, actively align the system where correspondence is missing, and retain the resulting models and mechanisms in the GEE. The governed surface grows around a system that was already running.

A greenfield project might appear to invite the opposite strategy: construct the models first, align implementation to them, and only then allow the system to emerge. That is sometimes appropriate when obligations are already well understood. It is not the general MAGE prescription.

Software engineering exists in part because software changes. Requirements turn out to be incomplete. Apparently obvious abstractions prove wrong. Interactions become consequential only after something runs. A specification can reduce degrees of freedom without eliminating uncertainty about which choices should ultimately be fixed.

Early in a project, some degrees of freedom therefore have information value. Cheap implementation can be used to explore them. A loose specification can produce one or several prototypes; those prototypes expose missing requirements, useful abstractions, resource constraints, awkward interactions, and assumptions that were invisible on paper. The engineer then has better evidence about what should become explicit structure. The parallel document-format implementations in §3.2 illustrate the exploratory route to Modeling in §2.1: they let me investigate common structure before deciding what should be shared.

docs.title: 4.1.4 What Cheap Implementation Changes
docs.text:
Agentic implementation makes this strategy unusually cheap. In that setting, even vibe coding has a legitimate engineering role: it can serve as a kind of 3D printer for software, rapidly realizing a loose specification so that engineers can learn about the system they actually need. The mistake is not using cheap implementation. The mistake is confusing an exploratory realization with a sufficiently governed one.

An exploratory implementation can become a production system. Engineers can recover models from the prototype, decide which properties must be preserved, and actively align the implementation with those obligations. Alternatively, they can use what the prototype taught them to construct a new implementation against explicit models. Either route is legitimate. Before a system is relied upon, however, its consequential properties need more than a successful demonstration: they need adequate evidence and, where justified, mechanisms that preserve them through subsequent changes.

Cheap implementation has another consequence: agents can produce unnecessary complexity at extraordinary speed. In my experience, coding agents readily introduce abstractions, architectural layers, and mechanisms that are reasonable in isolation but inappropriate for the system at hand. A design pattern may be sound, yet add more machinery than the problem warrants; a general solution may accommodate cases the system will never encounter. Empirical studies of AI-generated changes identify overengineering and poor contextual fit as reasons for rejection or reversion 34.3. Issam Oukhay et al., “When AI Code Doesn’t Stick: An Empirical Study on Reverted Changes Introduced by AI Coding Agents,” Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on Mining Software Repositories, 2026, 847–51, https://doi.org/10.1145/3793302.3793587.4. Daniel Ogenrwot and John Businge, “PatchTrack: A Comprehensive Analysis of ChatGPT’s Influence on Pull Request Outcomes,” Empirical Software Engineering 31 (2026), https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-026-10869-5. Agents can also explain and defend these choices convincingly. The engineer must judge whether the proposed structure fits the actual requirements, existing architecture, and likely evolution of the system. Parsimony is therefore an active engineering responsibility: deciding not only whether a design works, but whether its complexity is justified.

Much of my work with agents comes down to deciding what is an implementation detail and what is not. I generally do not care what a variable is called or how an ordinary function is organized, provided the result satisfies its obligations. I do care whether the implementation crosses an architectural boundary, introduces a new dependency, or changes the behavior of a service that other components rely on. The difficulty is that these distinctions are not always apparent in advance. Sometimes an agent makes a perfectly reasonable choice, I look at the result, and discover that I care about something I had never thought to specify. That is part of engineering. The next step is to decide whether the newly discovered obligation should become explicit, so that future work does not have to discover it again.

A useful rule is to distinguish three kinds of decisions. If a choice follows mechanically from an established model, generate it rather than asking an agent to reason it out repeatedly. If several implementations satisfy the obligations, delegate the choice and let the agent explore them. If experience reveals a consequential decision that later work will face again, preserve it in the engineering environment. That may mean recording a model, adding a constraint, or establishing a check. The point is not to eliminate judgment, but to spend it where it is needed rather than repeatedly making the same decision.

Cheap implementation changes engineering experience in three related ways.

Engineering phenomena — Implementation, comprehension, and connection amplification

Implementation amplification: compressed exploration. Commodity intelligence makes it cheap to implement, inspect, measure, and reject alternatives that previously would have been too expensive to try.

Comprehension amplification: compressed understanding. Rapid implementation helps engineers discover what they mean. Working software exposes misunderstandings that requirements and discussion leave hidden; agents make it cheaper to repeat the cycle of expressing an intent, inspecting the result, and revising the representation. You can only learn from what you can observe.

Connection amplification: compressed experience. Agents surface related failures, observations, and design consequences in dense succession, where conventional development would have separated them by days or weeks. Their proximity can make relationships visible: several local failures reveal one architectural gap; a measurement exposes a missing model; one change makes the consequence of another immediately apparent.

The limitation matters. A change can satisfy its functional goal while worsening performance, security, or maintainability. Fast implementation therefore increases the importance of measuring beneath the visible outcome. The DocAble case in §4.2 illustrates this through Ousterhout’s advice to measure one level deeper 5.5. John Ousterhout, “Always Measure One Level Deeper,” Communications of the ACM 61, no. 7 (2018): 74–83.

In DocAble, related failures sometimes arrived quickly enough that what first appeared to be separate defects became recognizable as symptoms of a missing architectural concept. The shared relationship became a system model, which in turn enabled static analyses that prevented several classes of failure. Speed had changed what the engineer could see.

The engineer still judges which alternatives are worth exploring and which apparent connections matter. When experience reveals a recurring lesson, governance conversion preserves it in the environment so that later work can use the resulting representation, procedure, or control.

Engineering move — Governance conversion

A recurring failure, a repeated judgment, or a newly discovered relationship is converted into durable engineering structure: a representation, a body of evidence, a procedure, or an enforced obligation. §3.4 develops the move in full.

It does not decide what deserves capturing; that judgment stays with the engineer. It names what follows the decision: the lesson stops living in one person's memory and starts living in the environment that governs the next change.

Figure 4.1-4 brings these recurring activities together. Alignment operates throughout the work, while governance conversion can preserve a consequential lesson wherever it arises.

Agentic Engineering Through Models Model, Realize, and Evaluate form a repeating cycle. A brace spans all three activities and is labeled Governance conversion: Make consequential lessons durable. Conversion can occur during any of the activities; it is not a fourth phase. Agentic Engineering Through Models Model Realize Evaluate Governance conversion Make consequential lessons durable Figure 4.1-4. Agentic engineering through models. Modeling, realization, and evaluation recur as a system evolves. Alignment operates throughout; governance conversion can make a consequential lesson durable during any activity.

The engineers supervising this process do not begin without understanding. They had enough understanding to state the problem, write the loose specification, judge the prototype, and recognize what it gets wrong. The task is to move consequential parts of that understanding out of human memory and into explicit representations that agents and the engineering environment can use. Because agents can perform both implementation and much of the mechanical work of model induction quickly, this transition need not be a long separate modeling phase.

Leave degrees of freedom open while variation produces useful information. Once a choice becomes sufficiently understood and consequential, represent it and, where justified, align the implementation to it. This applies to greenfield and brownfield engineering alike. The difference is where the first useful evidence comes from: exploratory implementations in one case, an existing system and its accumulated engineering knowledge in the other. §4.3 examines how to recover that knowledge from an inherited system.
