docs.title: §4.4 · Engineering the Environment
docs.text:
Chapter 4 — MAGE in Motion: Engineering Through Models  ::  §4.4§4.4 Engineering the Environment

The engineering environment accumulates models, controls, procedures, and evidence. Maintaining its usefulness requires four kinds of work: equip the reasoner, evaluate proposed work, operate the supporting machinery, and maintain what later tasks inherit.

docs.title: 4.4.1 Equip the Reasoner
docs.text:
There are two complementary ways to improve recurring engineering work. One is to improve the conditions under which a reasoner makes a judgment: give it better representations, domain knowledge, examples, procedures, tools, and context so that a satisfactory realization becomes more likely. The other is to enforce selected obligations in the environment so that satisfying them does not depend entirely on the reasoner choosing correctly.

Both effects can come from the same artifact. A model can guide an agent and state properties consumed by a validator. A runbook can brief a reasoner and trigger a gate. Evidence can inform a decision or feed a gate. A governed engineering environment composes these roles rather than assigning each artifact permanently to one side.

Distributed cognition provides a useful frame for this composition: reasoning can be performed by a system of people, representations, procedures, and artifacts rather than one isolated individual. The inset explains the connection 1.1. Edwin Hutchins, Cognition in the Wild (MIT Press, 1995).

COGNITIVE SCIENCE

Inset — The GEE as a Distributed Cognitive System

Studies of distributed cognition ask us to move the boundary of analysis outward. Edwin Hutchins's classic study of ship navigation, for example, does not explain navigation solely by asking what one navigator knows. Position is established through a system of people with different roles, instruments, charts, procedures, communications, and intermediate representations. The relevant cognitive system is larger than any individual participating in it 1.

The same perspective is useful for agentic engineering. A coding agent need not carry the whole engineering problem inside its context window. Models preserve selected facts about the system; skills preserve procedures; tools perform operations that need not be approximated through language-model reasoning; evidence records what occurred; people or agents supply judgments that remain difficult to evaluate mechanically. The capability of the resulting engineering system is therefore not simply the capability of its foundation model.

External representations matter for more than storage. Work on distributed cognitive tasks shows that the form of an external representation can change the operations required to solve a problem 2.2. Jiajie Zhang and Donald A. Norman, “Representations in Distributed Cognitive Tasks,” Cognitive Science 18, no. 1 (1994): 87–122, https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1801_3. A state machine exposes legal transitions; a dependency graph exposes reachability and coupling; a measurement model exposes a bound. The representation changes the reasoning problem presented to whoever—or whatever—reasons next.

A GEE adds another step. Its surrounding machinery can sometimes act on the represented property. A dependency model may help an agent understand the architecture, but a validator can also compare an observed dependency with an architectural obligation, and a gate can refuse the change. The environment therefore does not merely distribute cognition across reasoners and artifacts. For selected obligations, it can enforce what those representations express.

Organizational-learning research distinguishes correcting an error from changing the assumptions or rules that shape later action 3.3. Chris Argyris and Donald A. Schön, Organizational Learning: A Theory of Action Perspective (Addison-Wesley, 1978). Governance conversion is a concrete engineering move within that broader concern: a recurring gap becomes a model, procedure, check, or permission that later work inherits.

Some recent work automates parts of this improvement: analyzing traces to distil reusable skills, 44. Jingwei Ni et al., Trace2Skill: Distill Trajectory-Local Lessons into Transferable Agent Skills, arXiv preprint arXiv:2603.25158, 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.25158. diagnose harness defects, 55. Mengzhuo Chen et al., From Failed Trajectories to Reliable LLM Agents: Diagnosing and Repairing Harness Flaws, arXiv preprint arXiv:2606.06324, 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06324. or revise the harness from observability data 6.6. Jiahang Lin et al., Agentic Harness Engineering: Observability-Driven Automatic Evolution of Coding-Agent Harnesses, arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.25850, 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25850. Such techniques can supply candidates; engineers still decide which lessons and obligations the environment should preserve.

Some recurring judgments should remain qualitative. Others contain narrower obligations that can be enforced while the larger decision stays open. The unit of that decision is the obligation, not the entire task.

docs.title: Package Recurring Judgment
docs.text:
Skills preserve recurring procedures and judgment. Package the representations, examples, heuristics, decision procedures, and tools that help later work avoid reconstructing the same practice from general knowledge.

A skill can range from a compact procedure to a substantial body of domain knowledge and tools. It needs the representations used to reason about the work, the recurring decisions that matter, and a procedure for making them. What matters is what a fresh agent can use, not the package’s length or file format.

Prose, examples, models, and decision procedures make satisfactory judgments more likely. A skill can also invoke enforcing mechanisms or carry the models and correctness conditions they consume. Where an obligation requires independent enforcement, a constraint or gate must control the relevant action or admission decision; a checker may supply the evaluation used by that gate.

Delivering the packaged knowledge is its own engineering problem. Loading everything all the time is the obvious solution, and often a bad one: every rule, model, example, and failure lesson competes for attention, so a larger context can make navigation harder rather than easier. Separate the small standing context that must remain continuously salient from the richer slices retrieved when the task makes them relevant, and treat the delivery as an intervention whose effect can be measured. Context delivery changes what the reasoner can see; by itself, it does not change what the environment permits.

docs.title: 4.4.2 Evaluate the Work
docs.text:
Every engineering process must decide what evidence justifies accepting a change. Code review, testing, analysis, measurement, and expert judgment remain available; agentic implementation increases the rate at which the environment must use them. Start with the obligation the evidence must establish.

Validation begins with an obligation. If the obligation is settled, evidence can test whether the change satisfies it. If the obligation is still a hypothesis — whether users want the feature, which workflow they prefer, which tradeoff is acceptable — no test suite can manufacture the missing product knowledge. In that regime the evidence is experimental. MAGE can govern the experiment and preserve known constraints; it cannot turn an open question into a mechanical truth.

The obligation determines what must be represented; the representation determines which judgments are feasible. Start with the obligation and ask what representation makes it tractable, then use the cheapest judge adequate to the representation and the decision at hand. Representation can change that allocation: a judgment that initially requires expensive interpretation may become mechanically decidable once the relevant states, relations, or invariants are explicit. The converse failure also exists. A cheap judge can be perfectly reliable over an inadequate representation and still answer the wrong engineering question. In DocAble, pixel variance was easy to measure but could not decide whether a low-variance image carried semantic content; the representation had discarded the distinction the obligation required. Tightening the pixel-variance threshold would not recover the missing semantic distinction. DocAble instead routed that question to a judge capable of evaluating semantic content.

Use the weakest representation that preserves the distinction the obligation requires, and the cheapest judge adequate to decide it. Then decide, separately, whether the resulting judgment warrants enforcement. A deterministic check may remain advisory; a probabilistic evaluator may sometimes be reliable enough to support enforcement.

For a settled obligation, the producer's own report is rarely enough. A human says the change is correct; an agent says the tests pass; a tool announces completion. Each claim may be useful, but the strongest assurance comes from evidence generated independently of the judgment seeking admission. For consequential changes, prefer evidence that can challenge the producer's own claim rather than relying on self-report alone. Where the consequence warrants it, place admission control outside the producer's ability to redefine success.

That evidence can come from several sources. Where a model exposes a consequential property — a transition rule, a permitted edge, a declared bound — an appropriate analysis can produce evidence about whether that property holds; other models support navigation or reconstruction and need not carry an invariant at all. A model need not be an oracle to be useful. Evidence can equally come from outside a model: a test exercises a behavior, a compiler or type system rejects an illegal state, a reference implementation supplies a differential oracle, a metric reveals degradation, a human reviewer decides a property that remains judgment-laden. MAGE requires only that the obligation and the evidence be adequate to the claim.

In software testing, an oracle is the means of deciding whether an observed result is correct. It may be an expected output, a property the result must satisfy, a reference implementation, or a human judgment. An oracle is useful only to the extent that its verdict addresses the intended obligation. A perfectly reliable check of the wrong property is still an inadequate oracle.

SOFTWARE ENGINEERING

Inset — The oracle problem

A longstanding difficulty in software testing is that executing a program can be much easier than deciding whether its result is correct. Testing research calls this the oracle problem 7.7. Earl T. Barr et al., “The Oracle Problem in Software Testing: A Survey,” IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 41, no. 5 (2015): 507–25. For a sorting function, checking that the output is ordered is insufficient: an implementation that returns an empty list would pass that check. The oracle must also establish that the output contains the same values, with the same multiplicities, as the input.

Complex behavior may require properties, reference implementations, metamorphic relations, models, runtime evidence, or human judgment. Agents can cheaply produce implementations and test inputs, but more candidates do not supply the criteria for accepting them. Before expanding the search, the engineer must identify evidence that can distinguish an acceptable result from a plausible but incorrect one.

Existing behavior can stand in for a surprising amount of written specification. In a compatibility port or a structure-preserving migration, a reference implementation supplies an executable oracle: challenge a new realization with the same inputs and compare it against known behavior 891011.8. Anthropic, “How Anthropic Runs Large-Scale Code Migrations with Claude Code,” Anthropic, July 16, 2026, https://claude.com/blog/ai-code-migration.9. Nicholas Carlini, “Building a C Compiler with a Team of Parallel Claudes,” Anthropic, February 5, 2026, https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-c-compiler.10. Steve Faulkner, “How We Rebuilt Next.js with AI in One Week,” Cloudflare, February 24, 2026, https://blog.cloudflare.com/vinext/.11. Stephen Toub, “Migrating the GitHub Copilot Runtime to Rust, Using Copilot,” GitHub, September 16, 2026, https://github.blog/ai-and-ml/generative-ai/migrating-the-github-copilot-runtime-to-rust-using-copilot/. Tests, benchmarks, compatibility suites, and production traces close the target further. The implementation problem may stay enormous, but much less of the engineering question remains open.

Generative validation searches for counterexamples to a property, as discussed in §3.3. For sorting, generated empty lists, duplicates, and different input orders can test whether the result is an ordered permutation. A failure may reveal a law worth checking beyond the original example. A run without a counterexample still depends on which inputs the generator could reach; test count and line coverage alone do not establish that the property holds.

Docker's autonomous coding fleet separates producer from grader: the agent that writes a change does not grade it. An independent reviewer with its own model invocation, a determinized test suite, and a human gate stand between a pull request and main. The fleet may open a pull request; it may not merge one 12.12. Manuel de la Peña, “A Virtual Agent Team at Docker: How the Coding Agent Sandboxes Team Uses a Fleet of Agents to Ship Faster,” Docker, May 1, 2026, https://www.docker.com/blog/a-virtual-agent-team-at-docker/.

docs.title: Model-Aware Change Impact
docs.text:
As agents produce changes faster than engineers can evaluate them, validation can become a bottleneck. One way to reduce that burden is to determine which obligations a change might affect, then select the evidence needed to establish that they still hold. The models and traceability relationships developed through MAGE offer a basis for doing so: explicit relationships among models, implementation elements, and obligations can guide the selection of tests, analyses, and measurements.

Consider a proposed increase in DocAble’s worker concurrency. The changed code may be confined to the executor, but its consequences extend beyond it. The execution model describes which operations can run together; the memory model constrains the resources consumed by concurrent work; and the latency model predicts how scheduling choices affect completion time. Figure 4.4-1 follows these relationships from the proposed change to potentially affected obligations and the evidence needed to evaluate them. Correct execution order, peak memory, and latency may require different checks, even though the change originated in one part of the implementation.

Model-aware change impact A proposed increase in worker concurrency leads through execution, memory, and latency models to legal ordering, peak-memory, and latency obligations. Correctness tests, memory analysis or measurement, and performance tests supply evidence for admission. Models, obligations, and evidence form three shaded bands connected by single downward arrows on a central spine. Proposed change Increase worker concurrency Execution model (work and dependencies) Memory model (resource bounds) Latency model (response time) Related models: concurrency constrained by memory; latency depends on work and memory. Affected models Potentially affected obligations Required evidence (evaluation) Legal ordering (no violated dependencies) Peak memory (within budget) Latency budget (within target) Correctness tests (ordering and results) Memory analysis or measurement (peak RSS) Performance test (end-to-end latency) Admission decision Evaluate affected obligations with required evidence Figure 4.4-1. Model-aware change impact. A proposed concurrency change leads through related execution, memory, and latency models to potentially affected obligations and the evidence needed to evaluate them. These relationships guide validation effort; incomplete or stale relationships can require broader checks before admission.

This approach builds on established work in software change-impact analysis, requirements traceability, model-based impact analysis, and regression test selection 13141516.13. Shawn A. Bohner and Robert S. Arnold, eds., Software Change Impact Analysis (IEEE Computer Society Press, 1996).14. Orlena C. Z. Gotel and Anthony C. W. Finkelstein, “An Analysis of the Requirements Traceability Problem,” Proceedings of the First International Conference on Requirements Engineering, 1994, 94–101, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRE.1994.292398.15. L. C. Briand et al., “Automated Impact Analysis of UML Models,” Journal of Systems and Software 79, no. 3 (2006): 339–52, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2005.05.001.16. Gregg Rothermel and Mary Jean Harrold, “A Safe, Efficient Regression Test Selection Technique,” ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology 6, no. 2 (1997): 173–210, https://doi.org/10.1145/248233.248262. Its value in MAGE is that the models identify engineering questions, not merely implementation dependencies. A change to concurrency may warrant renewed memory analysis even if no memory-management code was modified. Conversely, sufficiently complete model relationships may justify omitting evaluations for obligations unaffected by the change.

The limitation is the completeness of the relationships being used. A missing dependency, an outdated model, or an incorrect link between a model and its implementation can conceal an affected obligation. Model-aware impact analysis therefore supplies evidence for selecting evaluations, not a guarantee that unselected checks are unnecessary. Where the relevant relationships are incomplete or uncertain, broader validation remains appropriate. An affected obligation may also require human judgment rather than an automated check.

Model-aware impact analysis extends the role of engineering models beyond directing implementation and evaluating its results. By connecting changes to the obligations they may disturb, those models can also help determine where evaluation effort is needed. The benefit grows as the rate of implementation increases, provided the cost of maintaining the relationships remains justified by the evaluation work they save.

docs.title: 4.4.3 Operate the Environment
docs.text:
A method has to survive terrible, horrible, no good, very bad days, too. Full disks, conflicted branches, vanished agents, stalled queues, flaking tests—the quotidian catastrophes of software engineering. Engineers often know how to recover, but that knowledge may live only in someone's head, where an autonomous agent cannot reliably reach it. Do not neglect operations when applying Modeling and Alignment.

Lifecycle models represent healthy progress and important failure states. Events make consequential transitions observable. Runbooks preserve sanctioned reactions, including where judgment remains. Metrics expose the quantities needed to judge whether the loop is healthy. Together they support an operating loop: recognize the state, surface the right reaction, take the appropriate action, and observe what happened next.

A lifecycle model starts with the healthy path of a recurring activity — how a bug moves from reported to fixed, how an agent moves from dispatched to landed — then names the failure states that matter and the sanctioned recovery from each. Pair prohibitions with recovery paths. "Never use this destructive merge command" leaves a stuck agent with a prohibition and no exit; "when this state occurs, do not use X; use Y because it preserves the already-applied work" supplies the missing path. DocAble learned this when agents used a destructive Git escape during stuck merges: the durable rule named both the forbidden action and the recovery that preserved already-applied work.

Operation improves further when an important transition can make the right procedure arrive at the right moment. Do not rely on an actor to remember to inspect the lifecycle, notice that a transition happened, retrieve the right procedure, and invoke it. Where a recurring event is mechanically observable and a standard response is useful, bind the reaction to the event. A mechanical trigger does not require a mechanical response: the firing can be deterministic while the payload still contains judgment. An agent reaches a context threshold, and a hook deterministically requests a handoff the agent must still compose. A deployment fails a health check, and the event opens a recovery path an engineer must still judge. Automate the arrival of the decision procedure, not every decision.

Runbooks preserve how an experienced engineer reasons through a recurring situation. Their steps can require different kinds of decisions:

  • Execute when a step is mechanically determined and can become an executable operation.
  • Delegate when a step requires bounded judgment. Supply the relevant state, choices, criteria, and required output.
  • Escalate when a decision requires human judgment or authority. Prepare the evidence and surface the decision explicitly.

Where possible, surround a step requiring judgment with deterministic work. Prepare the data mechanically before the decision, then execute and measure mechanically afterward. Preserve the rationale separately from the execution trace. The judgment remains judgment, but its inputs and consequences become easier to replay and check. Runbooks can drift, so their procedures need the same maintenance discipline as other engineering models.

Operational measurement should expose the state the decision actually depends on. A worker count may be a poor proxy for memory pressure; measure the pressure. A marker on disk may not establish liveness; record lifecycle state explicitly. Ousterhout's rule from §4.2 applies to operations unchanged: 1717. John Ousterhout, “Always Measure One Level Deeper,” Communications of the ACM 61, no. 7 (2018): 74–83. measure one level deeper. A whole-project cloud bill tells you what you spent; cost by service may tell you what to change. Keep measurement separate from enforcement: a metric supplies evidence, a validator may interpret that evidence against an obligation, and a gate may act on the resulting verdict.

docs.title: Scheduling Validation
docs.text:
Model-aware change-impact analysis addresses which evaluations a change requires. A separate problem is how to execute those evaluations without unnecessarily delaying engineering work. Even when the right checks have been selected, they consume time and computational resources. Running them synchronously can delay dispatch of subsequent development work—underutilizing agent capacity—while running them asynchronously can overwhelm the available infrastructure. The engineering environment must therefore determine when evaluations run, how they share resources, and which results must block further work.

DocAble’s agents eventually outpaced the infrastructure that checked their work. Before a November 2026 redesign, completed changes arrived in batches roughly every ten minutes, while the full test suite took about thirty minutes. The validation queue grew even though implementation was progressing well. I therefore asked which checks had to pass before each merge and which could examine several changes together.

An initial asynchronous arrangement launched expensive checks in the background after each merge. That removed the wait before the next merge, but it did not reduce the work being requested. Each merge still started another expensive run. A burst of merges therefore launched a burst of validation workers and overloaded the host. Moving validation off the critical path had exchanged waiting for resource contention.

The redesign separated broad validation from the arrival of individual changes, as Figure 4.4-2 shows. Inexpensive checks still ran before each merge. Broad repository checks ran every thirty minutes against the main branch, in an isolated worktree, with a lock permitting only one sweep at a time. Several merges could therefore be evaluated together. A blocking failure raised an alert and stopped new agent dispatch until the orchestrator acknowledged or handled it; acknowledgment permitted work to resume while repair was tracked separately. Before deployment, the full validation suite ran against the candidate being shipped.

The arrangement distinguishes three enforcement boundaries. Per-merge checks protect rapid integration, scheduled checks examine the accumulated changes without blocking each merge, and predeployment validation protects the released artifact. Asynchronous evaluation does not mean that its results are ignored: a scheduled failure can still interrupt subsequent work. The engineer chooses which obligations require immediate evidence and which can tolerate delayed evaluation, taking account of the consequences of failure.

Separating integration from broad validation Before, an agent merges with full validation before the next work. After, each change passes cheap checks and merges before next work; a thirty-minute timer triggers one broad check of main at a time, and blocking failure pauses dispatch for diagnosis and repair. Deployment requests require full validation to pass before deployment. Shading identifies validation work. Before: integration and validation coupled Agent Merge and full validation Next work Next work waits for full validation. After: separate triggers for different checks For each change Agent Cheap checks Merge Next work Every 30 minutes Timer Broad checks of main One sweep at a time Pause dispatch Diagnose; repair blocking failure For deployment Deployment request Full validation Deploy passes = validation is running (tests, analyses, or measurements) Figure 4.4-2. Separating integration from broad validation. Shaded boxes identify validation work; initially, full validation delayed subsequent changes. The redesigned pipeline runs inexpensive checks before each merge, broad checks periodically against accumulated changes, and full validation before deployment. Separating these schedules reduces repeated computation and blocking latency, but delays detection of failures that escape the per-merge checks.

The gain came at the cost of delayed defect detection and harder diagnosis. A defect could remain on the main branch until the next sweep found it. If several changes had merged since the last successful check, the failure had to be traced to one of them. The appropriate schedule therefore depends on how long the project can tolerate a broken main branch and how effectively the environment can diagnose and repair it. The same bottleneck reasoning used for document processing in §4.2 applies to the engineering environment itself: measure where work accumulates, distinguish latency from aggregate resource demand, and account for the consequences of changing the execution schedule.

Other stalls require different diagnoses. Before adding another mechanism, establish what kind of problem you have.

PRACTICE

Inset — When work stalls, diagnose before adding machinery

Repeated failure does not always call for another control. Before you build one, ask which part of the loop is limiting the work. Table 4.4-1 distinguishes four possible limits and the changes each calls for.

Table 4.4-1. Diagnosing stalled work. Four possible limits on engineering work and the changes each calls for.What may be limitingThe questionIf that is the gapSearcherCan the available intelligence find a good candidate?Change the foundation model, tools, decomposition, or search strategy.ModelIs consequential structure missing from the representation?Make it explicit.OracleCan the environment tell good candidates from bad?Strengthen the evidence, validation, or simulation.TargetDo we know what "good" even means?Stop building and learn.

A stronger reasoner does not settle an unknown requirement; another validator does not supply a missing abstraction; more modeling cannot answer a product question whose answer must come from users or deployment.

docs.title: 4.4.4 Maintain the Machinery
docs.text:
As engineers develop the governed environment, they create reusable models, controls, procedures, and evidence pipelines that make subsequent work easier to direct and evaluate. Keeping this engineering capital useful requires maintenance. A model may drift from the implementation, while a gate continues to enforce an obsolete policy. Noisy controls and broken evidence pipelines can make their verdicts difficult to trust; skills can preserve procedures whose assumptions have expired. Engineers therefore need to observe, reconcile, repair, and sometimes retire these structures, just as they do for the system those structures govern.

An audit of DocAble’s models found that ten providers appeared to have the required uniqueness checks. Every test passed. Closer inspection showed that all ten checks examined identifiers in a shared graph, where uniqueness was already guaranteed, rather than the source records belonging to each provider. Duplicate source records could therefore overwrite one another without triggering a failure. The checks established a true property of the wrong collection.

The repair changed both the checks and the evidence for trusting them. Each check examined its provider’s source records, and a test deliberately introduced a duplicate that the check had to reject. This suggests a general maintenance practice: construct a violation of an obligation, run the actual check, and establish that it detects the violation. Where enforcement is intended, also test whether the resulting verdict prevents the work from proceeding. A passing control should have evidence that it can fail for the right reason. In §3.3, the consumer mistook an incomplete validation for a clean result; here, the uniqueness checks examined the wrong records.

Audit models, mechanisms, procedures, and evidence pipelines together:

  • Does it still describe or govern the intended system? Check for changed assumptions, obsolete obligations, and evidence whose revision or operating conditions no longer match the work.
  • Who uses it, and for what decision? A representation may support reasoning, queries, generation, or checking. Where enforcement is intended, verify that the mechanism still consumes the current model and acts on violations.
  • Does its benefit justify its cost? Consider maintenance effort, false alarms, delayed work, and the consequence and recurrence of the failure it addresses.
  • Should it be repaired, replaced, or retired? Preserve useful knowledge while removing machinery whose original purpose no longer warrants its upkeep.

Retirement belongs to the same discipline as governance conversion. §4.3 applies the same test when deciding what inherited structure to recover.

docs.title: §4.5 · Summary
docs.text:
Chapter 4 — MAGE in Motion: Engineering Through Models  ::  §4.5§4.5 Summary

Modeling and Alignment are not one-time activities preceding implementation. The DocAble episodes showed how implementation, measurement, and failure can expose missing engineering knowledge, while explicit models and controls make that knowledge available to subsequent work. The resulting environment evolves alongside the system it governs. Five practices characterize this process.

  1. Use implementation to learn what should be modeled. Trying several implementations can reveal which choices matter and which can remain open. The results of a trial are evidence an engineer can use in deciding what to preserve and whether to accept the work.
  1. Establish an alignment kernel before undertaking consequential transformations. An alignment kernel protects the properties that a proposed transformation could put at risk. Those risks determine which models and controls must be in place before work begins.
  1. Introduce governance incrementally. In an existing system, recover the structure already in use and audit the proposed checks against it. Verify their coverage and resolve existing violations before making the checks blocking.
  1. Match representations and evidence to the obligation. Choose the simplest model that preserves the required distinction and the least costly evaluation that can reliably decide it. Independent evidence must be capable of exposing an error in the agent’s account of its own work.
  1. Maintain engineering capital rather than accumulating machinery. Revisit what each model describes and what each check actually measures. Repair misleading checks and retire controls whose benefit no longer justifies their upkeep.

These practices change more than the way an engineer directs individual agents. They create a production environment in which models, controls, evidence, and implementation machinery can be developed and maintained as reusable assets. Chapter 5 examines that environment as a software factory, using DocAble and published industrial accounts to investigate how organizations produce and govern software when implementation becomes inexpensive.

docs.title: §5.1 · The Software Factory
docs.text:
Chapter 5 — DocAble Among Other Software Factories  ::  §5.1§5.1 The Software Factory

Earlier in this book, I compared coding agents to 2D and 3D printers. The comparison was about fabricative technology: unlike a specific-purpose tool such as a stapler, a fabricator can realize a broad range of artifacts from a description of what should be made.

We can now expand that metaphor. A fabricator does not operate alone. Once fabrication becomes a means of production, it sits inside a larger system that determines what should be made, organizes how production proceeds, and determines whether what was produced is acceptable. The printer becomes one piece of the factory.

Factories developed to make production repeatable at scales that craft production could not support. Interchangeable parts allowed components made separately to participate in the same product. Mechanization increased the amount of work that machinery could perform. Machine tools increased precision and repeatability. Each advance also exposed a problem. Faster machinery could produce defects faster than people could inspect them; a design was of little use if the available machinery could not realize it accurately; interchangeable parts were not interchangeable if different shops produced incompatible dimensions. Scaling fabrication therefore required engineering the production system around the fabricator.

Software engineering has already made much of this move. Continuous integration and delivery organize building, testing, and deployment into repeatable processes, with automated checks governing what may proceed 1.1. Jez Humble and David Farley, Continuous Delivery: Reliable Software Releases through Build, Test, and Deployment Automation (Addison-Wesley Professional, 2010), https://www.informit.com/store/continuous-delivery-reliable-software-releases-through-9780321601919. Coding agents extend automation into the production of the changes themselves. The factory must now govern not only how software is built and delivered, but also how implementation decisions are delegated, what system knowledge informs them, and what evidence justifies accepting the result.

Two ideas from manufacturing help explain what this expanded software factory must do:

  • Process design determines how production proceeds. Work is decomposed and sequenced; responsibilities, machinery, and information are arranged; measurements and decision points occur at selected stages. The process carries knowledge about how production should occur rather than requiring each fabricator to reconstruct it. Scientific management made this separation explicit by moving planning, work methods, instructions, and standards into a deliberately designed production system 2.2. Frederick Winslow Taylor, The Principles of Scientific Management (Harper & Brothers, 1911).
  • Tolerance states which variation in the product is acceptable. A drawing can specify a dimension and its allowable variation without prescribing every motion of the machinist or every property of the finished part. Gauges and metrology then establish whether selected properties of the realized part fall within those bounds. The factory can therefore leave substantial freedom to the fabricator while retaining control over the properties that matter 3.3. Simon Winchester, The Perfectionists: How Precision Engineers Created the Modern World (Harper, 2018).

As §3.3 showed, measurement can establish not only whether a realization satisfies a tolerance but, for quantitative properties, how much margin remains. That evidence can inform the next engineering decision without prescribing how the fabricator must work.

Two problems of factory engineering Process design organizes engineering intent, context and work, the fabricator, and realization. Measurement evaluates possible realizations against tolerance. The acceptable region contains permitted variation; an inside point leads to admitted change and an outside point to revision or rejection. Its structure matches the probability-in-the-factory figure. SOFTWARE FACTORY PROCESS DESIGN: how production proceeds PRODUCTION PROCESS Engineering intent Context / work Fabricator Realization Context; tools; routing; authority; sequencing what process design determines Measurement: tests, PBT, analysis, simulation, human judgment POSSIBLE REALIZATIONS Acceptable region TOLERANCE acceptable product variation within tolerance outside tolerance Admitted change Revise / reject Figure 5.1-1. Two problems of factory engineering. Process design determines how production proceeds around the fabricator. Tolerance identifies acceptable variation in what the factory produces; measurement establishes whether a realization remains within those bounds. The two concerns are complementary: a production system may carry engineering knowledge in the organization of production, in explicit bounds on the resulting product, or in both.

Watt's improved steam engine shows why production capability and product tolerance must develop together. Its design required cylinders more accurately bored than ordinary eighteenth-century production could reliably make; Wilkinson's precision boring machinery made cylinders sufficiently true for the engine to perform as intended. The advance was therefore more than a faster way to make an existing artifact. A more capable production system made a different artifact practical.

docs.title: 5.1.1 What Does a Software Factory Produce?
docs.text:
The analogy requires one adjustment before we apply it to software. A physical factory commonly produces many instances of a product. Software usually does not. Another copy of a program may cost almost nothing, while a software service may consist of one continuously evolving system serving millions of users.

The output of a software factory is the next working realization of the product. Software organizations repeatedly change an existing system: adding features, repairing defects, adapting to new environments, migrating dependencies, changing architectures, and responding to new requirements. Each production cycle begins with a working software system and attempts to produce a changed system that still works.

The factory's job is to realize controlled change: creating and evolving software while preserving sufficient control over the properties and consequences that matter 4.4. James C. Davis, The Software Engineering Handbook: A Judgment and Decision-Making Approach, 1st ed. (2026), https://davisjam.github.io/model-based-agentic-software-engineering/book/se-handbook/index.html. A software factory is the production system through which that change occurs.

Software factory. The engineered production system through which software changes are realized from engineering intent and evaluated, admitted, deployed, and improved.

A software factory contains more than its fabricators. Models describe the product: architecture descriptions, service graphs, and the properties a change must preserve. Tools work on it: linters, test harnesses, validators, and analyzers. Controls bound what may be done and accepted through permissions, admission gates, and enforced policies. An agent can run a test and reason about its result. The test supplies evidence; a gate enforces a condition by requiring a passing result before admission. A failed test that is only reported leaves a different choice to the agent or reviewer. Fabricators build the product from models, using tools, subject to controls.

The governed engineering environment developed in Chapters 2–4 is part of this larger factory. It comprises the reusable representations, tools, procedures, and controls through which engineering work is directed and governed. The factory also includes the people and agents doing the work, the production activities they perform, and the organizational arrangements that determine what work is undertaken and who has authority over its consequences.

Process design organizes how changes are produced; tolerance determines which resulting changes are acceptable. Unlike a factory producing repeated copies of a fixed design, a software factory must preserve consequential properties while changing the system itself.

That task carries a cost that physical manufacturing can often amortize differently. A drawing for a manufactured part can remain useful across thousands of instances of that part. A representation of a software system describes a target that is itself being changed. Requirements, architecture descriptions, interface specifications, models, tests, and other engineering artifacts therefore incur a carrying cost: as the software changes, they may also have to change if they are to remain useful representations of it.

Software organizations have made different economic judgments about that cost. Some have found enough durable value in explicit models, specifications, interface definitions, and other representations to justify creating and maintaining them; others have found it cheaper to keep skilled human engineers close to implementation, where they can resolve open questions about behavior, structure, interfaces, failure handling, and performance as the software changes 5.5. Oliver Kautz et al., “Achievements, Failures, and the Future of Model-Based Software Engineering,” in The Essence of Software Engineering, ed. Volker Gruhn and Rüdiger Striemer (Springer, 2018), https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-73897-0_13. Neither choice is intrinsically irrational. The tradeoff depends on how much reusable engineering knowledge a representation carries, how expensive that knowledge would be to reconstruct during implementation, and how expensive the representation is to keep accurate.

The Agile movement placed greater weight on keeping knowledgeable engineers close to implementation 66. Kent Beck et al., “Manifesto for Agile Software Development,” 2001, https://agilemanifesto.org/. 7.7. Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, “The Scrum Guide: The Definitive Guide to Scrum: The Rules of the Game,” 2020, https://scrumguides.org/. Working software became the primary measure of progress; changing requirements were expected rather than exceptional; close collaboration was preferred to elaborate handoffs; and documentation was valuable insofar as it continued to serve the work. These choices make particular sense when the object of engineering is controlled change. A representation that does not change with the software can cease to describe the thing it is meant to govern. Keeping knowledgeable humans close to implementation accepts repeated human judgment partly in exchange for avoiding representations whose carrying cost may exceed their continuing value.

Earlier attempts to separate engineering judgment from implementation encountered the same tradeoff from the other direction. Moving decisions upstream could allow implementation to be performed by less experienced programmers, but only if sufficiently detailed requirements, architecture, interfaces, or models carried the judgment that those programmers would otherwise need to supply. Producing those representations required skilled engineering labor, and maintaining them as the software changed added further cost. Leave more decisions open, however, and the organization again needed skilled human fabricators capable of resolving them during implementation.

The economic question was where engineering judgment could be carried most economically without losing control. Craft production remains economical when transferring enough judgment out of fabrication would cost as much as leaving that judgment with the skilled human fabricator. Factory production becomes economical when reusable production structures can carry consequential judgment more cheaply than repeatedly exercising it during fabrication.

Commodity intelligence changes this tradeoff. In an agentic software factory, inexpensive agents can perform substantial realization work and resolve many ordinary implementation decisions. The production system can carry selected consequential judgments while leaving the agent substantial realization freedom, subject to the evidence required for acceptance.

docs.title: 5.1.2 Walking Through a Software Factory
docs.text:
Four questions orient a walkthrough without prescribing how the factory should be organized:

  1. What does the factory produce? What changes enter it, and where do they originate?
  1. What do people do? Which judgments and acts of realization do people retain or delegate?
  1. How is production organized? How does work move through realization, evaluation, admission, and deployment, and how do lessons change that process?
  1. What are the tolerances? Which properties must remain within bounds, how are those bounds represented, and what evidence establishes compliance?

Software tolerances include quantitative bounds, invariants, architectural constraints, and qualitative obligations that may still require human judgment; each identifies variation the factory must control while leaving other choices open.

These questions can be answered at different levels of detail. A longitudinal account can show how a factory’s arrangements developed, which problems prompted changes, and what the resulting machinery accomplished. Reports from established organizations can show how factories differ in their allocation of work, authority, and control, although they rarely expose the same development history. DocAble provides the first perspective; the industrial accounts provide the second.

docs.title: §5.2 · Inside DocAble's Software Factory
docs.text:
Chapter 5 — DocAble Among Other Software Factories  ::  §5.2§5.2 Inside DocAble's Software Factory

This section illustrates

✓ The Modeling Principle · ✓ The Alignment Principle · ✓ Governance Conversion · ✓ Residual Human Judgment

DocAble was built by one engineer (me) directing a fleet of coding agents. The product was a document-accessibility remediation service; the factory was the production system through which I directed changes to that service. I was engineering both. The product had to improve accessibility while preserving the document properties its users depended on. The factory had to organize implementation and preserve consequential engineering decisions as agents changed the system.

The record examined here spans 31 complete weeks, from March 12 through October 14, 2026. At the final snapshot, DocAble contained 615,395 lines of production code and 2,333,471 lines of supporting source, including tests, checks, tools, infrastructure, models, and indexed documentation. The history identified 143 model modules. These measurements describe the resulting system and its engineering environment; they do not measure how much useful work each line or model represents.

New work came from my goals for the system, user feedback, production failures, accessibility standards, public guidance from advocacy groups 11. National Federation of the Blind, Creating Nonvisually Accessible Documents, Access Technology Team, Jernigan Institute, Baltimore, MD, 2014, https://nfb.org/images/nfb/products_technology/creating_accessible_documents.docx., and the demands of institutional use. I decided which pressures warranted engineering work and made consequential decisions about requirements, architecture, validation, and deployment. Coding agents wrote every line of the implementation. I inspected almost none of the code they produced.

That division of work required process design and tolerance. Work had to be selected, planned, dispatched, integrated, and evaluated without making me the bottleneck for every implementation decision. At the same time, agents needed freedom to choose implementations without being free to violate consequential requirements. The factory therefore developed models, procedures, tools, and controls that carried selected decisions into later work. A failure could require two repairs: changing the product and changing how future changes to it were governed.

The case follows the factory’s development from initial requirements through production operation. Its chronology matters because the machinery did not arrive fully formed. Implementation, institutional use, and observed failures exposed engineering decisions that needed to persist; the factory changed to carry them.

docs.title: 5.2.1 The Problem
docs.text:
In 2024, the U.S. Department of Justice required state and local governments, including public universities and schools, to make covered web content and mobile applications conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA 2.2. U.S. Department of Justice, Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities, 89 Fed. Reg. 31,320, 2024. The original compliance date for larger public entities was April 24, 2026. Four days before that deadline, the Department extended it by one year 3.3. U.S. Department of Justice, “Extension of Compliance Dates for Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities,” Federal Register 91 (2026): 20902–12, https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/04/20/2026-07663/extension-of-compliance-dates-for-nondiscrimination-on-the-basis-of-disability-accessibility-of-web.

For a university, compliance creates a recurring production problem: courses distribute documents whose meaning must remain available to readers using assistive technology. Purdue trained undergraduates to remediate course materials, providing both a practical reference workflow and the corpus used in the evaluation below. A checker can identify some defects, but supplying a useful description of a diagram or restoring the structure of a document requires interpreting its content. Chapter 1 introduced that difficulty; here it becomes a specification for a service.

The requirements were ordinary production-software requirements. What was unusual was the implementation capacity available to one engineer.

§1.3 grouped these obligations by kind to establish the nature of the problem. Table 5.2-1 states the eight requirements: they explain why demonstrating semantic reasoning was only the beginning.

Table 5.2-1. What DocAble had to accomplish. The eight requirements, R1–R8 — the specification the factory had to satisfy, which §1.3 introduced by kind.RequirementDocAble must…R1 · Multi-format remediationRemediate educational documents in the formats people actually use, including Office (PowerPoint, Word, Excel) and PDF.R2 · Semantic remediationPerform semantic repairs that require understanding document content, not only syntactic, deterministic transformations.R3 · Preserve the documentRetain content, appearance, and behavior except where remediation requires a change.R4 · Standards-grounded accessibilityEvaluate and repair documents against their governing obligations (WCAG 2.1 AA), not proxy checker scores.R5 · EvidenceRecord what accessibility requirement motivated each change and what evidence supports the resulting document state.R6 · ReviewabilityMake outputs auditably traceable: consequential automated changes are inspectable and, where appropriate, reversible.R7 · Production operationProcess real documents at practical sizes, costs, and latency.R8 · Institutional deploymentOperate as a deployed service that scales to thousands of faculty at one institution, and preferably nationwide.

These requirements explain why the resulting system grew large. Semantic reasoning was only one requirement of eight. A frontier foundation model could supply a capability that had previously been missing. That capability alone did not establish preservation, reviewable changes, conformance, or dependable service operation; each remained an engineering obligation. Those obligations generated the engineering system around that capability.

docs.title: The Feasibility Probe
docs.text:
I tested the uncertain capability first. I gave a multimodal foundation model pictures of mathematical equations, technical slides, and handwritten notes. On those examples it produced useful transcriptions and alternative text. The results supplied initial evidence that generative AI could perform some of the semantic reasoning needed for remediation; they did not establish that it could reliably remediate arbitrary documents.

I decided not to make the foundation model the whole remediation system. To use its semantic capability in a service, I would also have to establish document preservation, reviewable changes, conformance, dependable operation, and practical cost.

docs.title: The Two Rules of Agentic Software Engineering
docs.text:
I began with two rules.

Reading the code is the last resort. If building DocAble required me to inspect the implementation produced by coding agents, then implementation throughput would remain bounded by my capacity to read code. I wanted to build an engineering environment in which I could direct work, understand the system, evaluate evidence, and decide whether changes were acceptable without routinely reconstructing those answers from implementation.

This did not mean that I refused to read source code. It meant that needing to read it pointed to a missing supervisory surface: a model, test, lint, instrument, architectural boundary, or other representation of the property I actually needed to reason about. Reading the code was the escape hatch, not the operating model.

The resulting system should be good, fast, and cheap. This was partly a requirement for DocAble and partly a test of agentic software engineering itself. I wanted to know whether agents could help build a production system that was not merely fast to develop, but good enough to trust, fast enough to matter, and cheap enough to deploy at scale. I therefore made all three requirements for the factory.

A fast factory producing poor software would fail the test. So would a high-quality system whose development or operation remained prohibitively expensive. Agentic implementation was valuable only if the engineering system around it could achieve all three.

docs.title: The Build, in Stages
docs.text:
I began with PowerPoint, then generalized the system to Word and Excel and added PDF support as colleagues brought other documents (R1). Each new format tested assumptions that my own files had not exposed. Putting DocAble online introduced authentication, deployment, institutional use, and unfamiliar workloads (R8). Users then found outputs that passed existing checkers while losing semantic equivalence, prompting validation grounded more directly in accessibility standards (R4). When the Department of Justice extended the deadline, I shifted more attention toward production hardening (R7).

Figure 5.2-1 records the sequence. The stages mark changes in the engineering problem, not merely larger quantities of implementation. Supporting another format could reveal a weakness in the shared architecture; serving users could reveal a missing obligation that no development fixture had exercised.

The seven build stages as a dated timeline of pressure and consequence A retrospective vertical timeline of seven build stages, each row naming the stage, its dates, the pressure that forced it, and the major engineering consequence that followed. Feasibility, March: vision-language capability became usable, so the build began. PowerPoint, March to April: colleagues supplied their own decks, producing the first real remediation pipeline. Format expansion, April: Word, Excel, and PDF broke one-size-fits-all assumptions, so the architecture differentiated. SaaS, April: real users on real documents forced authentication, quota, cost, security, and exposed fidelity limits. Standards, April to May: the need for a defensible accessibility claim forced standards-grounded validation. Hardening, May to June: time became available for structural work, producing models, tests, gates, and provenance. Deployment, iteration, and optimization, July to October: operating the production system exposed performance, cost, reliability, and architectural limits, forcing repeated measurement, redesign, optimization, and re-platforming. The stages are labels drawn afterward, not a preplanned roadmap. STAGE THE PRESSURE THE CONSEQUENCE 1 Feasibility March a probe in a meeting Vision-language capability became usable → the build began 2 PowerPoint March–April the first format Colleagues supplied their own decks → the first real remediation pipeline 3 Format expansion April Word · Excel · PDF New formats broke the one-size-fits-all assumptions → the architecture differentiated 4 SaaS April a deployed service Real users on real documents → auth, quota, cost, security — and the first fidelity limits 5 Standards April–May a defensible claim The need for a defensible accessibility claim → standards-grounded validation 6 Hardening May–June structural work Time became available for structural work → models, tests, gates, provenance 7 Deployment, iteration, and optimization July–October operating what shipped Production operation exposed limits on performance, cost, reliability, and architecture → repeated measurement, redesign, optimization, and re-platforming Figure 5.2-1. The build, in stages. DocAble expanded from a feasibility probe through format support, institutional operation, and hardening. Each stage introduced obligations that changed the product and the environment governing its implementation.

One operational surprise came from Google Cloud. I had asked Claude to deploy DocAble, and it did. What I had not specified was the full deployment lifecycle, including how obsolete deployments should be retired. Eventually I noticed that the service was costing roughly $40 per day when I expected something closer to $5. I asked Claude to investigate. It reported approximately 2,000 obsolete deployments that had accumulated without being cleaned up. The cloud bill was about $1,000.

The repair was to complete the lifecycle model by adding a cleanup step for obsolete deployments. Claude had done what I asked—and had neglected what I had omitted.

docs.title: The Build, Measured Weekly
docs.text:
The repository reconstruction covers 31 complete seven-day weeks from March 12 through October 14, 2026 4.4. James C. Davis, DocAble: Automated Document-Accessibility Remediation, Good Fast and Cheap, SEIP manuscript, October 28, 2026, 2026. Figure 5.2-2 brings four dimensions together: landed work commits, accumulated models and checks, recovered agent dispatches, and documented Epic completions. They describe the activity and structure of the factory; none alone measures productivity.

An Epic represented a substantial engineering intention with a rationale, design, relevant invariants, phases, and acceptance criteria. Nontrivial designs received separate review using another foundation model, and a Definition-of-Done review assessed completion. One Epic could require several dispatches and many commits. Across the complete window, the reconstruction recovers 36,578 work commits, 14,392 dispatches, and 428 affirmative completion claims.

Development activity and engineering structure over 31 weeks: (a) reconstructed landed work commits; (b) declared models, consumers of multiple models, and registered static and dynamic verifier files; (c) recovered dispatches; (d) documented Epic completions. Shaded intervals lack retained records and do not establish zero activity. Activity and inventory counts describe the factory’s growth, not the value or correctness of its output.

The final snapshot identifies 143 model modules, 45 consumers of at least two models, and 232 static and 153 dynamic verifier files. The inventory records an increasing investment in representations and checks; the examples below examine their engineering roles and consumers.

Week 11 marks a deliberate change in my engineering practice. Notes from May 22 and 24 describe replacing repeated agent audits with deterministic checks, supported by typing, lint-authoring, and repair campaigns. The commit subjects and emerging formal Epic records agree with that account. They support an interpretation of a hardening campaign; the first surviving Epic or dispatch record does not establish when I first used agents, planning, or checks.

The series require some care. Work commits are reconstructed from direct and expanded squash landings, with duplicates, empty commits, and integration bookkeeping excluded. Completion records are affirmative claims rather than independent outcome audits, and dispatch retention is uneven. Earlier model existence is traced by path so a later declaration convention does not create a false growth spike. Registered verifier files establish an available checking apparatus, not that every check ran.

docs.title: The Support Ratio
docs.text:
The source composition gives a different view of the investment (Figure 5.2-3). Production includes remediation, web processing, the frontend, and shared services. The supporting apparatus includes tests, lints, tools, agent infrastructure, infrastructure-as-code, models, and indexed documentation. Historical snapshots and generated copies are excluded.

Call apparatus divided by production the support ratio. At weeks 11, 21, and 31 it was approximately 2.6, 3.6, and 3.8, respectively; it reached about 4.5 at week 17. The last snapshot contains 2,333,471 apparatus lines supporting 615,395 production lines. These are measurements at ten sampled revisions, with interpolation between them. A larger ratio is not a target. Tests, models, and operating tools carry different obligations, and supporting source earns its upkeep only while later work benefits from it.
