Lines between samples interpolate; the apparatus’s size establishes investment, not its return.

Together, the measurements show sustained implementation accompanied by an expanding engineering environment. They do not isolate the cost of a requirement or the causal contribution of a control. They also leave a question for engineering judgment: would this project have been feasible under the same constraints without generative AI or the machinery built around it?

Field note — The counterfactual

Within the actual constraints of this project—one primary engineer, an academic budget, and the development interval reported here—DocAble was not feasible for me without generative AI. I would not have attempted a production system at this scope without commodity implementation capacity.

Sustaining that delegation posed a second problem. Once the change volume exceeded what I could inspect conventionally, continuing required explicit representations, independent evidence, constraints, and gates. My judgment is that GenAI made the project feasible and the machinery that became MAGE made delegation at this rate feasible. This is an account of the project I could undertake, not a controlled estimate of either contribution.

docs.title: 5.2.3 Inside the Factory
docs.text: As DocAble grew, source code alone stopped being an adequate engineering interface. Repository search could locate a symbol without explaining which services participated in a workflow, who owned a piece of state, or which resource bound a proposed change had to preserve. The growth in supporting source recorded in Figure 5.2-3 reflects my response to such problems. The following examples show what that investment made possible: representations that answered engineering questions directly, relationships from which the factory could derive checks and configuration, and controls that made selected obligations consequential for later changes.

docs.title: What the Factory Knows
docs.text:
The 31-week reconstruction identifies 143 model modules at the final snapshot. These representations change with the system and answer different engineering questions. Registries describe ownership and available operations; budgets make resource bounds explicit; state machines expose legal transitions; decision tables preserve policy distinctions. Some models describe the product, while others describe the agent fleet and its engineering environment. The factory represents both the software it produces and the process that produces it.

Each representation gives the engineer a purpose-built view of a consequential property. The model carries selected engineering knowledge that the supervisor can inspect directly, without reconstructing it from implementation. This applies the purposeful reduction developed in Chapters 2–4 to factory supervision. Table 5.2-2 shows six representative models, chosen for the variety of question, form, and consumer.

Table 5.2-2. Six representative engineering models. Each row: the engineering question, the representation that answers it, what consumes it, and what the supervisor no longer reconstructs from implementation.Engineering questionRepresentationConsumerSupervisory consequenceCan a job always terminate legally?Composed cross-service state-machine model with per-invariant factsExhaustive-state checkers; the workers' own transition tablesLegal progress and termination are reasoned over states and transitions, not a multi-thousand-line workerHow much memory can a job need?Peak-memory sizing model that upper-bounds a job and derives the deployment memory tierDeployment configuration; regression tests on the boundA resource bound is inspected directly rather than reconstructed from allocation behaviorWhich services exist, and what may call what?Deployment topology plus a typed inter-service call-edge modelDeploy machinery; agents localizing changesOwnership and boundaries are read from the map, not rediscovered per changeMay this user submit this document?Entitlement decision table — the single policy authority for the admission decisionThe front door at upload timeThe admission rule is one table; changing policy is editing a model, not hunting scattered conditionalsWhat may touch a document format's internals?Registry of external seams plus typed format models owning all mutationBuild-time ban checks on raw library accessRaw library access outside the typed boundary is rejected at build timeWhich step changed this document element?Per-mutation provenance stamps projected into a derived changelogThe customer-facing changelog; forensic queriesDiagnosis is a lookup over evidence, not a cross-file investigation

docs.title: The Joins: What the Factory Can Derive and Enforce
docs.text:
In §2.6, DocAble used shared identities to answer engineering questions, such as how a particular deployment performed. In the factory, these joins also determine which properties need checking, which mechanisms check them, and what evidence a change must supply before it can proceed. The architecture resembles proof checking in one limited respect: a producer is separated from the smaller mechanism that decides whether its evidence is sufficient for admission 5.5. Talia Ringer et al., “QED at Large: A Survey of Engineering of Formally Verified Software,” Foundations and Trends in Programming Languages 5, nos. 2–3 (2019): 102–281, https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.06458. Three joins show the difference in increasing order of reach.

Property facts → verification tier → required checker → blocking consequence. Each invariant in the cross-service state-machine model carries declared property facts: how many concurrent lanes touch it, whether it is a safety or a liveness property, what state it ranges over. From those facts the model derives a verification tier — an invariant crossing multiple concurrent lanes demands exhaustive state-space exploration; a single-lane invariant demands a property test; a temporal obligation demands a model checker run. The tier is not advice: a check walks the model and fails when a mandated checker does not exist on disk. The supervisor need not choose a checker class afresh for every invariant. The encoded rule derives that requirement from the declared property facts, and the environment rejects a missing checker.

Service relationships × deployment wiring × runtime identity → an access-grant plan. The typed inter-service edge model declares which service calls which, over which plane, under which identity. Deployment machinery consumes those edges and derives the invoker grants and token audiences each service needs — and a coherence gate asserts at deploy time that the granted permissions match the modeled relationships. Least-privilege wiring is not a checklist a human re-audits; it is a projection of the service graph.

Mutation → stamp → derived account. Every mutating operation in the remediation core writes a provenance stamp — the verb, the pass, the visibility of the change — and the customer-facing changelog is derived from those stamps rather than authored beside them. A wiring validator identifies mutating paths that fail to stamp their work. The derived changelog provides structured evidence of the recorded mutations; the wiring check guards the obligation to record them.

Modeling changed what the factory could know. Alignment changed what that knowledge could cause.

docs.title: The Computation Graph: a Representation That Took Over Execution
docs.text:
The remediation graph makes a further connection: its representation determines execution. Each pass declares typed input and output relationships; the graph derives dependencies from those declarations, and execution machinery uses the dependencies to determine when work is ready. A blocking parity check holds the declarations and projected graph together. Composition therefore need not be reconstructed from behavior scattered across pass bodies.

§4.2 develops the architectural history, including the large presentation that exceeded page-chunked execution. Here the consequence is the mature capability: the same stable computation identities support execution and analytical views of critical paths, mutation boundedness, cost, and coverage. An analytical view can answer a question execution itself does not need to answer.

Explicit models expanded the questions the environment could answer. A lifecycle model made illegal transitions explicit. An ownership model reduced a concurrency protocol to the states and interleavings needed to ask whether two workers could hold the same claim; a small purpose-built checker could then exhaustively explore that finite state space. Eventual termination — a property over executions, not states — was written as small temporal specifications and checked mechanically; with recovery disabled, the checker produced exactly the stranded execution the property was meant to exclude. Checking the model created a second obligation: why believe a property established over the model holds of the implementation? Conformance tests exercised production operations against the executable model, and when one such test drifted red for days after production changed, the durable response was correspondence machinery — model-to-implementation checks selected automatically when modeled surfaces change. The factory then added machinery to keep the map true.

docs.title: Substituting the Reasoning Engine
docs.text:
DocAble separates the reasoning that proposes a repair from the machinery that changes the document. The separation preserves much of the engineering investment when the reasoning strategy changes: a new strategy can reuse the document models, controlled operations, and validation machinery rather than reconstructing them. It also lets us ask whether more general reasoning earns its additional cost.

Substitution occurs at two levels. For individual tasks, ModelSelector assigns a foundation model using task-specific configuration and capability requirements. The remediation graph stays the same while the model supplying a judgment changes. A per-task benchmark compares candidate models on quality, cost, and latency. At a coarser level, a general-purpose agent can choose and sequence repairs instead of following the production graph’s orchestration.

Selecting a foundation model was itself an engineering decision: frontier foundation models were reserved for judgments where their additional capability earned their additional cost — the cheapest-adequate-judge rule of §4.4 applied to the fabricator rather than to the validator.

The PDF changeset interface gives these strategies a common way to request supported mutations. A proposed operation names its target and intended change; the applier resolves it against the current document, checks its preconditions, and records the outcome. The structured pipeline and an experimental agent can therefore reuse typed document operations, independent validation, and provenance while deciding differently what to repair. Human-directed editing uses the same operation vocabulary. Figure 5.2-4 shows these architectural alternatives; the experiments below concern automated strategies.

Substitutable reasoning, controlled mutation Three equal reasoning-strategy boxes—structured pipeline, general-purpose agent, and human-directed editing—converge on a typed changeset containing target, operation, and arguments from a closed mutation vocabulary. The PDF path continues through a controlled applier that resolves targets, checks preconditions, applies supported mutations, and records outcomes; a structured document model of typed PDF objects; and a result with applied-operation provenance and independent validation. A return arrow makes the model available to all reasoning strategies for inspection. A separate dashed note says that some PDF operations still mutate directly outside the common changeset interface. Other formats have their own model implementations. REASONING STRATEGIES Structured pipeline General-purpose agent Human-directed editing propose edits TYPED CHANGESET target · operation · arguments closed vocabulary of supported mutations CONTROLLED APPLIER resolve · check preconditions · apply · record STRUCTURED DOCUMENT MODEL Typed PDF objects · format-specific implementation RESULT AND EVIDENCE remediated document · applied-operation provenance independent validation Inspect document model Some PDF operations still mutate directly outside the common changeset interface. Figure 5.2-4. Substitutable reasoning, controlled mutation. Different reasoning strategies inspect the document model and propose supported edits through a common typed changeset interface. A controlled applier executes those edits; provenance and independent validation provide evidence about the result. The drawing shows the PDF changeset path. Some PDF operations still mutate directly outside this interface.

This interface was still incomplete in November 2026. Dozens of PDF remediation passes retained direct-mutation paths, including repairs whose effects required additional operation types or more substantial restructuring. The common interface made some reasoning interchangeable; it did not make the entire pipeline replaceable. Extending the operation vocabulary was itself engineering work, especially where an edit changed several related structures or depended on targets created by an earlier edit.

Experiments clarified the role of representation. Frontier agents inferred PDF structure through several tool interactions, while a foundation model given a prepared scaffold inferred structure in one pass on a separate prose fixture. The scaffolded pass achieved high agreement with its reference structure at much lower inference cost. Because the documents and interaction patterns differed, this was not a matched cost comparison at equivalent quality. It identified an architectural choice: which useful structure should the system supply, and which judgments should the foundation model make 4?

I had expected that a more capable agent might sometimes lower total cost by inspecting the document more broadly and avoiding repeated specialized calls. An experiment in September 2026 compared the pipeline with an agent using DocAble’s document tools on one handwritten PDF. It pointed the other way on cost. The pipeline’s metered inference cost was about $0.0419; the estimated agent execution cost was $2.29.** The agent figure was reconstructed from its transcript, including cached-input charges, rather than read from an API billing meter. A modeled minimal-context loop cost $1.24; charging the whole experimental session gave $6.92. These are alternative accounting scopes, not separate measured strategies. Repeated processing of the agent’s accumulated context accounted for much of the estimate. Both approaches had produced outputs with no failures on the evaluated veraPDF checks. The agent recovered more of the reference document structure, but had seen the reference sequence; this cost experiment could not establish an unbiased quality comparison.

A November evaluation tested a narrower question: could a coached repair loop improve an agent’s result? The loop inspected remaining findings and could request another repair pass. On two PDFs, it closed no additional findings beyond the single-pass agent. The harder document completed a second pass but retained the same 15 findings; its cost rose from $1.35 to $3.57. The other document had no remaining findings after one pass, so the loop stopped. The result did not justify promoting the loop to production. Both configurations already shared recently added document operations; a second round of reasoning supplied no measured benefit on this pair.

The unresolved question is where additional reasoning earns its cost. Difficult semantic cases may justify a frontier agent, and an agent can help investigate failures or test what the specialized pipeline misses. Those uses require evidence about the quality gained as well as the inference bill. DocAble’s architecture lets us investigate them while retaining the document representations, supported operations, and validation machinery already built. That retained work is engineering capital: a new reasoning strategy can inherit it without reproducing the engineering decisions it embodies.

docs.title: From a Priority to Completed Work
docs.text:
How does one engineer keep several agents working without continually prompting each one? The workflow described here is the factory’s November 3, 2026 configuration, following the measurements ending October 14. I record priorities and deployment prerequisites in a strategy document. An orchestrating agent selects ready work and coordinates its planning, implementation, and evaluation.

A planning agent develops an epic: a persistent work order recording the change’s purpose, scope, phases, dependencies, and completion criteria. Its design document identifies consequential properties and the tests or analyses required for them. A separate agent reviews the plan; unresolved engineering decisions return to me. The work order preserves decisions across dispatches while leaving implementation choices within the stated requirements to the agents.

The phase dependencies determine which agents can work concurrently, as Figure 5.2-5 shows. The orchestrator dispatches ready phases into isolated Git worktrees. Each agent first inspects its assigned component and records a refined plan, including target files, in its first commit. Before changing the implementation, it supplies those files to Query Repo, which retrieves the associated models, invariants, tests, and static checks. A pre-commit check requires a record that this discovery occurred. Known obligations can therefore inform the agent’s implementation choices from the outset.

DocAble: from a priority to completed work An engineer sets priorities and resolves open decisions. A reviewed work order records the design, phases, and dependencies. The orchestrator schedules ready phases across isolated agent worktrees. Their changes converge through integration and checks. An independent completion audit checks the work order and evidence. Deficiencies return to the orchestrator for repair. An optional dotted branch also returns unresolved problems to the engineer. The work order closes only when its criteria are met. Deployment is a separate decision. Worktree isolation separates concurrent edits; it does not establish correctness. Engineer Priorities and open decisions Reviewed work order Design, phases, dependencies Orchestrator Schedules ready phases Agent A Isolated worktree Agent B Isolated worktree Integration and checks Merge changes; gather evidence Independent completion audit Check work order and evidence Work order closed Escalateif needed Repair work Criteria met Deployment is a separate decision. Figure 5.2-5. From engineering intent to completed work. The orchestrator schedules independent phases from a reviewed work order, then a separate agent audits their combined result against the completion criteria and returns missing or defective work for repair. Closing the work order and authorizing deployment are separate decisions.

Completed changes pass inexpensive checks before integration. Broader validation runs periodically against the combined code, and the deployment process reruns the full validation suite. Two changes may each work in isolation and still fail when combined, so separate worktrees do not remove the need to check the integrated result. §4.4 explains the bottleneck that motivated this arrangement and the cost of delaying some checks.

Finally, an independent agent audits the epic against its completion criteria. It checks that the expected changes landed and that the required evidence supports completion. Missing work or failed checks lead to repair and another review. Problems the agents cannot resolve, including defects in the factory itself, return to me. The work order closes after the audit accepts the result.

docs.title: What Escalated Failures Became
docs.text:
Some of DocAble’s engineering models were designed from known requirements. Others arose when failures exposed missing distinctions or controls. Three episodes illustrate the latter process, involving document mutation, instructions to foundation models, and integration of concurrent development work.

Preserving document structure required a controlled mutation boundary. An early PDF-slicing operation used PyMuPDF to copy pages into smaller documents. The resulting pages rendered correctly, but the operation discarded the PDF’s accessibility tag tree, including /StructTreeRoot and the page-to-structure relationships. A library call that preserved visible content had silently destroyed information essential to accessibility.

The immediate repair replaced the slicing operation with one that preserved the tags. I then established a canonical-library policy and concentrated PDF mutations in typed operations under AdaTool.PdfModel. For example, structure insertion passes through PdfStructInserter rather than allowing arbitrary calls to the canonical PDF library’s tag-manipulation APIs. A blocking direct-access lint rejects those calls outside designated modules. The architectural model identifies where PDF structure may be changed; the lint checks that subsequent implementations preserve the boundary.

Semantic instructions required their own engineering model. Agents developing DocAble’s image-description prompts introduced numerical requirements, including a demand for at least three specific facts and a minimum description length. Some source images did not contain enough legible information to satisfy those requirements. In several evaluated cases, the foundation model invented plausible values or padded descriptions to meet the prescribed quantity. The problem was not the particular threshold: an unconditional demand for information absent from the source could produce the same failure.

I responded with a typed prompt-governance model. It classifies prompts by purpose, such as describing, transcribing, or extracting information, and classifies their instructions by the demands they impose. A decision table determines which combinations are permitted. For example, a minimum fact count is prohibited in a description prompt, while an extraction requirement may be permitted when conditioned on information actually present in the source. The model distinguishes requirements appropriate to a task from requirements that could make faithful completion impossible.

A deterministic lint checks registered prompt definitions against this model and blocks illegal combinations. An agent introducing another unconditional fact minimum into a description prompt encounters a failed check rather than relying on a reviewer to recognize the mistake. The lint governs the instructions, not the descriptions produced from them; it cannot establish that an individual output contains no fabricated content. It prevents a recurring class of inappropriate requirements from entering the remediation system 4.

Integration automation required a model of safe conflict resolution. DocAble’s agents worked concurrently in separate Git worktrees, often changing overlapping files. The integration machinery ordinarily rebased completed work onto the current repository. When a rebase encountered a conflict, an automatic retry used Git’s -X theirs option, favoring one side of each conflicting hunk. In June 2026, concurrent modifications to the integration machinery itself produced an incompatible combination of edits. The resulting Python code failed to load, disabling scheduled integration.

The failure exposed a decision that the automation had been making without an adequate policy: which conflicts may be resolved automatically? I distinguished three cases. A clean rebase can proceed. Certain narrowly defined additive conflicts can use an established resolution procedure. Other conflicts require escalation because the integration machinery cannot establish that combining the changes preserves their intended effects. This decision model separates the presence of a conflict from permission to resolve it automatically. A conflict is evidence that further work may be needed, not authorization to discard one side.

I removed the -X theirs retry and changed the integration procedure to follow this policy. Clean integrations and permitted additive resolutions could proceed automatically; unresolved conflicts produced a conflict-need-help disposition. That disposition made the remaining work suitable for delegation. Rather than having Git select a resolution without understanding the changes, the disposition provided a defined task that I could assign to an agent: examine the conflicting contributions, reconcile their intended effects, and produce a candidate for validation. The agent could perform the repair, but the integration procedure would not accept an arbitrary conflict resolution merely because it had been generated. The model thus governed both what the automation could decide on its own and how unresolved work could be handed back to an agent.

Across these episodes, I repeatedly observed that coding agents could diagnose defects and implement repairs but seldom proposed the larger changes to models, architecture, or controls that would prevent similar failures. Claude suggested replacing the offending library call, not establishing a controlled mutation boundary. Claude suggested revising the prompt, not modeling which instructions were appropriate to different semantic tasks. Claude suggested repairing the integration script, not reconsidering which conflicts the factory should resolve automatically. I generally had to identify and direct these larger changes, although agents could implement the resulting machinery. Once the decisions were represented explicitly, agents could also undertake work that the new structure made delegable, such as reconciling conflicts identified by the integration policy. Bui and Evangelopoulos distinguish this capacity to execute assigned work from the proactivity needed to recognize worthwhile work independently 6.6. Nghi D. Q. Bui and Georgios Evangelopoulos, Agentic Coding Needs Proactivity, Not Just Autonomy, Google Research, 2026, https://research.google/pubs/agentic-coding-needs-proactivity-not-just-autonomy/. My experience illustrates that distinction, although it does not establish a general limitation of coding agents.

docs.title: 5.2.5 The Supervisor's Job
docs.text:
As DocAble’s engineering environment developed, my role changed with it. Figure 5.2-6 summarizes that progression in three stages: co-coder, tech lead, and architect. The staircase represents two related developments: the models and controls available to govern agent work accumulated, allowing me to supervise implementation at increasing levels of abstraction.

Initially, I read, judged, and merged agents’ changes. As implementation outpaced my attention, I delegated evaluation to other agents, then replaced recurring decidable findings with deterministic checks. Specialized reviewers, named ownership zones, and boundary rules allowed me to direct work without inspecting every change. Eventually, architectural, behavioral, and ownership models provided system-level views for planning and evaluation. I could make decisions about the system without routinely reconstructing its implementation.

DocAble’s delegation staircase Three ascending staircase shelves show Co-coder with an ordinary repository; Tech lead with agent review, deterministic checks, ownership zones, and boundary rules; Architect with system models, traceability, and controls. A rising GEE-capability arrow identifies the accumulated models, checks, and controls. Aligned responsibilities progress from reading, judging, and admitting changes to directing work and resolving exceptions, then deciding system structure, consequential obligations, and strategy. GEE capability (models, checks, and controls) MY ROLE 3. ARCHITECT System models, traceability, and controls 2. TECH LEAD Agent review, deterministic checks, ownership zones, and boundary rules 1. CO-CODER Ordinary repository Decide system structure, consequential obligations, and strategy Direct work and resolve exceptions Read, judge, and admit changes Figure 5.2-6. DocAble’s delegation staircase. As the governed engineering environment (GEE) acquired models, checks, and controls, my work shifted from inspecting and admitting individual changes toward directing implementation and making system-level decisions. The three stages summarize DocAble’s development rather than prescribe a maturity model. Failures in the environment could still require direct inspection.

For example, a cross-format migration touching 58 files and rewriting 5,000 lines took about 5 hours of agent time over a dinner break. My decision was that those files should change; the agents performed the migration. I rarely needed to inspect the implementation, although model drift still required correspondence checks, and failures in the engineering environment could return me to direct inspection.

My attention shifted toward deciding what should change, which properties required representation or enforcement, and what anomalous evidence meant. The environment took over more of the routine work of directing and evaluating implementation, but decisions about system structure, acceptable risk, and unresolved failures remained mine.

docs.title: §5.3 · Evaluating the Product and Factory
docs.text:
Chapter 5 — DocAble Among Other Software Factories  ::  §5.3§5.3 Evaluating the Product and Factory

The engineering machinery described in the preceding section made substantial delegation possible. Its value, however, depends on the software it produces and the cost of producing and maintaining it. DocAble must improve document accessibility while preserving the properties its users depend on; the factory must accomplish that work economically. Purdue’s undergraduate remediation effort provides a practical reference for evaluating the resulting documents.

docs.title: 5.3.1 Human Remediation as a Reference
docs.text:
Across approximately six months, 42 trained undergraduates billed 1,303.4 hours, and the recovered corpus contains 382 identifiable before/after pairs from 20 courses. That is 3.41 billed hours per pair. At an assumed typical wage of $13, estimated direct labor is $44.36 per pair. These are corpus-level quantities; individual document timings and subsequent review effort were not measured 1.1. James C. Davis, DocAble: Automated Document-Accessibility Remediation, Good Fast and Cheap, SEIP manuscript, October 28, 2026, 2026.

The student outputs document an institutional workflow rather than expert-verified accessibility. I developed DocAble against standards using independently obtained documents and did not examine the students’ remediated files until near the end of development. Eligibility screening yielded 315 pairs, randomly split by document and stratified by format into 252 development documents and 63 validation documents. One validation spreadsheet had prior development exposure. DocAble produced outputs for 62 attempts and failed on one PDF.

The evaluation in Figure 5.3-1 compared the original, human-remediated, and DocAble-remediated versions of each document along two dimensions. Syntactic accessibility concerns selected mechanically testable properties, measured with veraPDF’s PDF/UA-1 checks and Microsoft Office’s October 2026 Accessibility Checker. For each document, the study calculated the signed reduction in findings relative to the original, then summarized those reductions by format. A reduction does not establish that every accessibility obligation holds.

Semantic accessibility asks what information the document conveys. A GPT-5.2 rubric assessment examined text transcripts, with the original identified and the two outputs presented under randomized labels concealing their provenance. The model judged individual criteria and supplied transcript evidence. A deterministic scorer credited improvements and penalized regressions relative to the original; an output-score difference within one point defined the parity band. The rubric was refined on the development partition before the validation run.

Human and DocAble comparison: per-document median checker reductions; increased-finding counts; semantic 20 better, 41 parity, 1 worse of 62; document-criterion gains and regressions. Remediation compared with the human reference: (a) median reduction in checker findings from the original; (b) frequency of increased findings; (c) semantic comparison of DocAble and human outputs under the project rubric; (d) criterion-level gains and regressions relative to the original. Percentage reductions exclude documents with no original findings. Parity denotes similar measured improvement, not equivalent accessibility.

DocAble achieved larger median checker reductions for PDF and DOCX; the human workflow achieved larger reductions for PPTX. Both workflows had the same frequency of increased finding counts. The spreadsheet had no original findings, so its percentage reduction was undefined. The failed PDF’s partial artifact was excluded from completed-output comparisons.

Across the 62 scored outputs, the semantic rubric rated DocAble better on 20, within the parity band on 41, and worse on 1. Gains in complex-image descriptions accounted for much of its advantage. These are weighted document scores; the gain/regression panel separately counts document–criterion judgments, not unique defects.

One presentation makes the distinction concrete. It contained an image of a thermochemical table. The human-authored alternative text repeated the table’s title, which satisfied a checker’s requirement for alternative text but did not communicate the entries. DocAble supplied a description and a transcription next in the reading order. In the same presentation, the human version transcribed mathematical content that DocAble missed. These author-inspected examples explain disagreements between the measures; they are not systematic expert adjudication.

The semantic assessment covered only part of the intended rubric. Of 3,392 criterion-level rows, 2,467 were inconclusive for DocAble, including 1,617 whose automatic adapters were pending. Inconclusive judgments contributed no points; they were not evidence of satisfactory accessibility. Two scoring passes agreed on 58 of 62 document classifications, but repeatability does not establish agreement with accessibility experts.

The evaluation did not include vision-tier or screen-reader assessments, nor systematically measure complete content preservation or visual fidelity. The Office checker had also changed since the students’ summer work, although all versions were evaluated with the same current tools. The findings show improvements on measured properties and identify remaining weaknesses. They do not establish full WCAG conformance or equivalent accessibility for outputs within the parity band.

docs.title: 5.3.2 Runtime and Cost
docs.text:
Median elapsed time across all 63 attempts, including the failed attempt, was 1.36 minutes. The 62 completed outputs had a median inference expenditure of $0.066, with a measured range of approximately $0.001–$0.440. Full cloud execution costs were not measured for this cohort. The paper separately reports coarse operating-cost estimates; those should not be mistaken for the measured distribution 1.

These quantities show that the specialized system can produce remediation outputs quickly and with little inference expenditure. The human reference required 3.41 billed hours per document pair, compared with 1.36 minutes of unattended DocAble runtime. These are different measures of production effort. Estimating labor savings would additionally require measuring the competent review and correction needed after automated remediation and human remediation. To the best of my knowledge, the faculty whose courses were manually remediated have not been surveyed regarding quality of the result and the need for subsequent changes. As to DocAble's outputs, so far, faculty describe a few up to tens of minutes of follow-up per output.

docs.title: 5.3.3 General-Purpose Agents and a Specialized Service
docs.text:
Could a general-purpose agent perform the remediation directly? A separate comparison in the DocAble study used community document tools, unlike the engineered DocAble operations reused in Substituting the Reasoning Engine. Opus and Fable each used one configuration on ten validation documents: five PDFs, two Word documents, two presentations, and one spreadsheet. Opus and DocAble completed all ten; Fable timed out on one PDF.

Quality varied by format. On the four PDFs completed by every configuration, DocAble had the largest median reduction in checker findings. Both agents exceeded DocAble’s reductions on the two Word documents, while human remediation led on the two presentations. Median runtime was 8.22 minutes for Opus, 7.77 for Fable, and 1.31 for DocAble; median agent inference costs were $2.466 and $3.977, compared with less than $0.50 for DocAble. These costs concern this ten-document cohort, not the larger cohort underlying the $0.066 median above.

The result concerns particular configurations, community tools, and automatic findings. It does not establish comparable semantic quality or a lasting capability boundary between a specialized service and a general-purpose agent. The engineering problem includes acquiring a useful rubric, providing suitable tools, and delivering a workflow users can operate. A specialized service packages that accumulated work and can reduce the cost of applying it repeatedly; its advantage depends on the quality of that work, operating economics, and usability.

docs.title: 5.3.4 What the Economics Establish
docs.text:
A factory’s startup cost, its marginal change cost, and its carrying cost are different numbers — a separation §6.1 develops formally. The DocAble study estimates approximately $110,000 to develop DocAble over six months: $90,000 in engineering labor and $20,000 in cloud expenditure. These are author-supplied estimates, not an independently audited ledger 1. Much of that expenditure purchased reusable capability. Dividing it by the documents processed during development would confuse the cost of building the factory with the cost of using it.

The alternatives incur costs in different places. Manual remediation purchases labor for each document. General-purpose agents need a rubric, tools, and supervision. A specialized service incurs development and maintenance costs to make the recurring workflow easier to run. Cheap output production is therefore only part of the return on the factory. Establishing that the outputs serve their readers, integrating the service into institutional work, and maintaining it remain engineering and economic obligations.

docs.title: 5.3.5 Limitations and Maintenance Costs
docs.text:
The engineering machinery that made delegation possible could also mislead the agents it was meant to support. One model named a code symbol that was later moved and renamed. Nothing invalidated the reference; the model continued to look authoritative, agents continued to reason from it, and the failure surfaced days later during deployment. A subsequent audit showed that the stale pointer was not an isolated defect: re-running closed work against current code found genuine model-to-code drift that a green definition of done had missed. This incident motivated correspondence checking between models and implementation. The factory needed machinery not only to preserve engineering knowledge, but also to establish that its representations remained connected to the system they purported to describe.

The apparatus requires maintenance of its own. Models drift, controls conflict, and evidence becomes stale as workloads change. A gate can continue enforcing an obsolete assumption long after the incident that justified it. Correspondence checks help detect some of these failures, but must themselves be operated and repaired. At the final snapshot, supporting source was about 3.8 times the production code. Its size is a liability as well as an investment; some of it will cease to justify its upkeep.

The evidence has clear limits. This is one longitudinal production case led by one primary engineer directing an agent fleet, using one contemporary model ecosystem, without a controlled comparison against another engineering process. It cannot establish that another organization will encounter the same failures, build the same mechanisms, or achieve the same economics — and checker scores do not establish complete end-user accessibility. What the case can establish is mechanism and sequence: these pressures occurred, these responses followed, and selected structures persisted long enough to be exercised under continuing change.

Appendix B offers a practical starting point for applying these techniques, including brownfield migration, operation of a governed engineering environment, and measurement.

DocAble provides evidence about one factory’s development, operation, outputs, and costs. It shows how an engineer can construct machinery that permits substantial delegation while preserving selected engineering obligations, but also how that machinery can fail or become expensive to maintain. These observations do not establish that other organizations need the same arrangements. They do, however, raise a question worth examining: when agents increase implementation capacity in other software organizations, what changes in the surrounding production system?

docs.title: §5.4 · Other Agentic Software Factories
docs.text:
Chapter 5 — DocAble Among Other Software Factories  ::  §5.4§5.4 Other Agentic Software Factories

DocAble provides a longitudinal account of one engineer developing and operating an agentic software factory. Other organizations begin with different resources and constraints: established engineering teams, existing production processes, accumulated institutional knowledge, and obligations distributed across many people. Their factories may therefore organize delegation, evaluation, and admission differently. The four questions from §5.1 guide the comparison: what the factory produces, what people do, how production is organized, and what tolerances the resulting software must satisfy. The public accounts illuminate different parts of those questions; they need not supply the same answer or document every part equally well.

These are my interpretive reconstructions of public reports, not claims that the companies adopted MAGE. Engineering blogs, talks, and product documentation describe mechanisms and operating experience, but also serve promotional purposes. I use MAGE to interpret the arrangements they describe; the reports do not independently validate the method. Reported measurements retain their scope, and missing information remains missing rather than proving that a mechanism does not exist.

docs.title: 5.4.1 Cloudflare
docs.text:
Cloudflare shows how an organization's policy can become a control over work performed across many teams. Its standards corpus had grown beyond what individual engineers could readily remember. An extraction agent turns each SHOULD or MUST into a structured statement with a stable identifier, so the obligation can be tracked when its containing document changes 1.1. Timo Reimann, “How Cloudflare Enforces Engineering Standards Using AI,” Cloudflare, August 4, 2026, https://blog.cloudflare.com/engineering-standards-enforcement/. That identity supports compliance records and explicit waivers. Standards then meet work at several stages: specification review before implementation, linters during editing, semantic review in CI, and incident review after production. The representation connects a human-authored obligation to machinery that can find and apply it; merely storing the original policy documents would leave more of that connection to each reader.

An approved statement does not automatically block work. Any employee may propose a standard, and a named domain owner approves it. A separate promotion moves it from advisory to enforced; the cited account does not identify who performs that step. For enforced standards, a coordinator agent orchestrates up to seven specialist reviewers, evaluates severity, and can approve a merge request, revoke an earlier approval, or block the merge. Only enforced MUST statements can block, and the rubric favors approval so that a lone warning does not 2.2. Ryan Skidmore, “Orchestrating AI Code Review at Scale,” Cloudflare, April 20, 2026, https://blog.cloudflare.com/ai-code-review/. This separates the decision to adopt an obligation from the decision to let an automated reviewer enforce it.

Human reviewers retain an exception path: commenting “break glass” forces approval and records the override. Cloudflare reports 288 such overrides, 0.6 percent of merge requests, from March 10 to April 9, 2026 2. The override count measures how the control was used. Review runs, findings, and blocked merges similarly describe its operation. The account makes the allocation of authority visible, while the effectiveness of the checking—including violations missed and defects prevented—remains incompletely measured.

Operating experience also changes what later work inherits. The November and December 2025 outages led to rules against calling .unwrap() outside tests and against assuming upstream dependencies were in an expected state. Dangerous configuration patterns can be enrolled in Snapstone's shared deployment machinery. The policy representation changed from Markdown to JSON when agents needed more reliable filtering 3.3. Jeremy Hartman, “Code Orange: Fail Small Is Complete. The Result Is a Stronger Cloudflare Network,” Cloudflare, May 1, 2026, https://blog.cloudflare.com/code-orange-fail-small-complete/. Semantic-review latency also encouraged moving suitable checks into deterministic linters earlier in the workflow 1. These are concrete instances of governance conversion: a failure or recurring cost leads to a reusable change in the environment. The sources describe those changes but do not measure their effect on later incidents.

docs.title: 5.4.2 Spotify
docs.text:
Spotify introduced agents into an established process for changing software across many repositories. Fleet Management selected repositories, ran transformations, opened and merged pull requests, and monitored the resulting deployments, alerting the change author when production failed 4.4. Matt Brown, “Fleet Management at Spotify (Part 3): Fleet-Wide Refactoring,” Spotify Engineering, May 15, 2023, https://engineering.atspotify.com/2023/05/fleet-management-at-spotify-part-3-fleet-wide-refactoring. In 2025, an agent replaced the transformation script at one station while the surrounding targeting, review, and merge infrastructure initially remained the same. The agent addressed changes that deterministic scripts had struggled to cover, including the remaining 30 percent of one fleet migration 5.5. Max Charas and Marc Bruggmann, “1,500+ PRs Later: Spotify’s Journey with Our Background Coding Agent,” Spotify Engineering, November 6, 2025, https://engineering.atspotify.com/2025/11/spotifys-background-coding-agent-part-1. This lets us examine which production structures could be reused and which later required revision.

The late-2025 configuration bounded both the agent's actions and its route to a pull request. It exposed selected Git commands that excluded pushing, shell commands from an allowlist, and a verification tool. Users supplied relevant context in prompts; code-search and documentation tools were withheld 5. The verification tool selected checks from repository contents, and failure prevented a pull request from being opened. The agent could choose how to implement a change within those bounds, but its own assessment could not waive the required checks. After unwanted changes such as disabled tests, Spotify added an LLM judge that compared the diff with the original request. In December 2025, the company reported vetoes in about a quarter of thousands of sessions, with agents correcting their work after about half of those vetoes 6.6. Max Charas and Marc Bruggmann, “Background Coding Agents: Predictable Results Through Strong Feedback Loops (Honk, Part 3),” Spotify Engineering, December 9, 2025, https://engineering.atspotify.com/2025/12/feedback-loops-background-coding-agents-part-3.

A March 2026 report of Spotify's QCon talk describes a further separation between the agent runtime and verification runtime, with pull requests created only after CI checks. It also reports that the judge sometimes rejected valid changes and was later removed as foundation models improved and verification instructions in prompts proved sufficient for its role 7.7. Daniel Curtis, “QCon London 2026: Rewriting All of Spotify’s Code Base, All the Time,” InfoQ, March 18, 2026, https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/03/spotify-honk-rewrite. This is a secondary account of the talk, and it does not imply that the required checks or review disappeared. The sequence shows why maintaining a control includes reassessing both the failures it catches and the valid work it rejects. An engineering response to one generation of agent behavior need not remain economical unchanged.

The inherited process also supports different admission decisions for different producers. Spotify reports more than 2.5 million automated maintenance pull requests, most automatically merged; that cumulative figure chiefly describes the deterministic fleet machinery, not agent-authored work 8.8. Niklas Gustavsson, “Coding Is No Longer the Constraint: Scaling Developer Experience to Teams and Agents at Spotify,” Spotify Engineering, June 3, 2026, https://engineering.atspotify.com/2026/6/code-with-claude-coding-is-no-longer-the-constraint. The QCon account says agent-authored changes still required human review 7. People define migration scope and maintain prompts as tested, version-controlled artifacts. They can also reserve particular decisions: in one migration, the agent was instructed to leave fields unchanged and annotate them whenever a judgment call was needed 59.9. Devon Edwards Joseph, “Background Coding Agents: Supercharging Downstream Consumer Dataset Migrations,” Spotify Engineering, April 22, 2026, https://engineering.atspotify.com/2026/4/background-coding-agents-dataset-migrations-honk-part-4. Delegation therefore varies within the production process rather than being one decision to automate the whole line.

Spotify's later measurements make the limits of that process visible. Its refined rework measure did not rise during the AI ramp-up, while code complexity and pull-request size did; the company kept its thresholds unchanged. Incident retrospectives found no material direct contribution from AI-authored code, yet change volume had grown faster than some verification controls could adapt. One automated dependency upgrade passed its checks and still failed in production 10.10. Tyson Singer, “AI Changed How Spotify Builds. What We Learned (and Fixed) About Quality at Higher Velocity,” Spotify Engineering, September 16, 2026, https://engineering.atspotify.com/2026/9/ai-changed-how-spotify-builds-what-we-learned-and-fixed-about-quality-at-higher-velocity. These observations concern different properties and should not be collapsed into a single quality score. Producing more changes has exposed a capacity problem as well as a check-coverage problem.

docs.title: 5.4.3 Shopify
docs.text:
Shopify's case concerns how work performed in one session becomes knowledge available to later sessions. River, its internal agent, operates in Slack and refuses direct messages. An employee starts work by mentioning it in a channel, leaving a public transcript that colleagues can inspect 11.11. Javier Moreno and Burke Libbey, “Under the River,” Shopify Engineering, May 28, 2026, https://shopify.engineering/under-the-river. This makes the work and its difficulties observable beyond the person who initiated it. It does not ensure that every failure attracts attention, but it provides a shared record from which people can identify missing knowledge instead of depending entirely on a later report.

People use that record to change what later agents receive. They watch River work, identify what it should have known, and add a skill, revise an AGENTS.md file, or record another reusable instruction in the monorepo 11. These artifacts sit alongside code, conventions, intent documents, and runbooks. River's reported merge rate rose from 36 to 77 percent over two months while its foundation model stayed the same 12.12. Tobi Lütke, “Learning on the Shop Floor,” May 9, 2026, https://x.com/tobi/article/2053121182044451016. The improvement occurred with the foundation model unchanged, as people deliberately preserved lessons for later work. The report does not isolate the contribution of those changes. Unlike DocAble's one-engineer account, this mechanism distributes observation and knowledge maintenance across an organization.

The shared knowledge also requires maintenance. Instruction files apply through the monorepo's directory hierarchy, while different agent tools read different files. Shopify describes divergence between those conventions: a directory can contain instructions for one tool and omit the corresponding file for another, so engineers working on the same code supply different context to their agents 1314.13. Tobi Lütke, “Split Brain Problems When Different Team Members Use Different Tools,” X, August 25, 2026, https://x.com/tobi/status/2092259436538495186.14. Amanda Caswell, “Shopify’s CEO Threatened to Ban Claude Code. Anthropic Had Already Closed the Feature Request,” The New Stack, August 25, 2026, https://thenewstack.io/shopify-claude-code-agentsmd/. Automation repairs that drift. Recording a lesson has therefore created another engineering artifact whose continued value depends on keeping it available and consistent. The cost follows from the mechanism that makes the knowledge reusable.

A security-workflow account shows why recording an instruction may be insufficient. River violated a prompt-stated enumeration requirement and acknowledged the omission in its report. Shopify's response was to require rules governing vulnerability closure to be enforced in code. The same account describes draft-only agent output, merge authority held by the engineers responsible for the affected code, a merge queue requiring fresh evidence, and a post-merge check that the default branch contains the fix. Use of that queue rose from about 10 to 80 percent 15.15. Erin Son and Kaiyi Li, “How River Takes Security Work from a Fix to Merge,” Shopify Engineering, September 2, 2026, https://shopify.engineering/river-vulnerability-remediation. That measures adoption of the queue, not the rate at which vulnerabilities escaped. The controls are described for security work; the account does not establish what evidence ordinary River pull requests must carry or how often they fail in production.

docs.title: 5.4.4 Uber
docs.text:
Uber treats the factory itself as something to measure and improve. Its managed agents perform work such as CI repair, review, alert triage, and maintenance; operational signals and schedules can initiate tasks as well as people 16.16. Uday Kiran Medisetty and Adam Huda, “Agentic SDLC at Uber — Building Blocks for Uber’s Software Factory,” AI Engineer World’s Fair, 2026, https://ai.engineer/talks/17-YSUHo6Lk-agentic-sdlc-at-uber-building-blocks-ubers. The relevant question is what it costs to complete useful work through that arrangement. A token reduction, a cheaper foundation model, and a shorter review queue affect different parts of the answer.

Uber adjusts context delivery, tool access, and coordination. Moving deterministic orchestration from repeated agent turns into executable code reportedly cut token use by more than half for common workflows and by more than 90 percent for bulk cases. Real workloads become benchmarks, foundation models are selected against cost and reliability, and managed agents are evaluated in units such as cost per merged pull request, review, alert, or cleanup 1716.17. Uday Kiran Medisetty, “Running a Software Factory Efficiently at Uber Scale,” Uber Engineering, 2026, https://www.uber.com/us/en/blog/efficient-software-factory/. Those units connect resource use to an outcome rather than counting agent activity alone. They also make the surrounding engineering choices visible: some work is cheaper when executed directly than when repeatedly reconstructed through model interactions.

Evaluation begins inside the producing agent's loop, with static-analysis repair, simulator screenshots compared with design specifications, and staging integration. The resulting pull request carries a table of checks and evidence assembled by that agent. The account does not say that independent machinery re-derives every entry 16. Additional model-based review, CI, and human approval follow. Uber describes a possible move toward partial automatic approval, but does not publish the qualifying evidence or eligibility criteria 18.18. Will Bond and Ameya Ketkar, “Building uReview, Uber’s Multi-Agent Code Review Engine,” AI Engineer World’s Fair, 2026, https://ai.engineer/talks/EL123UNokkI-building-ureview-ubers-multi-agent-code-review. The reported review layers therefore tell us how evaluation is arranged without establishing the assurance of every proposed change.

Reviewer attention has its own capacity limit. Time to first review rose from three hours in 2024 to nine in 2026 as volume and change size grew 18. Uber schedules maintenance jobs on Sunday to use spare CI capacity, but separately caps the diffs engineers will face on Monday 16. This is a concrete process-design decision: spare compute can produce more work than the next human stage can absorb. The organization also tracks revert rate, F1, and time to recovery alongside production cost, although the cited accounts do not publish a complete outcome series.

docs.title: 5.4.5 Amazon
docs.text:
Kiro supplies a reusable workflow for making intent explicit before implementation. A feature specification records user stories and acceptance criteria, develops an architectural design, and divides implementation into tasks that engineers can review 19.19. Kiro, “Specs,” Kiro Documentation, 2026, https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/. In MAGE's vocabulary, these requirements and design artifacts are engineering models. DocAble arranged related work through project-specific work orders and design documents; Kiro makes a specification workflow part of the harness. Adopting it still leaves a team responsible for the content of those artifacts and their connection to its system.

The workflow can connect specifications to evidence and enforcement. Kiro's IDE can extract properties from requirements and generate property-based tests, whose execution is optional by default and whose results are explicitly distinguished from proof 20.20. Kiro, “Correctness with Property-based tests,” Kiro Documentation, 2026, https://kiro.dev/docs/specs/correctness/. Configured hooks can run checks after edits or block tool calls when preconditions fail 21.21. Kiro, “Hooks,” Kiro Documentation, 2026, https://kiro.dev/docs/hooks/. Engineers must decide which properties matter, whether the tests express them correctly, and where failure should prevent work from proceeding. A supplied workflow makes these connections possible; its presence does not establish that a particular project enabled them.

Amazon's Bedrock account makes some of that adopting-team work visible. Six senior engineers rebuilt part of the inference engine in 76 days, using small modules, reviewable commit-sized tasks, focused operational tools, tests, end-to-end canaries, and senior inspection of generated code 22.22. Kiro, “Six engineers completed a 30-person project in 76 days,” Amazon Web Services, accessed November 6, 2026, https://kiro.dev/case-studies/bedrock/. AWS reports a twentyfold increase in normalized commit velocity, from two to forty commits per developer per week 23.23. Swami Sivasubramanian, “How frontier teams are reinventing AI-native development,” Amazon Web Services, June 10, 2026, https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/how-frontier-teams-are-reinventing-ai-native-development/. That is a production-activity measure. It does not establish defect reduction or separate Kiro's contribution from team selection and workflow redesign.

Amazon also reports experiments on improving Kiro itself. Kiro-trace proposes prompt or tool changes from recorded runs. A separate deterministic gate screens targeted failures, checks regression assertions, and compares candidates with an unchanged control on the full benchmark. It requires gains on selected tasks without losses beyond a specified margin elsewhere; a person decides whether to merge. One apparent improvement was rejected after it proved to be a lucky run. Evaluation mistakes became checks, and confirmed fixes add regression assertions 24.24. Myeongsoo Kim et al., “How Kiro fixes itself, and how we keep the fixes honest,” Kiro, October 20, 2026, https://kiro.dev/blog/how-kiro-fixes-itself/. These internal experiments illustrate the same engineering problem at another level: improving the fabricator requires evidence about the improvement and maintenance of the machinery that evaluates it.

docs.title: 5.4.6 GitLab
docs.text:
GitLab illustrates how an integrated development workflow can bring existing organizational knowledge and controls to agent work. Repository instructions, chat rules, review skills, CI configuration, and workflow definitions supply different kinds of context 25.25. GitLab, “Customize GitLab Duo Agent Platform,” GitLab Documentation, 2026, https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/customize/. The documented security-review flow can report findings but cannot approve a change 26.26. GitLab, “Security Review Flow,” GitLab Documentation, 2026, https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/flows/foundational_flows/security_review/. For human-triggered flows running on runners, composite identity limits access to the intersection of the service account’s and triggering user’s privileges 27.27. GitLab, “Composite Identity,” GitLab Documentation, n.d., https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/composite_identity/. Tool-governance rules can also constrain actions; project rules may tighten but not loosen a group rule 28.28. GitLab, “Agent Tool Governance,” GitLab Documentation, n.d., https://docs.gitlab.com/user/ai-governance/tool-governance/. These are distinct functions: instructions inform the work, permissions restrict actions, and the approval boundary reserves a consequential decision.

GitLab's internal playbook also makes acceptance depend on the surrounding pipeline. Its failing-test-first practice is backed by a CI job that fails when the test count decreases unless an explicit bypass label is present, addressing agents that remove tests to obtain a passing result 29.29. GitLab, “AI-Assisted Development Playbook,” GitLab Handbook, 2026, https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/workflow/ai-assisted-development/. A test-count check cannot establish that the remaining tests express the right requirements. It does make one recurring way of evading them consequential at admission.

docs.title: 5.4.7 What the Factories Share, and Where They Differ
docs.text:
The four factory questions reveal different arrangements rather than a common maturity sequence. The organizations differ in where they place engineering judgment, what they permit agents to decide, and which decisions remain with people or independent controls. Their measurements answer different questions: override frequency, veto and correction rates, merge rate, token cost, review delay, and engineering-health indicators cannot be combined into a single ranking of factory effectiveness.

One important difference is where the authority to accept work resides. Cloudflare distinguishes standards that advise reviewers from those whose violations can block a merge, while retaining a recorded human override 2. Spotify inserted agents into an existing production process but kept required verification and, in the reported configuration, human review of agent-authored changes 57. Shopify’s security workflow reserves merge authority to the engineers responsible for the affected code 15; GitLab’s documented security-review flow can report findings but cannot approve a change 26. These arrangements reserve admission authority in different ways, but none treats the producing agent’s claim of completion as sufficient authority to admit consequential changes. Process design determines who or what may make the admission decision; tolerance and its evidence determine what that decision must establish.

Two recurring costs cut across those arrangements. The first is supervisory capacity. Uber's Sunday maintenance schedule would be incomplete without its separate limit on Monday's review load. Spotify's ability to generate more changes exposed limits in verification even when its measured rework did not rise. A factory therefore has to organize evaluation and admission alongside realization. Increasing the rate of one stage can shift delay or risk to another; the production system must be assessed through the work it can accept and sustain.

The second cost is maintaining what later work inherits. Shopify repairs divergent instructions; Cloudflare revises policy representations and moves suitable checks earlier; Kiro's improvement experiments acquire new regression assertions. Each preserved lesson can reduce future reconstruction or repeated judgment, but the resulting artifact must remain connected to the work it governs. This is the carrying-cost question from §5.1 in operational form. Improvements in foundation models can also change that calculation, as Spotify's retired judge illustrates; Shopify's rising merge rate with an unchanged model shows that the surrounding factory can improve independently.

docs.title: §5.5 · Coda: Engineering the Factory
docs.text:
Chapter 5 — DocAble Among Other Software Factories  ::  §5.5§5.5 Coda: Engineering the Factory

Process design and tolerance help explain the different arrangements observed in this chapter (Figure 5.1-1). DocAble's accessibility obligations and one-engineer staffing made explicit requirements and automated rejection especially valuable: I had little inherited human process to accommodate and no spare reviewers for every implementation decision. Coordinating agents still required work orders, scheduling, and completion checks. In an established organization, the factory must also fit existing teams, knowledge, and authority. Both settings require judgments about which properties to preserve and how to organize work around them. A more capable agent may change the process needed to produce a system without changing its memory bound or deployment restriction. Engineers can leave implementation choices open within those bounds, while weighing the cost of supervision against the cost of maintaining the representations and checks that support it.

Organizations need not begin with fully autonomous implementation. Some use agents to review pull requests or propose changes that people still inspect. Others allow agents to implement and validate changes before routing selected decisions to human reviewers. These arrangements delegate different amounts of work and authority, but they face the same engineering questions: what must remain true, what evidence establishes it, and which decisions require human approval? MAGE applies to those questions even when most implementation remains under direct human supervision.

Capability also does not settle accountability. Organizations delegate consequential judgment to people partly through incentives and responsibility, including professional obligations and institutional consequences 1.1. James G. March and Herbert A. Simon, Organizations (Wiley, 1958). An agent does not bear those responsibilities or respond to those incentives in the same way a human engineer does. Its instructions and permissions can be changed, and its work can be stopped, but those actions do not transfer human accountability to it. Engineering authority must therefore decide which judgments to delegate, what evidence to require, and which obligations need controls. Chapter 6 examines the costs and effects of these choices: how representation and independent evaluation change the economics of realization, and how experience changes the engineering structures worth maintaining.
