docs.title: §6.1 · From Production to Cumulative Progress
docs.text:
Chapter 6 — The Theory  ::  §6.1§6.1 From Production to Cumulative Progress

Agentic engineering must preserve engineering intent while delegating implementation. Modeling makes that intent available for reasoning; Alignment supplies independent evidence and enforcement. Chapter 5 examined the software factory as a whole. We now focus on its governed engineering environment (GEE): the reusable engineering structure through which people and agents direct, evaluate, and control implementation. Three questions organize the theory, moving from individual production to engineering over time (Table 6.1-1).

Table 6.1-1. Three perspectives on engineering progress.Perspective and engineering questionFaithful production. Did the representation capture the intended obligations, and did the implementation fulfill them?Economical production. What did correct, admitted delivery cost, including failed attempts and upkeep?Cumulative progress. How does today’s work change the environment inherited by later engineering?

docs.title: 6.1.1 What Makes Production Faithful?
docs.text:
Recall the entitlement failure from Chapter 2. The client based its upload decision on a finite-credit total, ignoring a separate unlimited-status flag. That scalar could not distinguish exhausted finite credit from unlimited access. An implementation could faithfully compare the scalar with the upload cost and still make the wrong admission decision. The representation used for the decision had omitted a consequential distinction available elsewhere in the system.

This illustrates two ways delegated implementation can fail. The engineer may encode the wrong obligations, or the agent may fail to fulfill correctly encoded obligations. Let E mean that the encoding captures the consequential intent and F that the resulting artifact fulfills the encoded obligations. For a representation R, the probability of both is

pR=P(E∩F∣R)=P(E∣R)⏟Encoding: engineers statewhat must holdP(F∣E,R)⏟Realization: agents fulfillthose obligations

This encoding–realization decomposition applies the probability chain rule to separate two engineering questions: whether the representation captures the intended obligations, and whether the resulting artifact fulfills them.** In general, the probability that two events A and B both occur is the probability of A multiplied by the probability of B given A: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B∣A). This is the probability chain rule; it does not require the events to be independent. Here we apply the same identity conditional on the representation R, with A=E (correct encoding) and B=F (fulfillment), yielding P(E∩F∣R)=P(E∣R)P(F∣E,R). The distinction lets us examine how representations, agent capabilities, and production processes affect faithful realization.

Figure 6.1-1 distinguishes encoding from realization within the software factory. The encoded property also defines which realizations are acceptable, allowing the result to be evaluated independently of the agent that produced it.

Probability in the software factory Engineering intent is encoded as a property and fulfilled through a fabricator to produce a realization. The encoded property also supplies tolerance for possible realizations; independent measurement informs admission or rejection. SOFTWARE FACTORY PROCESS DESIGN: how production proceeds PRODUCTION PROCESS Engineering intent Encoded property Fabricator Realization P(E) correct encoding P(F | E) fulfill encoded obligations Engineers authorize intent. Agents interpret, implement, and correct. Supplies the tolerance Measurement: tests, PBT, analysis, simulation, human judgment POSSIBLE REALIZATIONS Acceptable region TOLERANCE acceptable product variation within tolerance outside tolerance Admitted change Revise / reject Figure 6.1-1. Probability in the software factory. Engineers encode consequential intent; agents fulfill the encoded obligations. The two probability terms condition on representation R, omitted for legibility. The encoded property also defines the acceptable region for realizations, allowing independent evidence to inform admission or rejection.

The two terms distinguish failures in what the agent was asked to produce from failures in producing it. Holding the task population and production setup fixed, R names the representation choice; probabilities range over the encodings and realizations produced through it. The first question is whether the representation captures the consequential intent the engineer authorizes. The second is whether the resulting artifact fulfills those obligations.

Realization includes interpretation, planning, implementation, and correction. An agent may initially misunderstand an obligation and then correct its work after a check or review exposes the error. Conversely, it may infer an obligation that the encoding omitted. The event E∩F therefore describes faithful production through the representation; observed task correctness must be assessed separately.

The first term is easy to overlook in an agentic setting. A structured model may help a machine interpret intent more reliably than prose, and it can also help the engineer express the intended property correctly in the first place. Different representations make different distinctions visible, force different decisions to be made explicitly, and make omissions easier or harder to notice. A representation can therefore improve P(E∣R) even if it leaves P(F∣E,R) unchanged. This is one reason Modeling is an engineering activity rather than merely a technique for supplying context to an agent.

Representation is not the only route to that term. A realization that misses the engineer's meaning can provide evidence about the encoding, although the failure may instead lie in realization. The comprehension amplification of §4.1 can help the engineer diagnose the cause and revise the encoding when needed. In that way, capable agents can contribute indirectly to P(E∣R).

Process design changes the conditions under which agents realize intent: context, tools, decomposition, routing, permissions, and other features of the harness can change P(F∣E,R), its cost, or both. A better agent can improve the same term. Explicit tolerances help engineers state the intended property and make it available for independent evaluation. Tests, analysis, measurement, or human judgment can assess whether a realization falls within that tolerance. Where the evidence supports enforcement, a gate can reject work that violates the obligation. This separates helping production succeed from deciding whether its result should be admitted.

A stronger reasoner can sometimes recover meaning that a weaker one misses. A terse requirement may be enough for an agent that knows the domain and can inspect the surrounding system. Better retrieval, tools, and feedback can also help it discover what the representation leaves implicit. These possibilities affect the cost and reliability of realization; they are reasons to compare richer representations with more capable inference rather than assume that either must win.

The entitlement failure also shows the limit of inference from an inadequate representation. A reasoner using only the finite-credit total could not recover the distinction between exhausted credit and unlimited access. Better reasoning could help only by revisiting the decision representation or consulting the existing unlimited-status signal.

Even perfectly reliable realization cannot, by itself, establish that the encoded obligations were right. Holding encoding quality fixed, as conditional realization approaches certainty, faithful production approaches P(E∣R). The practical consequence is to examine the encoding when better agents keep faithfully producing the wrong thing.

The appropriate degree of specification depends on the work. Some transformations leave little useful freedom, and the cost of ambiguity may outweigh any benefit from delegation. Elsewhere, specifying nearly every realization decision in advance recreates much of the specification cost discussed in Chapter 5. It also sacrifices a major advantage of commodity intelligence: agents can explore implementation choices that engineers need not make themselves. The engineer can specify consequential obligations, leave other choices open, and let the agent find a satisfactory realization. The economic value of Modeling and Alignment therefore depends partly on how much useful freedom the environment can preserve while maintaining adequate control.

docs.title: 6.1.2 What Makes Production Economical?
docs.text:
The engineering question is what useful delivery costs. A cheap attempt may leave an engineer with hours of repair; an expensive model may support hundreds of later changes. To compare those arrangements, we need to count the work that went into delivery, including the work that never produced an acceptable result.

For N requested changes, let DN count the changes independently verified as correct and admitted within a declared evaluation horizon. Each requested change can include several attempts. The total cost and the cost per correct admitted change are

CN=Cbuild+∑i=1N(Crun,i+Ccarry,i),cN=CNDN,DN>0.

Construction covers the initial investment in the engineering environment. Running costs include production, checking, human review, and repair across all attempts; carrying costs cover the upkeep needed to keep the environment useful. A failed or abandoned task still contributes its costs to the numerator. If nothing correct is delivered, report that result and the expenditure rather than assigning a cost per delivery. Shared costs need an explicit allocation, and human effort and machine expenditure need declared valuations before they can be added. Elapsed time remains a separate outcome.

This accounting does not assume that tasks cost the same, that retries are independent, or that the environment stands still. It does require comparable work. An engineering process that accepts only easy changes may have an attractive cN while leaving important requests unfinished. Comparisons should therefore hold the requested work and evaluation horizon fixed, report what was delivered and left unresolved, and measure escaped failures and false rejection alongside cost. Repeated attempts often change the specification, tools, or next plan; observed delivery costs can count that learning without pretending that every retry starts over under identical conditions.

Admission adds the cost of gathering evidence and acting on it. A gate can provide the same protection while one representation causes agents to collide with it much more often than another. Each rejected candidate may require further inference, diagnosis, or human attention. These costs belong in Crun,i, whether the rejection catches a real defect or mistakenly turns away correct work.

Carrying cost completes the comparison. The factories in Chapter 5 preserve engineering knowledge in models, instructions, policies, skills, tests, and context systems. All require some effort to remain useful as the software changes. A structured model earns its construction and upkeep when it enables valuable work or reduces later reconstruction, realization, failure, or assurance costs enough over its useful life. For a simple or infrequent task, a natural-language description may already do the job at very little cost.

The alternative is often to buy inference when the question arises. A capable agent may reconstruct a dependency from source cheaply enough that a maintained graph would not repay its cost. For another task family, reconstructing that same dependency hundreds of times may be much more expensive than keeping it explicit. The comparison depends on the work, the available reasoner, the assurance required, and the expected reuse of the representation. A model can also repay its cost in a single use when the question is sufficiently consequential.

This gives packaged agent systems a place in the theory. A capable reasoner and generic supervisory machinery may economically replace some structure that a weaker reasoner would need. How much can they replace, and for which obligations? We can compare what those arrangements deliver, what escapes their assurance, and what they cost, while also asking what engineering knowledge survives for the next task.

This accounting makes alternative engineering arrangements comparable, but it does not tell us which arrangement to choose. A stronger foundation model may reduce the need for explicit representations; a better representation may let a cheaper foundation model perform the same work. A gate may reduce escaped failures while increasing rejection and repair costs. The engineering problem is to choose among these arrangements under requirements for correct delivery, acceptable risk, and human attention. The cheapest implementation attempt need not be the cheapest way to deliver acceptable work.

Human attention is part of this accounting. A production system that generates changes cheaply but requires an expert to reconstruct each one has moved work onto that expert. The relevant cost includes the time needed to interpret the evidence, diagnose failures, and decide whether the result is acceptable. The following inset explains why increasing output can make this cost decisive.

HUMAN FACTORS

Inset — Human Attention Is Not a Free Control

Moving work from human execution to machine execution does not eliminate the cost of human attention if people must inspect the resulting stream. Software engineering has long relied on one engineer reviewing another's work, but code review is imperfect. Studies document the improvements reviewers prompt and associate review coverage and participation with post-release quality 12.1. Moritz Beller et al., “Modern Code Reviews in Open-Source Projects: Which Problems Do They Fix?” Proceedings of the 11th Working Conference on Mining Software Repositories, 2014, 202–11, https://doi.org/10.1145/2597073.2597082.2. Shane McIntosh et al., “The Impact of Code Review Coverage and Code Review Participation on Software Quality: A Case Study of the Qt, VTK, and ITK Projects,” Proceedings of the 11th Working Conference on Mining Software Repositories, 2014, 192–201, https://doi.org/10.1145/2597073.2597076. At Microsoft, reviews spanning more files had a lower proportion of useful feedback, and developers reported that such reviews required more time and effort 3.3. Amiangshu Bosu et al., “Characteristics of Useful Code Reviews: An Empirical Study at Microsoft,” Proceedings of the 12th Working Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR), 2015, 146–56, https://doi.org/10.1109/MSR.2015.21. As agents assume more implementation work, software engineering faces a problem familiar to industries that automated earlier. Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation described how automation can leave human operators responsible for monitoring rare failures and intervening when something goes wrong 4.4. Lisanne Bainbridge, “Ironies of Automation,” Automatica 19, no. 6 (1983): 775–79, https://doi.org/10.1016/0005-1098(83)90046-8.

As agentic output grows, proportional human inspection becomes a bottleneck. Where recurring obligations can be represented explicitly and checked or enforced adequately, reusable mechanisms can reduce the inspection required for each change. Engineers can then concentrate their attention on ambiguous evidence, novel failures, tradeoffs, exceptions, and decisions whose consequences require expert judgment. Human attention is an engineering resource.

The return on an engineering environment depends on the value of the work it enables and its cost over time. Product work may deliver new capabilities, security work may retire risks, and reliability work may prevent failures or shorten recovery. The environment also incurs costs between production episodes as its models, controls, and other assets require maintenance. Some structures remain useful for years with little attention; others lose fit quickly.

docs.title: 6.1.3 What Makes Progress Cumulative?
docs.text:
Choosing the least costly arrangement for the next change is not necessarily the best decision for the next hundred changes. A model, validator, or procedure may cost more to construct than the immediate task justifies, yet repay that investment through later work. Conversely, a locally inexpensive change can introduce architectural irregularity or obscure information that subsequent engineers and agents must reconstruct.

Winters et al. characterize software engineering as “programming integrated over time”: software is developed, modified, and maintained as both the system and its environment change 5.5. Titus Winters et al., Software Engineering at Google: Lessons Learned from Programming Over Time (O’Reilly Media, 2020). Each realization therefore changes the architecture, conventions, representations, tests, and other structure inherited by subsequent work. The lifecycle account totals these costs, but does not yet explain how earlier work changes the conditions for later production. We need to represent that inheritance explicitly.

Let Ti be the task at step i, M the foundation model, and Gi the governed engineering environment inherited at that step. The GEE includes the task-relevant representations, tools, procedures, and controls available to direct and evaluate the work. Let ai denote the work performed during the episode and the changes it leaves behind:

pi=p(Ti,M,Gi),Gi+1=f(Gi,ai).

Here pi is the probability of faithful production for task Ti, extending the earlier encoding–realization account to include the inherited environment. The second relation describes how the episode can change that environment. A failed attempt may leave a useful diagnosis or a new control even when it produces no admitted change. Holding the foundation model fixed lets us examine how changes to the GEE affect subsequent work; over a longer sequence, the foundation model can change as well. These are schematic relationships describing inheritance, not calibrated laws or a claim that every episode improves the environment.

This coupling creates path dependence. A locally acceptable change can increase architectural irregularity, obscure structure, or introduce inconsistent conventions, leaving later agents a worse reasoning surface. A change that improves representations, architecture, constraints, or other engineering capital can instead make later work easier to reason about and govern.

Agentic capacity and the GEE jointly shape what a software factory can accomplish, but they play different roles. Work orders specify the intended changes; foundation-model capability, concurrency, and implementation speed determine the available agentic capacity. The GEE supplies the representations, procedures, evidence, and controls through which that capacity is directed and governed. Figure 6.1-2 relates these inputs to attempted work and realized performance, then shows how experience can change the environment inherited by later work.

The MAGE Dynamic Model Prior knowledge seeds the governed engineering environment. Work orders, agentic capacity and the environment shape attempted work and its outcomes. Observed problems can lead to diagnosis and adaptation. Corrective feedback revises the inherited environment, which may enable larger tasks and greater concurrency. Prior engineering knowledge standards, requirements, existing assets, prior lessons seeds Governed engineering environment 𝒢 representation · coverage · coherence · economy Expanding task frontier may enable larger tasks and greater concurrency Work orders task, intent, acceptance criteria Attempted work changes undertaken, task frontier Agentic capacity model capability, concurrency, implementation speed specify intended work enables execution produces Realized performance durable throughput, defect escape, human attention provides evidence Experience and adaptation Observed problems churn, recurring failures, interventions, control friction Diagnosis local defect? structural gap? inadequate enforcement? Governance adaptation convert, reconcile, retire Corrective feedback revises inherited structure Figure 6.1-2. The MAGE Dynamic Model. Prior engineering knowledge seeds the governed engineering environment (GEE). Work orders specify intended changes, agentic capacity enables their implementation, and the GEE governs attempted work. Observed problems can prompt diagnosis and governance adaptation, revising the environment inherited by later work. An improved GEE may also support more ambitious tasks, exposing new demands on its representations and controls.

The corrective feedback path begins when attempted work exposes recurring failures, escaped defects, repeated human intervention, or friction from existing controls. Engineers diagnose whether the problem is local to an implementation or reflects a deficiency in the GEE. A structural problem may warrant a new representation, stronger enforcement, reconciliation of conflicting mechanisms, or retirement of an obsolete control. Improving the GEE’s fit may require removing machinery rather than adding it. When such changes address the underlying cause, subsequent work can avoid repeating the same failure. Without diagnosis and authority to revise the shared environment, the organization may instead repeat local repairs indefinitely.

The expanding task frontier is a related effect. As the GEE becomes better suited to existing work, engineers may attempt larger changes, increase concurrency, or undertake work previously too expensive to supervise. A GEE that supports ordinary changes may make cross-service migrations practical, exposing obligations and failure classes that simpler work never encountered. Corrective feedback can improve the environment’s fit to current work; an expanding task frontier changes the work against which that fit is judged. Neither effect guarantees improvement.

The GEE need not begin empty. Existing standards, requirements, architecture descriptions, tests, and lessons from other projects can provide useful structure before local experience reveals a gap.

More machinery does not mean a better GEE. Ten thousand lines of stale checks are worse than one hundred lines that govern the obligations that matter. The four properties identified in Figure 6.1-2 provide ways to assess that fit:

  1. Useful representations. The information needed for the work is explicit at an appropriate level of abstraction.
  1. Adequate coverage. Important obligations have appropriate evidence and enforcement.
  1. Coherence. Models and mechanisms reinforce one another rather than contradicting or needlessly duplicating.
  1. Economy. Their future value justifies their maintenance, friction, and context cost.

Coverage does not require mechanizing every obligation. Some belong in a compiler rule or gate; others require statistical evidence, semantic evaluation, or human judgment. A strong GEE makes clear where judgment belongs and where repeatedly buying the same judgment is wasteful.

These properties describe different ways a GEE can support the work, rather than stages of a maturity model 6.6. Terry B. Bollinger and Clement L. McGowan, “A Critical Look at Software Capability Evaluations,” IEEE Software 8, no. 4 (1991): 25–41, https://doi.org/10.1109/52.300034. The appropriate investment depends on what is limiting progress. Repeated reconstruction of important state suggests a representation problem; escaped failures call for examining evidence and enforcement. When existing controls impose more friction than protection, reconciliation or retirement may improve the GEE more than adding another mechanism.

A theory of agentic engineering should distinguish activity from progress. Durable throughput is useful system progress that survives rework, integration, and operation. Defect escape records consequential failures that reach later lifecycle stages or production. Human-attention burden measures the scarce engineering judgment consumed per unit of durable progress. Table 6.1-2 gives candidate observables; §6.4 returns to how comparisons can distinguish the effects of representation, enforcement, and inherited capital.

Table 6.1-2. Outcomes of the theory. Raw implementation activity is an input. The theory is interested in how much survives as durable progress, what failures escape, and how much scarce human judgment that progress consumes.OutcomeWhat it measuresCandidate observablesDurable throughputRaw implementation converted into lasting system progresslanded changes net of rework; churn share; the slope of sustained throughputDefect escapeRelevant failures reaching later lifecycle stages or productionescaped-defect rate; reopen rate; silent-corruption escapeHuman-attention burdenHuman judgment required per unit of durable outputinterventions per landed change; review time; conversion effort

Several easy-to-count quantities measure activity or investment rather than outcome: commits, lines changed, control files, model-sync events, and support ratio. They can help explain what an environment is doing; they do not establish that it is producing a return.†† The activity-versus-outcome gap also appears in industry data. LinearB's 2026 benchmark covers 83,000 developers across 253 organizations and compares merge rates from June 2025 to May 2026 7.7. LinearB, “The Engineering Productivity Gap: How Elite AI Teams Are Pulling Away from the Rest,” LinearB, 2026, https://linearb.io/resources/ai-engineering-productivity-gap. Among the heaviest AI users, merge rates roughly doubled while pull-request yield—the share of opened requests merged within 30 days—fell. The association does not establish that AI caused either change, and neither measure establishes durable progress. An industry analyst reads the same period as rising AI spend without proportionate shipping velocity, the difficulty having moved from comprehension to confidence 8.8. Jennifer Riggins, “AI Coding Got Faster. Why Didn’t Engineering?” The New Stack, August 9, 2026, https://thenewstack.io/ai-productivity-measurement-gap/.

None of these descriptions supplies a measured effect size. Together they support a more focused question: under what conditions do representations, independent enforcement, and inherited engineering judgment turn additional agentic capacity into useful progress? The next section develops four propositions that evidence could challenge.

docs.title: §6.2 · What the Theory Predicts
docs.text:
Chapter 6 — The Theory  ::  §6.2§6.2 What the Theory Predicts

The theory makes four connected propositions. A useful representation can change the work required to reason about a system. It can also make selected obligations available for independent enforcement. When the resulting knowledge and mechanisms remain useful, later work inherits engineering capacity. Additional agentic capacity then acts through that inherited environment, amplifying its fit or exposing its inadequacy.

These are theoretical relationships, informed by the cases rather than established as general findings. Each needs a mechanism, conditions under which it should matter, and a way evidence could show it to be wrong. §6.4 develops a compact set of comparisons for that purpose.

docs.title: 6.2.1 P1: Representation Leverage
docs.text:
Trustworthy, task-relevant representations can reduce reconstruction and extend the work that humans and agents can complete at a given quality and resource budget. They do so by exposing the distinctions and relationships needed for the task while suppressing implementation detail that would otherwise have to be reconstructed. The benefit depends on what the representation preserves, how it is used, and what it costs to build and maintain.

DocAble encountered this problem when representing large documents for remediation. One document produced roughly 590,000 tokens of reasoning representation against a 272,000-token context window. A more costly foundation model with a larger context window was one possible response. Another was to change the representation: windowing and whole-document compression reduced the information required for each judgment. The engineering choice was not simply how much context to purchase, but how much reasoning the representation could save.

Research on external representations has long shown that how information is organized changes the work required to reason with it 12.1. Jill H. Larkin and Herbert A. Simon, “Why a Diagram Is (Sometimes) Worth Ten Thousand Words,” Cognitive Science 11, no. 1 (1987): 65–100, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1551-6708.1987.tb00863.x.2. Jiajie Zhang and Donald A. Norman, “Representations in Distributed Cognitive Tasks,” Cognitive Science 18, no. 1 (1994): 87–122, https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1801_3. Models apply that principle to engineering questions by exposing consequential structure directly. A dependency graph, for example, can make permitted service relationships available without requiring an engineer or agent to reconstruct them from scattered implementation details.

This can shorten the reasoning path, rather than merely make each step cheaper. The environment preserves some work that would otherwise be repeated before the engineering question could even be addressed. State machines expose transitions; contracts expose obligations; assurance arguments relate claims to evidence. Such representations may bring a demanding task within the human-agent system’s effective reasoning horizon, or make an already tractable task cheaper. They cannot provide distinctions they omit, and an agent still has to use the representation appropriately.

Once a model exists, maintenance becomes a second problem. “Keep the model equal to the code” is too crude. A model of permitted dependencies should disagree with code that violates them. A requirements model may intentionally describe an intended state the current implementation has not reached. The engineering problem is to state and maintain the correspondence each model claims—for architecture, behavior, process, invariants, lineage, or other views—cheaply enough to expose meaningful divergence near the change that created it.

A synchronized model can still be useless for the question at hand. Test suites provide the familiar warning: an oracle may faithfully reproduce implementation behavior while failing to express the requirement.** Automation that optimizes against a visible oracle can satisfy that oracle while violating properties it does not check 4.4. Edward K. Smith et al., “Is the Cure Worse Than the Disease? Overfitting in Automated Program Repair,” Proceedings of the 2015 10th Joint Meeting on Foundations of Software Engineering (ESEC/FSE), 2015, 532–43, https://doi.org/10.1145/2786805.2786825. A recent audit of a coding benchmark likewise identified flawed tests alongside contamination 5.5. OpenAI, “Why SWE-bench Verified No Longer Measures Frontier Coding Capabilities,” OpenAI, February 2026, https://openai.com/index/why-we-no-longer-evaluate-swe-bench-verified/. Neither fidelity to an artifact nor success against a visible test establishes that the intended obligation was adequately represented. Model evaluation must therefore ask both whether the claimed correspondence is trustworthy and whether the representation preserves the distinctions needed by the decisions that use it. Stale or poorly chosen models can confidently direct reasoning toward the wrong result, adding cost rather than saving it.

The proposition does not require engineers to design every representation in advance. Chapter 4 showed how implementation signals and commodity intelligence can help recover latent models. Repeated structures may reveal a domain concept that the implementation already embodies but has never named. Recovery makes that structure explicit, leaving engineers to determine whether the observed behavior is the behavior the system ought to have.

A more ambitious possibility is representation innovation. A reasoner may propose a different decomposition, relation, or state space that makes an engineering question tractable, even when that representation was neither supplied by an engineer nor plainly latent in the implementation. The innovation is useful when it exposes consequential structure that existing representations did not make practically available. A novel diagram alone would not establish that result.

Discovery does not confer trust. Like any model in Chapter 2, a machine-proposed representation claims a relationship to the system and must earn the trust placed in that claim. A recovered model can be checked against the implementation it purports to summarize; a genuinely novel abstraction poses the harder question of what evidence establishes that it preserves the distinctions required by its intended engineering use. The stronger the reasoning, assurance, or enforcement built on the representation, the stronger that evidence must be.

P1 would be challenged if these representations add interpretation and maintenance work without lowering reconstruction cost, preserving quality, or extending the scale of work completed. The comparison must include their construction and useful life. More capable agents may reduce the need for some representations by reconstructing the relevant knowledge cheaply; they may also make other representations economical to discover and maintain. The proposition concerns the value of the representation for the work, not the quantity of models an organization accumulates.

docs.title: 6.2.2 P2: Representation-Enabled Enforcement
docs.text:
An explicit representation can make a selected obligation mechanically decidable, allowing Alignment to enforce it independently of the producing agent’s compliance. Modeling supplies a form in which the property can be evaluated; Alignment supplies the mechanism that makes the result consequential. These contributions can reinforce one another, but neither should be mistaken for the other.

Suppose an architectural rule forbids a service from depending on a database directly. Giving the agent a dependency model can help it choose a permitted design. A separate gate can compare the resulting dependency graph with the rule and reject a change that violates it. The first intervention helps the agent produce acceptable work; the second governs what is admitted when production goes wrong. The gate can still reject the forbidden dependency even if the agent never consulted the model.

The distinction also explains why equal protection can come at different cost. A producer without the model may repeatedly propose changes that the gate rejects. Supplying the model can reduce these collisions without changing the gate’s guarantee. Conversely, a clear model without enforcement still leaves fulfillment dependent on the producer and whatever subsequent review occurs. Table 6.2-1 separates these possibilities.

Table 6.2-1. Modeling and Alignment are separable levers. Modeling changes the economics and tractability of reasoning; Alignment changes whether the result can acquire consequence. The cells describe their primary contributions, not an exhaustive account.Modeling ↓ / Alignment →No AlignmentAlignmentNo ModelingRepeated reasoning from a poor surface; residual failure can escapeCovered failure cannot escape, but rejection and regeneration may be expensiveModelingSatisfactory realization becomes cheaper or more likely, but residual failure can still escapeSatisfactory realization becomes cheaper while covered failure remains independently blocked

The strongest assurance claim is local to a covered property. If a sound admission mechanism rejects every violation of that property, admitted work cannot contain that violation, regardless of how often the producer makes the mistake. That does not establish that the property is the right one, that the representation covers every consequential concern, or that the mechanism’s implementation is sound. Those remain engineering obligations.

Most assurance is less decisive. Tests can miss failures, validators can reject useful work, and statistical checks can be uncertain. A lower escape rate may simply reflect rejecting more candidates. Comparisons therefore need independent assessment of correct delivery and false rejection as well as escaped failure, with the cost of sustaining delivery included. Independence here concerns the mechanism’s ability to act without relying on the producer to obey; it does not mean that every source of error is statistically independent.

Modeling can change which obligations admit such mechanisms. The dependency rule may be difficult to assess by repeatedly asking a reasoner to interpret source files, configuration, and conventions. Once an appropriate model exposes the relevant services and dependency edges, checking the forbidden relation becomes a repeatable predicate. The engineer still has to establish the graph’s claimed correspondence with the system; the mechanical check is only as relevant as that correspondence makes it.

The determinization frontier separates judgments that require fresh interpretation from those that can be evaluated by a repeatable procedure. Alignment can mechanize an obligation that is already decidable. Modeling can change the representation so that a previously difficult judgment becomes decidable, after which Alignment can enforce it (Figure 6.2-1). This distinction is also economic. On one side are judgments the factory must make repeatedly through probabilistic reasoning; on the other are properties it can evaluate through reusable machinery.

The Determinization Frontier Repeated judgment follows either an already-decidable route or a route through Modeling to change the representation and expose a decidable property. Both join before Alignment, where sensors provide evidence and validators evaluate it before a gate applies the result. REPEATED JUDGMENT property requires reconstruction property already decidable MODELING Change representation Decidable property (predicate over model) ALIGNMENT Encode and evaluate the predicate Sensors and Validators Gate REPEATABLE DECISION The determinization frontier: change what is decidable (Modeling), then bind the decision (Alignment). Figure 6.2-1. The Determinization Frontier. Alignment can bind a property that is already decidable. Modeling can change the representation so that a property previously requiring semantic reconstruction becomes decidable and can then be bound by Alignment. Both routes move repeated judgment into machinery.

DocAble illustrates the distinction. Determining what an image means and writing an adequate description require semantic judgment. Once a description is attached to an object in the document model, checking its presence and placement can be mechanical. That check does not establish that the description is adequate. Modeling has made a narrower property decidable, and Alignment can enforce it without repeating the original semantic judgment.

The frontier does not imply that every judgment can become mechanical. Better representations may improve human or agent evaluation even when no definitive predicate is available. Where a property does become mechanically decidable, the question is whether the resulting evidence and enforcement are trustworthy enough for the consequence attached to them. P2 would be challenged if the proposed representation fails to make the important property checkable, or if apparent assurance gains disappear once coverage, false rejection, correct throughput, and cost are compared fairly.

docs.title: 6.2.3 P3: Governance Conversion and Engineering Capital
docs.text:
When engineering judgment becomes trustworthy, reusable structure, later work can inherit productive capacity rather than purchase the same reasoning again. Governance conversion is one route to this engineering capital. A recurring failure can become a validator; an architectural distinction can become a model; an operational lesson can become a procedure. Up-front engineering and lessons transferred from other systems can create the same kind of inheritance before a local failure occurs.

The return is broader than defect reduction. An architectural model may let an engineer assess a change that would otherwise be too expensive to understand. A typed operation can make a previously risky mutation routine. A validator can provide evidence earlier, and a recovery procedure can make a failed experiment cheap enough to attempt. In each case, earlier work has changed what later engineers and agents can accomplish, what they must reconstruct, or what risk they must bear.

This is why the metaphor is capital rather than memory. A record can preserve information without changing the productive capacity of later work. An engineering asset becomes capital when later work can use it to gain capability, reduce cost, or control risk. A useful record can certainly do that; its format does not decide the question. The test is what the next engineer or agent can inherit.

That inheritance need not depend on the continued presence of the engineer who supplied the original judgment. When an architectural distinction becomes a trustworthy model, a review judgment becomes a validator, or an operational lesson becomes a reliable procedure, some of the originating engineer's productive capacity now lives in the GEE. A later engineer or agent can benefit from the result without reconstructing the reasoning that produced it.

The transfer is necessarily partial. Durable structure carries only the judgment it successfully represents or mechanizes. When requirements change, a new failure appears, or the representation itself becomes inadequate, engineering judgment is needed again. Engineering capital therefore does not eliminate expertise; it changes how often the organization must pay again for expert judgment on the same question.

The organizational path matters. If an engineer diagnoses a recurring boundary error but can only repair the current patch, later agents may encounter the same problem. If that diagnosis changes the shared model and its validator, later work can inherit the distinction without waiting for the engineer to explain it again. The theory therefore predicts more consistent propagation where diagnosis is connected to authority over shared engineering structure. It does not require all authority to reside in one person.

The analogy to technical debt is intentional. Debt makes future change more expensive; capital makes future change more productive. Neither status is permanent. Capital depreciates as systems, obligations, and tools change. A validator can become noise, a model can drift, and a once-useful constraint can begin blocking legitimate work. Governance therefore includes maintenance, reconciliation, and retirement. Accumulation is not the objective; productive capacity is.

Estimating the return on engineering capital requires comparing later work with what the same work would have cost without the asset, under comparable capability, quality, and task conditions. The comparison must include construction and maintenance, the asset’s useful life and loss of fit, and the value of human attention. Changing foundation-model capabilities and prices affect both sides: cheaper agents may lower the cost of constructing and maintaining an asset, but also the cost of reconstructing the same knowledge on demand. Inherited capacity pays where the value of the work it enables or saves justifies those costs over its useful life. The proposition identifies what must be measured without claiming known coefficients.

This account also connects to Storey’s distinction among technical, cognitive, and intent debt in AI-assisted software 3.3. Margaret-Anne Storey, “From Technical Debt to Cognitive and Intent Debt: Rethinking Software Health in the Age of AI,” Queue 24, no. 2 (2026), https://doi.org/10.1145/3807966. A team can accumulate implementation faster than it maintains shared understanding or preserves why the system should behave as it does. Explicit models and evidence can give consequential understanding and intent a durable place to live. They do not remove the need for expertise when requirements change or the representation itself becomes inadequate.

P3 would be challenged if later work gains no useful capacity over local repair or on-demand reconstruction once the asset’s full costs are counted. A decline in recurrence alone is insufficient: the engineer may have become more experienced, or the work may have changed. Reuse by later engineers or agents, including work performed without the originator, provides a stronger test of what the GEE actually preserves. The research agenda returns to how these comparisons can be made.

docs.title: 6.2.4 P4: Governable Acceleration
docs.text:
The effect of additional agentic capacity depends on the GEE through which it acts. Where representations and assurance adequately support the work, added capacity can produce more durable progress without proportionate growth in human inspection. Where the GEE fits poorly, the same capacity can instead produce more churn, intervention, or escaped failure. Raw implementation activity may rise in either case.

Consider two agents making more changes against the same service boundary. An explicit dependency model may spare both agents repeated reconstruction; a gate may keep the covered architectural violation out of admitted work. Those mechanisms can support a higher rate of acceptable changes. If the model is stale or the gate enforces the wrong rule, more activity can instead multiply the resulting repair and review. The proposition concerns these mechanisms and their fit to the tasks, rather than a blanket advantage for a GEE described as stronger.

To test that claim, GEE quality has to be characterized independently of the outcomes it is supposed to explain. The four dimensions in §6.1 provide questions about representation usefulness, obligation coverage, coherence, and economy. They do not yet supply a validated universal score. Counting checks would be easier, but an overgrown collection of conflicting checks can make the GEE less useful. A comparison must identify which relevant properties differ, then observe what additional capacity does under those conditions.

Several outcomes are plausible. A good representation might let a weaker model perform work that previously required a stronger one. A stronger model might benefit more because it can exploit relationships that the weaker model cannot. Or capable agents might reconstruct the required knowledge so cheaply that maintaining the representation contributes little to production efficiency. Independent assurance may still matter in that last case, because being able to produce a result does not establish that it should be admitted. These possibilities are reasons to compare capability and GEE together, not to assume that more Modeling must always accompany better agents.

Acceleration can also change how quickly inadequacy becomes visible. Failures that would arrive months apart may occur close enough together for an engineer to recognize their common structure. That creates an opportunity for governance conversion, not an automatic learning mechanism. Without diagnostic capacity, the organization may simply produce patches faster. Without authority to change the shared GEE, a correct diagnosis may remain local. Useful adaptation can also be subtractive when the pressure comes from obsolete constraints or duplicated controls.

An improved GEE can in turn make larger tasks and greater concurrency economical. The organization may then attempt work that exposes different obligations and new failure classes. This is the expanding task frontier in Figure 6.1-2: engineering capital can support more ambitious work, which renews the need for diagnosis and adaptation. It does not imply unlimited improvement or that every increase in capacity is worth purchasing.

P4 would be challenged if added capacity has essentially the same effect on durable throughput, escape, and human-attention burden across otherwise comparable GEE conditions, or if the apparent advantage disappears when task difficulty and quality are matched. Faster approvals alone are not evidence of governable acceleration. The relevant result is more useful work admitted with adequate assurance, while the costs and unresolved demands remain visible.

Table 6.2-2 collects the four propositions. They overlap in an engineered system, but they ask different questions: what reasoning the representation changes, what an independent mechanism can enforce, what later work inherits, and how those conditions affect the use of additional capacity.

Table 6.2-2. Four theoretical propositions. Each identifies a mechanism, its conditions, and a comparison needed to assess it. These are claims to investigate, not measured effects.PropositionMechanismWhat a comparison must establishP1 Representation leverageTask-relevant structure reduces reconstructionReasoning reach or cost at matched quality, including fidelity and upkeepP2 Representation-enabled enforcementRepresentation makes an obligation checkable; Alignment enforces itEscape, false rejection and correct delivery for adequately covered obligationsP3 Governance conversion and engineering capitalLater work inherits useful engineering judgmentReused capacity and propagation net of construction, carrying cost and lost fitP4 Governable accelerationCapacity acts through the environment’s fit to the workCapacity-by-environment effects on durable throughput, escape and human attention« Table of contents« Beginning of chapter« Previous section§6.2 · What the Theory PredictsNext section »Next chapter »Index »© James C. docs.title: §6.3 · Scope Conditions
docs.text:
Chapter 6 — The Theory  ::  §6.3§6.3 Scope Conditions

The four propositions are conditional. A representation can be expensive to keep current, a control can enforce the wrong obligation, and an organization can recognize a structural problem without being able to change it. These limits are part of the theory: they identify where the proposed engineering moves should earn their cost and where another arrangement may be better.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Return, Governability, and Authority
docs.text:
Whether MAGE applies to a given engineering surface comes down to three questions:

  1. Will it earn a return? Is there enough recurrence or consequence to repay the investment?
  1. Can the obligation be governed adequately? Can the property be represented, evidenced, and evaluated well enough?
  1. Can the organization act on what it learns? Can it distinguish structural pressure from local defects, and does it have authority to change the shared environment?

Recurrence is the usual source of return. If the same architectural knowledge, review judgment, or failure class will be encountered hundreds of times, making it explicit once can avoid paying for the same reasoning repeatedly. But recurrence is not the only justification. A rare obligation with catastrophic consequences may warrant extensive modeling and assurance because preventing a single failure can repay the investment. The economic question is therefore broader: does the expected reduction in future reasoning, risk, or recovery cost justify the construction and carrying cost of the asset?

Some properties can be represented precisely and settled mechanically: a schema conforms, a dependency is permitted, an invariant holds. Others admit statistical evidence but not a definitive predicate. Still others depend substantially on aesthetic, scientific, organizational, or social judgment. Governability is the degree to which an important obligation can be made explicit, supplied with relevant evidence, and evaluated with adequate reliability and acceptable cost. Deterministic checking is its strongest region, not its definition.

The residual probabilistic surface is therefore not necessarily technical debt. Some judgment belongs there. The objective is not to minimize it blindly, but to avoid repeatedly purchasing expensive probabilistic reasoning or residual risk where a cheaper, adequate, and trustworthy representation or mechanism can do better.

The organization also needs diagnostic capacity and authority to adapt. Repeated failures become useful evidence only when someone can recognize the missing abstraction, boundary, invariant, or control. That diagnosis must then have a path into the shared environment. A contractor may identify a recurring failure without permission to modify the client’s development pipeline. A packaged agent system may allow task instructions while preventing changes to its underlying controls. The engineer can see the problem in either case, yet be unable to convert the diagnosis into a durable intervention.

MAGE therefore requires sufficient control over the engineering environment rather than ownership of the software being developed. An engineer working on a proprietary platform may hold extensive governance authority, while a contractor with full source-code access may hold almost none. Authority need not reside in one person; it has to connect diagnosis to the environment.

A single system can contain obligations suited to durable enforcement alongside obligations that still require expert judgment. The practical question is therefore not whether a project “uses MAGE,” but which properties deserve durable representation or enforcement, how strong the evidence should be, and which decisions should remain with experts.

docs.title: 6.3.2 The Expanding Frontier of Explicit Engineering
docs.text:
Consequence does not imply governability. Some important obligations admit precise models and strong evaluation: structural loads, resource bounds, protocol states, or dependency relations may support calculation, exhaustive analysis, or proof. Other obligations remain substantially qualitative even when an organization has strong reason, or a legal duty, to evaluate them carefully.

ENGINEERING PRACTICE

Inset — Hard Obligations, Judgment Calls

An explicit, consequential obligation can still require judgment. Consider a historic building. The Secretary of the Interior's Standards for Rehabilitation require certified projects to preserve historic character, and new work must be compatible with the historic building in its massing, size, scale, and architectural features. Replacement features may need to match the original design, color, texture, and other visual qualities 1.1. U.S. Department of the Interior, National Park Service, The Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for Rehabilitation, Historic Preservation Tax Incentives, 2024. These are real requirements that can determine whether a project is approved, but there is no complete test for “compatible with the historic character.” Engineers and architects can measure dimensions, identify materials, record features that must be preserved, compare photographs and drawings, and use precedent and design rules. These make the judgment better informed and more consistent. They do not remove the judgment.

Software has the same problem. The Department of Justice's 2024 accessibility rule generally requires state and local governments to make their web and mobile content conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, including conventional electronic documents where the criteria apply 2.2. U.S. Department of Justice, Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities, 89 Fed. Reg. 31,320, 2024. Many resulting requirements can be checked mechanically, but the rule also permits an alternative technique when it provides “substantially equivalent or greater accessibility and usability.” Whether it does so can depend on the information and functionality preserved, the users and tasks involved, and the barriers the alternative introduces. DocAble sits on this boundary. It can mechanically check many properties that its document models make observable and use probabilistic models for semantic work such as interpreting figures and generating descriptions. But neither proves that every blind student will receive a substantially equivalent experience from every remediated document. Some judgment remains.

The historic-building and accessibility examples illustrate obligations that are important, explicit, and legally binding while still requiring judgment. Engineering can improve those judgments by making the obligation explicit, mechanizing the parts that can be checked, and gathering good evidence for the rest. The boundary can also move. Better models and measurements can turn judgments that once required an expert into properties the environment can check; better GenAI may make us willing to entrust increasingly difficult judgments to an artificial expert. Here, expert means a reasoner capable of making the judgment well enough for the consequence at stake, whether human or artificial. The goal is to give each obligation the strongest form of evaluation and enforcement the available evidence can support.

Two considerations guide the investment decision. First, how much value would making an obligation explicit provide? Recurrence, consequence, and avoided reasoning or recovery costs can all justify greater investment. Second, how much of the obligation can be mechanized? Some properties admit reliable constraints, validators, or gates; others still require substantial judgment. The propositions in §6.2 explain how explicit engineering can create value; Figure 6.3-1 asks when that value justifies investment and how much of the resulting governance can be mechanized. High-value obligations may justify explicit models, evidence, and procedures even when reliable automation is unavailable. Where mechanization is feasible, its benefits must still justify its construction and carrying costs.

Choosing where to invest in explicit engineering Columns run from low to high mechanizability. Rows run from low to high value of making an obligation explicit. Low value suggests leaving judgment informal or mechanizing selectively. High value suggests investing in explicit judgment or in enforcement. Mechanizability From judgment-intensive to reliably mechanized (e.g., constraints, validators, or automated checks) Low High Value of making it explicit Higher value justifies more engineering machinery. Low High Leave judgment informal Example: A one-off internal naming choice. Mechanize selectively Example: Prototype formatting— automate when it is cheap enough to maintain. Invest in explicit judgment Example: Historic building design— document its fit with standards and precedent. Invest in enforcement Example: Service dependency— block changes that violate the modeled dependency rule. Figure 6.3-1. Choosing where to invest in explicit engineering. The value of making an obligation explicit and its mechanizability suggest four responses, illustrated by examples. Better models and evaluation can increase mechanizability, while cheaper engineering machinery can make investment economical at lower expected benefits. Neither change implies that every obligation should be mechanized.

Commodity intelligence can change this decision in two ways. First, it can lower the cost of constructing and maintaining models, validators, and other engineering machinery. An investment that was previously uneconomical may then become worthwhile, even though the obligation itself has not changed.

Second, better representations, instrumentation, and evaluation can increase mechanizability. An obligation that initially required repeated expert judgment may yield narrower properties that can be checked reliably. For example, an architectural restriction reconstructed from source code may become a repeatable predicate over a dependency model. This is the determinization frontier from §6.2: Modeling changes what can be decided mechanically, and Alignment makes the resulting decision consequential.

Not every obligation can or should become mechanical. Some judgments remain contextual or admit only probabilistic evidence; others can be automated but do not justify the investment. Explicit engineering can still improve how the remaining judgments are represented, informed, and reviewed.

Neither movement implies a destination for software engineering as a whole. Many consequential questions remain open because the system’s appropriate shape is still being discovered: which abstraction matters, which tradeoff users will accept, or which failure will dominate in operation. Implementation can be an experiment that produces information about the specification. Even a question that is closed today may reopen as users, dependencies, workloads, regulations, or adversaries change. Software evolution remains an outer loop around increasingly capable episodes of automated realization 3.3. M. M. Lehman and J. F. Ramil, “Software Evolution—Background, Theory, Practice,” Information Processing Letters 88 (2003): 33–44.

The failure mode is premature closure. An explicit representation can make the wrong target easier to optimize. A small probabilistic surface is therefore not itself evidence of good engineering. MAGE asks which questions can be governed adequately now, which still need investigation, and what structure would help the next decision. It does not predict convergence toward complete specification.

docs.title: 6.3.3 Scope Beyond Software
docs.text:
The mechanisms described here do not intrinsically require software. Other engineering work also uses representations, independent evidence, reusable procedures, and inherited judgment. Transfer requires useful representations of the consequential state, credible correspondence between those representations and the system, and mechanisms adequate to govern the relevant obligations. Where those conditions are weak, better agents or expert judgment may remain the appropriate means of doing the work.

These scope conditions are theoretical, informed by Chapter 5; they are not estimates of how often MAGE will succeed across a population. Chapter 7 examines other domains and what the account implies for engineers. The research agenda asks how to test the relationships first, before treating that wider application as established.
