docs.title: §6.4 · Research Agenda
docs.text:
Chapter 6 — The Theory  ::  §6.4§6.4 Research Agenda

The next step is to find out when these mechanisms matter, by how much, and at what cost. The central experimental difficulty is to distinguish improvements in the reasoning engine from improvements in the engineering environment through which it works. Three research directions organize that problem: representation engineering, governance and engineering capital, and the interaction between capacity and environment.

Lines of code have long served as a convenient measure of software production, although their relationship to engineering effort and value is imperfect. Agentic implementation weakens that relationship further: large quantities of code can be produced with little human effort, while substantial engineering work may produce no code at all. Token expenditure offers another readily available measure, but it describes resource consumption rather than engineering output. Agarwal and colleagues 11. Shyam Agarwal et al., The AI Era’s Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer’s Token Spend Measures, 2026, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2611.13396. found that token expenditure varied widely across weeks with similar commit counts. Engineers also reported using agents for analysis, research, and planning as well as implementation.

Model-based engineering offers a broader measurement perspective. Prior work has examined model maturity, traceability, verification, rework, and engineering effort 234.2. Gustavo Garcia et al., “Measuring Progress and Productivity in Model-Driven Engineering for Capital Project Delivery,” Journal of Construction Engineering and Management 147, no. 4 (2021), https://doi.org/10.1061/(ASCE)CO.1943-7862.0001969.3. Kaitlin Henderson et al., “Towards Developing Metrics to Evaluate Digital Engineering,” Systems Engineering 26, no. 1 (2023): 3–31, https://doi.org/10.1002/sys.21640.4. Kelly X. Campo et al., “Model-Based Systems Engineering: Evaluating Perceived Value, Metrics, and Evidence Through Literature,” Systems Engineering 26, no. 1 (2023): 104–29, https://doi.org/10.1002/sys.21644. MAGE extends the objects of measurement to the governed engineering environment itself: its models, relationships, controls, and ability to support subsequent engineering work. Table 6.4-1 organizes candidate measures into four categories. These measures describe different aspects of engineering activity, output, and capability; they are alternatives and complements for empirical investigation, not components of a prescribed productivity score.

Table 6.4-1. Candidate measures of agentic engineering. Implementation measures describe changes to the product; modeling measures describe explicit engineering knowledge; GEE measures describe the machinery supporting controlled change; activity measures describe resources consumed and work performed. Examples are illustrative rather than exhaustive.Measurement targetCandidate measuresWhat they characterizeImplementationLOC added, deleted, or retained; code churn; commits and merged changes; completed features; escaped defects; rework; accepted changes per unit timeProduct change, delivery, and durabilityEngineering modelsModel elements or size; model maturity; represented requirements and properties; model coverage; relationships across views or abstraction levels; traceability completeness; properties analyzed or validatedExplicit engineering knowledge, relationships, and evidenceGoverned engineering environment (GEE)Number and coverage of constraints, sensors, and gates; obligations with independent checks; model–implementation correspondence; violations detected or blocked; false rejections; human interventions; control maintenance cost; changes admitted without human inspectionCapacity to direct, evaluate, and govern implementationEngineering activity and resourcesAgent invocations; tokens consumed; inference expenditure; agent execution time; human engineering and review time; dispatches; retries; tool calls; validation runsWork performed and resources consumed

These categories need not move together. A migration may change thousands of lines while preserving the product’s externally visible behavior. Adding a model may make an architectural obligation explicit without changing the implementation, while introducing a gate may prevent future violations without producing a new feature. Conversely, an agent may complete substantial implementation work without adding to the engineering environment. Measurements should therefore be interpreted according to the engineering question: an experiment on implementation capacity may emphasize accepted changes and their durability; one on Modeling may examine represented properties and the analyses they support; and one on Alignment may examine enforcement coverage, violations, and the human attention required to govern changes.

The distinction also matters when measuring productivity over time. Durable throughput concerns useful work that survives subsequent change, but useful work may take the form of product functionality or reusable engineering capability. Code retained without churn, a model that continues to answer consequential questions, and a control that remains effective across later changes are different forms of durability. None is adequately measured by its size alone. Their costs and subsequent uses provide additional evidence for interpreting what was accomplished.

Table 6.4-2 collects four useful comparisons. Each holds the proposed move against an alternative that could plausibly work. Independent acceptance and the lifecycle accounting of §6.1 provide a common basis: include failed work and upkeep, report unresolved requests, and compare delivery under declared quality requirements and evaluation horizons.

Table 6.4-2. Four comparisons connecting the theoretical propositions to observable outcomes.QuestionComparisonWhat to measureRepresentation (P1)Structured representation versus prose containing the same obligationsCorrectness and reasoning cost across task families and agent capabilitiesAssurance (P2)Independent model-derived checks versus existing checksEscape and false rejection, alongside correct deliveryConversion (P3)Corrections retained as instructions versus conversion into durable controlsLater capability, recurrence and cost per correct delivery, including construction and upkeepCapacity × environment (P4)Different model capabilities crossed with different engineering environmentsDurable throughput, defect escape, and human attention

docs.title: 6.4.1 Representation Engineering
docs.text:
To test representation leverage, compare agents given structured models with agents given prose containing the same obligations. Hold the task, foundation model, tools, and admission mechanism fixed. Measure correct delivery, reasoning cost, and the human effort required to interpret or repair the result. This isolates the effect of representation form on fulfillment. A separate elicitation experiment should test whether structured representations help engineers discover or express obligations they would otherwise omit, rather than assuming that every treatment begins with an equally complete specification.

The admission mechanism should also be varied independently. With a sound gate, covered violations cannot enter admitted work regardless of whether the producing agent receives the model, but the representation may reduce the number and cost of rejected attempts. With imperfect checks, compare escaped defects, false rejection, and correct delivery under each representation condition. Crossing representation and admission mechanism in a factorial design would distinguish their individual contributions and reveal whether they reinforce one another.

A second set of experiments should compare representations designed by engineers, recovered from existing implementations, and proposed by agents as new abstractions, using raw implementation as a common baseline. The six model classes in Chapter 2 were offered as useful, not proved necessary, sufficient, or minimal. Recovery should faithfully expose consequential structure already present in the system. Innovation should make useful relationships available that the existing representations did not.

For either route, discovery is only the beginning of evaluation. Use held-out engineering questions and failures to test usefulness; assess claimed correspondence independently; measure reconstruction cost, reasoning success, human comprehensibility, and maintenance. A representation that solves the demonstration question but misleads later work has not established leverage. The comparison should also ask whether any added structure is more economical to retain or to reconstruct when needed.

Representation studies should also examine whether the resulting models improve human engineering decisions, a question taken up in the review experiment below.

docs.title: 6.4.2 Governance and Engineering Capital
docs.text:
Governance research asks which interventions leave capacity that later work can actually inherit. One practical design follows a recurring failure class from first occurrence through diagnosis, local repair, any durable conversion, later reuse, and eventual maintenance or retirement. Record what the intervention enables as well as which failures recur: a model may make larger changes tractable, and a validator may make independent operation possible.

That history can show when later work began to inherit an intervention, but a decline in recurrence alone cannot establish its cause. The engineer may have become more experienced, or the work may have changed. Comparing similar work that received only local repair, or observing later work without the originating engineer, helps distinguish these explanations. Across organizations, the same design can examine how authority connects a local diagnosis to changes in the shared environment.

The economic comparison must include construction, carrying cost, and the work spent reconciling or retiring assets that lose fit. Several assets may contribute jointly to a result: a model, a typed operation, and an admission check can reinforce one another. A credible return estimate needs an explicit allocation or a comparison of the bundle, rather than assigning the entire gain to whichever asset was added last. The aim is to learn when inherited capacity pays and how organizations can preserve that value without merely accumulating controls.

docs.title: 6.4.3 Capacity and Environment
docs.text:
A factorial study can vary foundation-model capability and GEE quality independently over matched task families. GEE conditions should differ in specified representations, controls, or evidence pipelines, with their adequacy assessed independently of the measured outcomes. The study should measure correct admitted work, escaped defects, human intervention, and lifecycle cost over a common horizon. Interactions would show whether improvements to the GEE substitute for model capability, complement it, or contribute little under the tested conditions. Repeating the comparison as tasks and GEEs evolve would test whether the observed effects persist.

For example, two engineering environments could operate on the same codebase and task population, with the same foundation model and production tools. One could provide a validated dependency model and an admission check covering a declared set of architectural obligations; the other could rely on existing source files and ordinary review. The experiment would assess the model’s correspondence and the check’s coverage independently, before measuring delivery outcomes. Both conditions would use the same independent outcome assessment. This tests a specific engineering investment without assuming that GEE quality can be reduced to a universal score.

I expect the marginal value of a stronger reasoner eventually to be dominated by the value of a better engineering environment. Indeed, I suspect we have already reached that point for some classes of software-engineering work. A more capable agent may implement a change faster, but if the surrounding environment cannot preserve intent, supply adequate evidence, and govern acceptance, the additional capacity may produce little durable progress. The comparison is not between intelligence and engineering, but between investing in more intelligence and investing in the conditions under which intelligence becomes useful.

Human review deserves a direct comparison within this design. Give engineers the same review-time budget, but vary whether they begin with code or with changed models and verification evidence, retaining access to code when needed. Include cases where a passing check rests on an incorrect obligation or stale evidence; a reassuring display can make the wrong decision easier. As agent output increases, measure whether engineers still distinguish acceptable changes from faulty ones and how much correct work is admitted. Faster approval alone would not support P4 if more violations enter the system.

docs.title: 6.4.4 Optimizing the Engineering Environment
docs.text:
These comparisons could eventually inform engineering routing: choosing how a task should be engineered for realization, including its representation, foundation model, tools, iteration, and admission mechanisms. A routing decision may favor a stronger foundation model, a cheaper foundation model with better structure, or a deterministic operation for a sufficiently specified task. Across repeated work, the decision also concerns what to invest in the GEE. The engineer must allocate resources among reasoning, representation, implementation, and assurance while accounting for the environment that later work will inherit.

Let π be an engineering policy that selects a production arrangement and any investment in the GEE for each task. Its choices depend on the inherited environment, the available evidence, and current conditions, including the capabilities and prices of available foundation models. Let Π be the set of policies available to the engineer. For a declared task sequence and evaluation horizon of H engineering episodes, let Ci denote the total cost incurred in episode i: production, checking, repair, valued human attention, and investment or maintenance attributable to that episode. Charge initial construction to the first episode and allocate shared costs once across the horizon. One formulation of the investment problem is

minπ∈ΠEπ[∑i=1HCi]subject toEπ[DH]≥Dmin,A(π,H)=acceptable,Eπ[AH]≤Amax,Gi+1=f(Gi,ai),i=1,…,H.

Here DH counts independently assessed correct admitted delivery and Dmin>0 is the minimum required delivery. AH is total human attention consumed over the horizon, measured in a declared unit such as engineer-hours, and Amax is the available attention budget. The expectation is over the outcomes under policy π. Human attention is both a valued cost and a limited resource; its constraint does not add a second charge. The condition A represents the declared assurance obligations, which may combine invariants, probabilistic failure bounds, and required human authorization. These obligations must also specify which requests or task classes require delivery when an aggregate count would permit the policy to select only easy work. The positive delivery minimum rules out rejecting everything; coverage requirements address selective avoidance.

The final relation retains the schematic inheritance model: episode work ai, including any engineering investment, changes the GEE available to later work. The policy generalizes the earlier fixed-foundation-model comparison by allowing the reasoning engine and production arrangement to change between episodes. This is an illustrative problem formulation; particular settings will require their own assurance conditions, resource budgets, and valuations of useful delivery.

We do not know the optimal policy. Cost and transition functions remain uncalibrated, and the effects of representations and controls depend on the tasks. Foundation-model capabilities and prices keep changing. Better agents may make some maintained representations unnecessary by reconstructing their information cheaply. They may also make other representations economical to build and maintain. Requirements, dependencies, and organizational authority change as well. An engineering arrangement that is economical today may not remain so.

The formulation gives the research agenda a decision problem to address. The propositions identify mechanisms that can affect its objective and constraints; the proposed experiments can begin estimating those effects. Such evidence may eventually support policies that choose where to invest in durable structure, where to rely on probabilistic reasoning, and where human judgment remains necessary. The economically appropriate division of labor is an empirical question whose answer can change as the available technology and work change.

These experiments would establish effects only for the tasks, agents, and engineering environments studied. Replication across organizations and task families would show how far the relationships extend. Testing them outside software would require additional evidence that the relevant obligations can be represented and evaluated adequately, as the scope conditions above suggest.

docs.title: §6.5 · Summary
docs.text:
Chapter 6 — The Theory  ::  §6.5§6.5 Summary

The chapter’s account of MAGE rests on five connected ideas.

  1. Agentic capacity acts through an engineered environment. Capability alone does not determine engineering progress. Representations, process, evidence, constraints, and controls shape how much raw capacity becomes durable output.
  1. Modeling and Alignment act on different parts of the problem. Modeling changes the reasoning surface and can make satisfactory realization more likely or cheaper. Alignment gives selected obligations independent evidence and enforcement, reducing the probability that covered failures escape.
  1. Engineering work changes the environment inherited by later work. Realizations are not independent. They can degrade the reasoning surface or leave behind models, constraints, sensors, architecture, and other engineering capital that make later work easier to govern.
  1. Engineering can move judgment into machinery. Alignment can bind obligations that are already decidable. Modeling can change the representation so that some judgments previously reconstructed through inference cross the determinization frontier and become repeatable decisions.
  1. The engineering problem is economic. Durable structure costs something to build and carry. The objective is therefore not maximum Modeling or Alignment, but an economical division of labor among probabilistic reasoning, deterministic machinery, and human judgment.

Together, these claims explain the dynamic at the center of MAGE. Commodity intelligence increases what an agent can attempt. Engineering determines how much of that capacity becomes reliable, governable, and cumulative. As the relative costs of reasoning, representation, and assurance change, so may the work engineers choose to perform themselves. Chapter 7 examines what those changing choices mean for the profession.

docs.title: §7.1 · The Reorganization of Software Work
docs.text:
Chapter 7 — The Profession  ::  §7.1§7.1 The Reorganization of Software Work

In software, MAGE is software engineering under changed economics. The analysis in Chapter 6 leaves a practical question: how should the profession reorganize its work when implementation and routine analysis become cheaper?

docs.title: 7.1.1 Was Implementation Ever the Bottleneck?
docs.text:
A reasonable objection begins with a fact: software engineers do not spend most of their workweek typing code. This result predates generative AI. Meyer et al., drawing on 5,971 responses from professional developers, found that software work spans a much broader mixture of development and non-development activities. More recently, Kumar et al. separated the developer workweek into sixteen activities; in their Microsoft sample, coding new features occupied roughly 11 percent of the actual week, alongside debugging, architecture and design, code review, testing, refactoring, environment work, security, communication, and other activities.** André N. Meyer et al.; 11. André N. Meyer et al., “Today Was a Good Day: The Daily Life of Software Developers,” IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 47, no. 5 (2021): 863–80, https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.2019.2904957. Sukrit Kumar et al. 2.2. Sukrit Kumar et al., “Time Warp: The Gap Between Developers’ Ideal vs Actual Workweeks in an AI-Driven Era,” Proceedings of the 2025 IEEE/ACM 47th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice (ICSE-SEIP), 2025, 12–22, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICSE-SEIP66354.2025.00007. Kumar et al. distinguish sixteen activities and report approximately 12 percent of the actual week in communication and meetings, 11 percent in coding, 9 percent in debugging, 6 percent in architecture and design, and 5 percent in pull-request and code review.

Butler et al. turn that observation into a critique of contemporary GenAI.†† These developer-time studies describe how work was allocated before today's stronger autonomous coding agents; I use them as evidence about work allocation, not as an empirical ceiling on what later bounded agents can perform. If the technology merely makes the coding slice faster, its whole-job effect has a low ceiling. Even if coding occupies only roughly 10–15 percent of the workweek, doubling performance on it cannot double developer productivity; faster source production can simply move pressure downstream into review, testing, integration, and other work. Their criticism applies well to GenAI used as individual code-generation assistance. It also supports a broader point MAGE shares: lines of generated code are not an engineering outcome, and handing developers a tool does not by itself redesign the system of work around them.‡‡ Jenna Butler et al. 3.3. Jenna Butler et al., “Eight Myths on Software Engineering and GenAI,” Queue 24, no. 2 (2026), https://doi.org/10.1145/3807963. The article's "Writing Code Is the Bottleneck" discussion explicitly frames the problem as GenAI used primarily to accelerate code creation while the surrounding development loop remains unchanged.

The disagreement begins when that fixed slice is treated as a bound on agentic engineering. Time categories are not independent production stages. Software engineers learn about a design by realizing it: implementation exposes missing abstractions; debugging changes what we believe about behavior; tests expose underspecified obligations; refactoring discovers structure; deployment reveals couplings that static design did not anticipate. This interleaving is not a new observation. Ralph's Sensemaking–Coevolution–Implementation theory models software development as repeated movement among understanding the context, revising the problem and design together, and constructing, debugging, and deploying the artifact; a later multi-method study using more than 1,300 developers and four longitudinal cases strongly supported that process account.§§ Paul Ralph, the Sensemaking–Coevolution–Implementation theory, 44. Paul Ralph, “The Sensemaking–Coevolution–Implementation Theory of Software Design,” Science of Computer Programming 101 (2015): 21–41, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scico.2014.11.007. and its multi-method follow-through, 55. Paul Ralph, “Software Engineering Process Theory: A Multi-Method Comparison of Sensemaking–Coevolution–Implementation Theory and Function–Behavior–Structure Theory,” Information and Software Technology 70 (2016): 232–50, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.infsof.2015.06.010. which combined a survey of more than 1,300 developers with four longitudinal case studies and reported strong support for the SCI account. For an older and deliberately stronger version of the "implementation is design" argument, see Jack W. Reeves 6.6. Jack W. Reeves, “What Is Software Design?” C++ Journal, 1992, https://www.developerdotstar.com/mag/articles/reeves_design.html.

MAGE therefore uses implementation capacity in an economic rather than time-sheet sense. Every design hypothesis that has to be realized before the team can learn from it imposes a cost, even if the eventual keystrokes occupy only a small fraction of the calendar. Reduce that cost sufficiently and more alternatives become affordable, feedback arrives sooner, and intelligence can participate in more of the surrounding loop. Modern coding agents already reach beyond source generation into repository inspection, debugging, test construction, refactoring, tool execution, and multi-step changes. Whether they can safely take on still more of that loop is exactly the engineering question MAGE addresses.

This makes the disagreement empirically testable. If assistance accelerates only code writing while the surrounding work stays unchanged, the fixed-slice argument largely holds. If governed agents can assume meaningful portions of debugging, testing, refactoring, integration, migration, and operation without proportionate growth in human review, a fixed coding-time slice is no longer the right model of attainable leverage. The relevant boundary is the work delegated and the supervision it requires. MAGE asks how to cross that boundary without losing engineering control.

DevOps offers a particularly close precedent. Infrastructure as Code and Policy as Code moved knowledge that once lived in operating practice into executable artifacts. MAGE generalizes the move without insisting on code as the form: an engineering decision might become a type, model, schema, validator, permission, workflow, or documented review obligation. Useful engineering knowledge increasingly becomes structure later work can inherit; residual semantic judgment remains with people.

docs.title: 7.1.2 Agents Entered an Implementation-Centered Discipline
docs.text:
The first generation of agentic software-engineering research inherited the engineering object already in front of it: a repository and a software-development task. The central question was how to make an increasingly capable reasoner perform that task more effectively.

The progression is instructive. Early agentic software-engineering research improved agents' ability to work with existing software artifacts. Repository retrieval made relevant code and documentation available during implementation 7.7. Fengji Zhang et al., “RepoCoder: Repository-Level Code Completion Through Iterative Retrieval and Generation,” Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (Singapore), 2023, 2471–84. Purpose-built interfaces improved an agent's ability to navigate repositories, edit files, and execute tests 8.8. John Yang et al., “SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering,” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37, 2024. Program analysis helped agents locate and reason about changes by exploiting program structure rather than treating a project as a collection of files 9.9. Yuntong Zhang et al., “AutoCodeRover: Autonomous Program Improvement,” Proceedings of the 33rd ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA ’24) (New York), 2024, https://doi.org/10.1145/3650212.3680384. More recent work has also attempted to infer specifications from existing artifacts 10.10. Haifeng Ruan et al., “SpecRover: Code Intent Extraction via LLMs,” Proceedings of the 47th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Software Engineering, 2025, https://doi.org/10.1109/ICSE55347.2025.00080. These developments improve how agents understand and modify software, and establish important foundations for autonomous implementation. They share an orientation: improving the machinery an agent uses to act on the software artifact.

Research on agent governance provides another important antecedent. Existing methods translate organizational and regulatory obligations into technical controls and assign those controls across design-time, runtime, and assurance layers 11.11. Christopher Koch, From Governance Norms to Enforceable Controls: A Layered Translation Method for Runtime Guardrails in Agentic AI, arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.05229, 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05229. Other frameworks evaluate a proposed action against policies that depend on the agent's execution history 12.12. Maurits Kaptein et al., Runtime Governance for AI Agents: Policies on Paths, arXiv preprint arXiv:2603.16586, 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.16586. Governance-by-construction systems demonstrate how policy enforcement can be integrated into an agent's operating environment 13.13. Segev Shlomov et al., Governance by Construction for Generalist Agents, arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.20874, 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20874. These approaches develop architectures and methods for governing agentic systems. MAGE's governance-conversion process additionally accounts for how failures encountered during implementation reveal missing obligations or controls, and how engineers preserve those lessons for subsequent work.

MAGE accepts that machinery and enlarges the engineering object. The question is no longer only how an agent should navigate a repository, retrieve context, use tools, or construct a patch. It is what durable environment should be engineered around autonomous implementation: which system properties deserve explicit representation; which obligations deserve enforcement; what evidence work must produce; how representations remain in correspondence with the implementation; and how recurring judgment becomes machinery inherited by later work.

The difference is one of level, not opposition. Repository retrieval, structured code search, agent-computer interfaces, tests, and tool use all belong inside a governed engineering environment. MAGE's claim is that they are pieces of a larger engineered substrate rather than accessories to a coding agent.

docs.title: 7.1.3 The Old Dream, with a New Substrate
docs.text:
The ambition predates today's coding agents. In the 1980s, Charles Rich and Richard Waters's Programmer's Apprentice envisioned an AI system not merely as a programming tool but as an agent in the software process. The engineer would share programming knowledge with the Apprentice and delegate work across implementation, design, requirements, verification, explanation, and documentation 14.14. Charles Rich and Richard C. Waters, “The Programmer’s Apprentice Project: A Research Overview,” Computer 21, no. 11 (1988): 10–25, https://doi.org/10.1109/2.86782. Its internal representations made programming concepts explicit so that routine questions could be answered from represented knowledge rather than reconstructed from first principles.

The project realized important pieces of that vision, but under different constraints. Its intelligence depended heavily on programming knowledge deliberately encoded into specialized representations; Rich and Waters themselves observed that the economics failed when too much knowledge had to be supplied for each problem. Commodity intelligence changes that premise. A general-purpose reasoner can now arrive with substantial prior competence, enter an unfamiliar repository, use tools, interpret natural-language intent, and construct substantial implementations without the engineering organization first encoding everything it might need to know.

Earlier systems could demonstrate pieces of that vision; today's systems realize enough of it to expose the next-order engineering problems: keeping representations trustworthy, deciding which obligations deserve enforcement, producing evidence at agentic velocity, and converting recurring judgment into machinery that later work inherits.

docs.title: 7.1.4 Where Engineering Effort Moves
docs.text:
As commodity intelligence assumes more implementation and routine engineering work, human effort shifts toward directing that work and governing its results. Figure 7.1-1 illustrates two related changes: delegation transfers work to agents, while governance conversion preserves recurring engineering judgment in durable structure. The latter calls for Modeling to represent consequential knowledge and obligations, and Alignment to establish evidence, constraints, and controls. These are broad directions rather than a fixed allocation of effort; their relative importance depends on which capabilities improve and what investments become economical.

Where engineering effort moves Delegation shifts implementation and routine work to agents, while engineers retain judgment. Governance conversion turns recurring judgment into models, controls and evidence in the governed engineering environment. Pre-GenAI allocation Agentic engineering Implementation is a major claim on human effort. More implementation is delegated, and more judgment is preserved in structure. Human engineering work Requirements and intent Design and abstractions Implementation Review and acceptance Operation and adaptation Human engineering judgment Intent and abstractions Modeling: consequential knowledge and obligations Alignment: evidence, constraints, and controls Tradeoffs and acceptance Adaptation Commodity intelligence Implementation Analysis Transformation Routine remediation Delegation Shifts more implementation and routine work to agents. Engineering tools and processes CI/CD and build automation Tests and test infrastructure Static analysis and quality checks Repositories and code review Coding standards and policies Governed engineering environment Models and context Constraints and permissions Evidence and validators Admission Operational controls Governance conversion Turns recurring judgment into durable, reusable structure. Figure 7.1-1. Where Engineering Effort Moves. As the fleet assumes work across the lifecycle, the engineer increasingly works through the surrounding engineering environment: specifying intent, choosing consequential abstractions, evaluating evidence, resolving tradeoffs, and adapting the environment itself.

Where that displaced effort settles depends on which parts of the production system become cheaper and more reliable. Chapter 6 supplies the distinctions. Faithful production through a representation R depends on whether consequential intent is encoded in it (P(E∣R)) and whether the agent fulfills those obligations (P(F∣E,R)). Interpretation contributes to the second term. Governance separately concerns which unacceptable results the mechanisms detect, reject, or prevent. Cost includes realization attempts and the work required to keep representations and controls useful as the software changes. The engineer chooses the representation and the Alignment strategy together against those quantities.

Technological progress can move these terms independently. Reasoners can improve. So can the machinery for constructing and maintaining representations, the machinery for realizing them, and the machinery for detecting and refusing unacceptable results. These four are not a taxonomy of tools. They are the independent variables that prevent a single confident forecast. Table 7.1-1 sketches how each would redirect engineering effort. The correspondence is deliberately not one term per row: an improvement can change several terms at once, and representation machinery changes probabilities and costs alike.

Table 7.1-1. Possible movements of engineering effort. Improvements in different parts of the production system act on different terms of the Chapter 6 engineering problem. The trajectories can proceed independently and in combination, so the rows describe the pressures each would create rather than a forecast of a single future process.Technological trajectory and terms affectedWhat becomes economicalEngineering effort moves towardReasoners improve: P(F∣E,R)↑Reasoning successfully from less complete representations, and leaving more legitimate choices unresolved until realizationChoosing consequential distinctions, bounding degrees of freedom, and judging results rather than specifying every realization choiceRepresentation machinery improves: P(E∣R)↑, P(F∣E,R)↑, lower upkeepConstructing, maintaining, reconciling, and querying explicit representationsChoosing abstractions, validating representations, and maintaining correspondence among them and with the systemRealization machinery improves: P(F∣E,R)↑, lower realization costReliably transforming sufficiently complete representations into implementations, potentially deterministicallySpecifying and validating what should be realized rather than supervising how it is implementedGovernance machinery improves: less escaped failure, lower upkeepDetecting, rejecting, or preventing unacceptable realizations independently of the producing reasonerChoosing which obligations require enforcement, placing controls, and judging residual risk

Because these trajectories need not proceed together, commodity intelligence does not fix a single destination for software engineering. Better reasoners let engineering leave more legitimate freedom unresolved. The engineer states the consequential distinctions and lets realization choose among the acceptable possibilities. As Chapter 6 shows, faithful production approaches P(E∣R) when conditional realization approaches one and encoding quality is held fixed. Agents may infer omitted intent, but reliable fulfillment alone does not establish that the encoded obligations were right. Capability therefore moves effort toward deciding which distinctions are consequential; it does not retire the obligation to encode them.

If explicit representations become cheap to construct, maintain, and reconcile, engineers can profitably externalize more consequential knowledge. The modeling work developed in Chapter 2 then becomes economical for more questions: choosing useful abstractions and maintaining their claimed correspondence with the system.

Retrieval and representation engineering address different questions. Retrieval selects information to place before a reasoner; representation engineering asks whether a different form would make the engineering question easier to answer. An agent might retrieve enough source to reconstruct an architectural dependency, or work over a dependency model in which that relation is already explicit. The first improves access to the implementation; the second changes the representation over which reasoning proceeds. The two can be combined: a context pipeline may retrieve the dependency model itself.

Program comprehension and architecture recovery make this economic choice concrete. Their established methods recover higher-level views from source, execution, and other evidence 151617.15. Elliot J. Chikofsky and James H. Cross II, “Reverse Engineering and Design Recovery: A Taxonomy,” IEEE Software 7, no. 1 (1990): 13–17, https://doi.org/10.1109/52.43044.16. Stéphane Ducasse and Damien Pollet, “Software Architecture Reconstruction: A Process-Oriented Taxonomy,” IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 35, no. 4 (2009): 573–91, https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.2009.19.17. Bas Cornelissen et al., “A Systematic Survey of Program Comprehension through Dynamic Analysis,” IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 35, no. 5 (2009): 684–702, https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.2009.28. If agents make accurate recovery cheaper, they can lower the cost of realization and improve P(F∣E,R) by reducing reconstruction cost and exposing the dependencies relevant to a change. Recovery does not automatically improve P(E∣R): existing structure and observed behavior do not establish what the system ought to do. Engineers must compare recovering a view on demand with retaining it as engineering capital, whose future reuse must justify its construction and carrying costs.

This trajectory changes the price of representation work, not its nature. It makes a larger investment in representations economical without establishing that such an investment will dominate software engineering.

If realization from a sufficiently complete representation becomes cheap and reliable, engineering effort moves further upstream. Little consequential freedom then remains downstream of the representation, and transformation or generation can replace autonomous realization wherever the representation determines the implementation. §7.2 examines the engineering tradition that already works this way.

If strong controls become cheap, engineers can tolerate more freedom in realization while independently checking the consequential results. Validators, monitors, and admission checks can reduce the chance that unacceptable work is admitted when they detect violations and trigger an effective rejection or intervention. Lower cost makes that coverage more economical to construct and maintain; it does not by itself make a check sound. Effort then moves toward deciding which obligations deserve enforcement, placing the controls that enforce them, and judging the risk that remains. Under this trajectory an organization can become far more governed without becoming more model-driven.

Real engineering environments will combine these trajectories, often differently for different properties of the same system. A system might maintain an authoritative state model where invalid transitions are consequential, allow an agent wide implementation freedom locally, derive architectural views when a question needs them rather than maintain them, and enforce security and dependency obligations at admission.

The appropriate unit of analysis is therefore usually the engineering question or obligation, not the development methodology.

Model-driven engineering is one plausible destination, reached when improvements in representation and realization machinery reinforce one another. Cabot's proposal for vibe-driven model-based engineering keeps models as the pillar of development while letting AI assist their construction and, where a model determines the implementation, their realization through deterministic generators 18.18. Jordi Cabot, Vibe-Driven Model-Based Engineering, arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.10645, 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10645. That is one combination of the trajectories in Table 7.1-1: AI lowers the cost of constructing and manipulating explicit models while model-based realization stays attractive. MAGE includes that future. It does not predict it. The opposite combination is equally available. If reasoners become good at reconstructing trustworthy task-specific representations from implementation, carrying separately maintained models may become less attractive for many questions.

Commodity intelligence changes the economics of representation and control without determining their eventual form.

More modeling need not mean more permanently maintained models. Agents can make it economical to construct a dependency graph, a state abstraction, a quantitative model, or another purposeful reduction for one consequential question and discard it afterward. Construction cost must be repaid by the value of the reasoning it enables. Repeated reuse is one way to earn that return; answering a sufficiently consequential question once is another. Cheaper construction expands the range of one-off questions for which a model pays. A model can matter because reasoning passes through it today; an organization need not preserve it forever.

Whichever trajectory dominates, recurring judgment remains an opportunity for governance conversion. The conversion and ratcheteering developed in Chapter 4 let later work inherit that judgment while keeping the resulting structure open to correction. The professional question is whether the judgment belongs in the next reviewer's head or whether future work should inherit it from the environment.

The answer is not always "mechanize." Guidance remains useful where interpretation is semantic; human review remains appropriate where consequence or ambiguity warrants it; and every new mechanism adds carrying cost. The goal is to mechanize where doing so pays. Engineers make that choice one obligation at a time, under economics that have not finished moving.

docs.title: 7.1.5 Review When Implementation Is Abundant
docs.text:
Code review does not disappear when agents produce the code. Its center of gravity moves.

At low change volume, an experienced engineer can treat the diff itself as the principal reasoning surface. Read the implementation, reconstruct the surrounding architecture, infer the affected behavior, inspect the tests, decide whether the change belongs. That strategy stops scaling as implementation becomes abundant. The scarce resource is no longer the ability to produce another diff. It is the engineer's ability to determine what the change means.

This pressure predates agents. Long before agentic programming, empirical work at Microsoft found that larger changes were harder to review well: as more files were touched, the proportion of useful reviewer feedback declined, and large changes imposed greater reviewer effort 19.19. Amiangshu Bosu et al., “Characteristics of Useful Code Reviews: An Empirical Study at Microsoft,” Proceedings of the 12th Working Conference on Mining Software Repositories (MSR), 2015, 146–56, https://doi.org/10.1109/MSR.2015.21. Agentic generation makes that problem larger; it does not change its basic cognitive shape. The older result establishes that large changes tax human review and reduce useful feedback. It does not establish that explicit models would relieve the strain; models as the remedy are MAGE's proposal.

Greiler's more recent SCOPE proposal responds by changing the review operating model: detailed implementation review moves increasingly into the developer–agent loop, and team review becomes risk-proportional assurance over code together with higher-level artifacts and evidence 20.20. Michaela Greiler, “From Peer Review to Self-Review: The Epistemic Risk of Agentic Development,” July 2026, https://www.michaelagreiler.com/code-reviews-from-team-to-individual/. That proposal already includes agent review, developer attestation, risk-based team assurance, and accountability. SCOPE changes the operating model for review; MAGE additionally changes the surfaces available to the reviewer. When the environment holds explicit models of structure, behavior, ownership, execution, measurement, and provenance, those models become review surfaces in their own right. The engineer need not reconstruct every relevant property from the diff.

Explicit models provide intermediate review surfaces. A change can be projected onto component ownership, permitted dependencies, service edges, lifecycle states, deployment placement, user journeys, measurement obligations, and provenance. Deterministic mechanisms discharge the obligations that are mechanically decidable before scarce human attention is spent. The reviewer then spends attention on the remainder:

  • Is the intended change desirable — the question a diff could never answer on its own.
  • Do the models capture the relevant concern — or has the change moved a property no current representation exposes.
  • Is the evidence sufficient — do the checks that ran actually bound the risk this change carries.
  • Should the tradeoff be accepted — the residual judgment that stays with a person.

Implementation becomes one evidentiary surface among several, rather than the origin from which every system property must be reconstructed. The reviewer still examines implementation details when they are necessary to evaluate the risk. The models supply an index into the engineering significance of a change.

In the terms of Chapter 6, these representations can reduce the cost of evaluating a realization without necessarily improving the probability that the agent produces an acceptable one.

Review moves upstream, from inspecting realization toward evaluating intent, consequence, evidence, and the judgment that remains. Some argue that capable coding agents will eliminate human code review altogether 21.21. Martin Monperrus, The End of Code Review: Coding Agents Supersede Human Inspection, arXiv preprint arXiv:2606.13175, 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13175. Even if code review disappears, engineers must still evaluate the models, evidence, and tradeoffs that govern the resulting software.

Appendix A examines selected DocAble models, their consumers, and the checks that maintain correspondence with the implementation. These examples illustrate the engineering surfaces available for review without prescribing a fixed catalog of models.

This shift in review surfaces has a broader implication: effective engineering capability may increasingly be a property of the environment as well as the foundation model. A weaker reasoner operating over accurate representations, well-routed context, strong tools, and independent evidence may outperform a stronger reasoner over an opaque repository. MAGE does not establish that substitution quantitatively; §6.4 asks how capability and environment substitute for or complement one another, and how those comparisons might inform engineering routing.

docs.title: 7.1.6 Engineering the Production System
docs.text:
Chapter 5 distinguished two places engineering attention can go as realization becomes abundant. Engineers can spend increasing effort operating agentic machinery: supplying work and context, coordinating agents, inspecting output, and resolving exceptions. They can also engineer the production system around that machinery so that selected knowledge, evidence, and controls persist across acts of realization.

Both futures can contain capable agents and very little human implementation. They differ in where scarce engineering judgment goes. MAGE predicts increasing value in designing and revising the production environment: deciding what it must preserve, how it establishes acceptability, and which choices it can safely leave to agents.

Making agents easier to operate is not the same as making software easier to engineer.

This is not a new lifecycle phase. Requirements, design, validation, operation, and maintenance remain. What changes is that engineers increasingly exercise those responsibilities through the production system in which agents work. The next section places that arrangement within the longer history of engineering through explicit representations and controls.

docs.title: §7.2 · Back to Models, but Not Back to Waterfall
docs.text:
Chapter 7 — The Profession  ::  §7.2§7.2 Back to Models, but Not Back to Waterfall

MAGE asks engineers to invest deliberately in models, specifications, and controls while delegating more implementation to agents. Does that mean software engineering is returning to waterfall: specifying the system in advance, then handing the specification to a fabricator? The resemblance is understandable. Much of software engineering's history has involved moving away from the expectation that a sufficiently complete design could precede implementation. Yet the iterative development examined in Chapter 4 showed the opposite of a fixed handoff: implementation exposed missing knowledge, models were revised, and recurring failures changed the engineering environment inherited by later work.

The distinction is between working through models and requiring models to settle the implementation before work begins. Engineers have long used representations to make consequential decisions without expecting those representations to describe every detail of the finished artifact. Software engineering developed a different balance because code itself served as an unusually powerful representation and because maintaining additional models imposed costs. Commodity intelligence changes those costs. To understand what MAGE changes, and what it inherits, we need to examine why software engineering historically organized representation and implementation differently from other engineering disciplines.

docs.title: 7.2.1 Engineering Through Representations
docs.text:
The account of Modeling in Chapter 2 belongs to a much older engineering practice. Civil, mechanical, electrical, aerospace, and systems engineers work through load models, schematics, state-space models, simulations, drawings, and analyses.

Models are the building blocks of engineering.** Here I mean model in the broad sense developed in Chapter 2: a purposeful reduction that preserves distinctions needed for some question. The claim is close to axiomatic under this book's definition of Engineering. A consequential system sufficiently simple to understand and direct without reasoning through reduced representations does not present the complexity for which engineering, in this sense, is required. A circuit schematic is not a circuit; a finite-element model is not a bridge; a process-flow diagram is not a refinery. The representation is useful because it leaves most of reality out.

Physical engineering makes the separation vivid. Fabrication can be expensive or irreversible, full-scale trials can be destructive, and physical iteration can take weeks or months. A structural model answers a loading question before concrete is poured. Circuit simulation exposes a design error before a mask set is fabricated. Realization cost makes the gap between representation and artifact obvious.

The common engineering move is simple: ask the question over the cheapest representation that preserves the property you care about, then use evidence to justify realization. Mature engineering still uses prototypes, experiments, and direct inspection. Models do not replace the artifact. They organize the reasoning around it.

Software engineering already combines explicit obligations with rapid iteration. Test-driven development, for example, states an expected behavior in a test before implementing it, then revises the implementation through repeated test–code–refactor cycles 1.1. Kent Beck, Test-Driven Development: By Example (Addison-Wesley Professional, 2003). Specifying an obligation before implementing it is not the same as specifying the entire system before development begins. Likewise, agile methods do not dispense with planning. They favor delivering useful results early, learning from them, and revising subsequent plans as evidence accumulates 2.2. Kent Beck et al., “Principles behind the Agile Manifesto,” 2001, https://agilemanifesto.org/principles.html.

Software makes the same move through its own traditions. Requirements engineering externalizes obligations. Architecture exposes consequential structural relationships. Type systems and intermediate representations make selected program properties explicit. Formal methods construct representations over which stronger claims can be established. Model-driven and model-based approaches go further and make selected models primary engineering artifacts. These traditions differ substantially, and they share one move: represent the property at a level where it can be reasoned about.

The medium varies; the purpose does not. The analysis serves a decision. Salado makes this point directly by treating engineering as disciplined decision-making under uncertainty and competing objectives, rather than technical problem solving alone 3.3. Alejandro Salado, Rethink Engineering: Revolutionize the Way You Make Decisions (Educating Thinkers Press, 2026). Engineers model, calculate, measure, and experiment because consequential choices must be made: which design to pursue, what evidence to gather, which tradeoff to accept, or whether the resulting system is fit to proceed. A model earns its place when it stands in service of such a decision. MAGE shares that emphasis, and asks what happens when much of the work downstream of those decisions can be delegated to commodity intelligence.

docs.title: 7.2.2 Why Software Often Modeled Differently
docs.text:
Software engineering did not reject models in favor of iteration. Its economics made implementation itself an unusually attractive surface for engineering reasoning.

Software realization was extraordinarily cheap; detailed design and implementation labor were not. Once source code existed, another compilation, execution, or copy of the program could usually be produced at negligible marginal cost. Producing, understanding, debugging, and changing that source consumed skilled engineering labor. The source was already a precise, executable representation through which engineers reasoned about the system.

That blurred a distinction the older disciplines could make more cleanly. A structural engineer reasons through a design before concrete is poured; a semiconductor designer simulates a circuit before fabrication. In software, the artifact handed to the cheap realizing mechanism, the compiler, is itself the product of an iterative design process. Reeves made the strongest version of this argument by calling source code the final software design. MAGE does not require that full claim. It requires only the narrower one: software design and implementation have historically been tightly coupled, and code has served simultaneously as realization, executable specification, and a primary surface for further reasoning.†† Jack W. Reeves's "code is design" argument 44. Jack W. Reeves, “What Is Software Design?” C++ Journal, 1992, https://www.developerdotstar.com/mag/articles/reeves_design.html. is a useful historical extreme; MAGE relies only on the narrower claim that software design and implementation have traditionally been tightly coupled.

Code's malleability then works against the engineer as a system evolves. Architecture, intent, constraints, and operational knowledge can stay implicit in an artifact whose structure keeps changing, and the system stays executable long after the knowledge needed to govern it has become hard to recover. The disciplines named in the previous section exist partly to hold that knowledge where continual change cannot quietly erase it.

Those secondary models faced an unusual economic test. The implementation was already precise, executable, and immediately available, while an architectural, behavioral, or process model imposed an additional correspondence burden. A model could be useful when authored and misleading after the implementation moved beyond the relation it claimed. Many projects therefore kept such representations thin unless their communication, reasoning, or assurance value repaid that standing synchronization cost.

Commodity intelligence changes both sides of that ledger. It lowers the skilled labor required to realize and revise software, and parts of the labor required to derive, update, reconcile, and check additional representations. Implementation and live modeling can become cheaper together, making model-mediated software engineering economical over surfaces where the synchronization tax once exceeded its return. The construction and carrying costs examined in §6.3 still determine where that investment pays.

Lower construction and maintenance costs can make additional representations worthwhile without determining which should become primary. The alternatives in §7.1 remain open: maintain a model, derive a view when needed, or reason directly over implementation. The choice depends on the engineering question, the value of the representation, and the cost of keeping its claimed correspondence trustworthy.

Implementation remains an important source of truth, and some properties are most naturally reasoned about there. A useful representation need not become authoritative. What changes is that code need no longer bear the whole burden of being the realization, the repository of system knowledge, and the surface over which engineering reasoning occurs.

docs.title: 7.2.3 Model-First Engineering as One Point in the Design Space
docs.text:
Model-first engineering occupies one end of the representational design space: sufficiently complete models determine much of the realization that follows.

The Siemens reconstruction demonstrates one such equilibrium in a mature engineering culture. The public account describes persistent models carrying geometry, requirements, behavior, physical relationships, allowable change, and traceability before an agent enters the picture. Software can appear downstream as one realization among others. The agentic question is therefore not how to recover engineering structure from source code, but how to let autonomous tools operate safely through structure the organization already made explicit.

Model-first engineering does not, by itself, imply waterfall. A model can be revised after a prototype, simulation, test, or deployment exposes a mistaken assumption. The distinction concerns how much engineering intent the representation determines, not whether development proceeds through a single pass. In a model-first system, a sufficiently complete representation may support deterministic generation of much of the implementation; in MAGE, the representation may instead preserve selected obligations while leaving substantial implementation freedom to an agent. Both arrangements can be iterative. What differs is how much the engineer chooses to settle before a particular act of realization.

That inversion clarifies MAGE's position. Software-first agent systems largely ask, How do we make a codebase legible to an agent? A model-first discipline can ask, How do we let the agent work through the same engineering representations we already trust?

Degrees of freedom locate MAGE along this axis. A sufficiently complete model can determine realization closely enough that transformation, generation, or synthesis is the natural next step. MAGE includes that case, but does not require it. Its models can instead specify the obligations that matter and the tolerances those obligations permit while deliberately leaving other realization choices open. Those degrees of freedom are not defects in the model; they are choices engineers have no reason to settle in advance. Where tolerances become narrow and little consequential freedom remains, deterministic generation may be preferable. Where substantial freedom remains, autonomous realization can choose among acceptable implementations.

Cabot's vibe-driven model-based engineering proposes a contemporary software route toward the same end of the space, placing agents downstream of models much as a model-first engineering culture already does 5.5. Jordi Cabot, Vibe-Driven Model-Based Engineering, arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.10645, 2026, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10645. §7.1 weighed that proposal as one plausible equilibrium among several. What it adds here is the observation that the software proposal and the systems-engineering practice describe one arrangement approached from two directions.

MAGE includes this organization but does not privilege it. Which representations become primary is an empirical question about where the new prices land. A discipline may settle at different points for different systems, or for different properties of the same system.

docs.title: 7.2.4 Established Traditions, New Composition
docs.text:
MAGE combines two established lines of work around delegated realization. Engineering disciplines developed ways to represent systems, justify consequential claims, and control realization. AI developed ways to extend reasoners through external representations, memory, and tools. Figure 7.2-1 shows how these contributions meet in an agentic production system.

Established traditions, new composition Engineering and AI traditions feed MAGE. Modeling makes knowledge explicit and Alignment enforces selected obligations. Both contribute to a governed engineering environment that contains engineering capital. Subsequent work inherits that capital, with trustworthy autonomy as the intended outcome. ENGINEERING TRADITIONS AI TRADITIONS MBSE / MDE explicit models PL / compilers Types · DSLs Knowledge representation explicit knowledge Memory · planning state external state Formal methods specs; verification Systems / safety boundaries; control Structured reasoning intermediate structure Tools · interfaces reasoner support MAGE New economics → new composition Modeling make knowledge explicit Alignment enforce selected obligations Governed engineering environment representations · tools · procedures · evidence · constraints · controls where both traditions meet Engineering capital recurring judgment, made durable inherited by subsequent work Trustworthy autonomy intended outcome Figure 7.2-1. Established traditions, new composition. MAGE draws on two long-running traditions. Engineering disciplines developed explicit models, constrained representations, verification, and external control; AI repeatedly extended reasoners through knowledge representation, planning state, memory, structured reasoning, tools, and surrounding machinery. MAGE brings these inheritances together around autonomous software work: Modeling makes engineering knowledge explicit, Alignment enforces selected obligations independently, and both meet in the Governed Engineering Environment. Governance conversion carries recurring judgment into durable engineering capital within that environment.

Engineering supplies the first inheritance. Across its disciplines it externalized consequential knowledge into representations, constrained realization against those representations, established evidence that the constraints held, and controlled the transitions that carry consequence: a release, a certification, a change to a system already in service.

AI supplies the second. Its long history of improving reasoners runs substantially through structure placed outside the reasoner: knowledge representations holding what the system knows, planning state and memory holding what it is doing, tools and interfaces extending what it can act on, and intermediate reasoning structures holding partial work. §7.1 traces that line through recent systems. The reasoner improved because its surroundings did.

Commodity intelligence brings the two traditions into the same production system. The engineering environment itself becomes an object of design: the representations, evidence, constraints, and controls around autonomous work must be engineered and maintained together.

The conversion and ratcheteering developed in Chapter 4 keep this arrangement open to correction as experience reveals missing knowledge or controls.

docs.title: 7.2.5 What MAGE Claims Is New
docs.text:
MAGE neither restores a sequential development process nor requires a complete model before implementation begins. Its components have deep precedents: models, constraints, verification, external memory, structured reasoning, and autonomous software agents. The contribution lies in their architectural and disciplinary composition, made newly practical by commodity intelligence.

Much recent agentic software engineering asks how increasingly capable agents can perform work within the software-engineering environment they inherit. MAGE asks how that environment itself should be redesigned when autonomous implementation becomes a primary productive substrate.

Its answer is to make purposeful models, Alignment machinery, and the governed engineering environment first-class objects of software engineering, and to treat recurring judgment converted into durable structure as engineering capital. Consequential semantic judgment stays with engineers wherever representation and mechanism cannot responsibly carry it.

The claim is bounded in two directions. MAGE does not depend on inventing new modeling or verification techniques, and it does not hold that model-first organization is where software engineering must arrive. MAGE makes selected engineering representations authoritative within an increasingly automated production system, and applies the same approach to the production process itself. Commodity intelligence changes the cost of constructing and maintaining that arrangement. The engineering task is to decide where it pays and to build the production environment accordingly.
