docs.title: The question I asked
docs.text:
In the Preface, I asked:

How do we safely grant autonomy to commodity intelligence?

Software engineering provided a concrete setting for the question: if an agent can perform consequential work at extraordinary speed, what must the surrounding environment provide before we can safely grant that capability useful autonomy?

The seven chapters developed an answer at different levels. Modeling established how to represent consequential engineering knowledge; Alignment showed how to enforce selected obligations independently of the producing agent. MAGE in Motion developed the method through which experience becomes durable engineering structure. DocAble Among Other Software Factories examined that method in production, while The Theory explained its mechanisms and economic consequences. Finally, The Profession considered what changes for engineers when implementation can increasingly be delegated.

I developed this answer through software engineering because that is where my engineering expertise lies. The underlying question reaches beyond software and perhaps beyond the conventional engineering disciplines. Its answer in another domain will depend on the representations, evidence, and controls available there.

docs.title: The core of MAGE
docs.text:
MAGE makes three engineering moves.

  1. Work at the right representation. Choose the reduction that makes the engineering question answerable without carrying unnecessary detail. A purposeful model can expose properties that humans and agents would otherwise have to reconstruct from implementation, making them available for analysis, review, and evidence. Build the model when those benefits repay its cost, and maintain the correspondences on which its use depends.
  1. Put enforcement where the obligation can be represented and decided adequately. Guidance influences behavior; enforcement determines which actions or results the environment will accept. Some obligations can be enforced directly through types or permissions that restrict actions or artifacts. Where tests or validators check an obligation, a gate can reject work when the check fails. Others become decidable only after a suitable representation exposes the relevant semantics. Leave consequential decisions to human judgment when the environment lacks the meaning or evidence needed to decide them adequately.
  1. Make useful judgment reusable. When a recurring or consequential engineering decision is worth carrying forward, convert it into a model, mechanism, architecture, procedure, or body of evidence that later work can inherit. Such structures become engineering capital when they improve later engineering work. Ratcheteering preserves the consequential concern while allowing the particular structure that carries it to be corrected, replaced, or retired.

Together, these moves produce the governed engineering environment. Models represent consequential knowledge, controls constrain actions or evaluate results, and evidence supports engineering judgments. People remain responsible for the resulting system. In software, the representations include requirements, architectures, behavioral models, dependencies, provenance, and measurements; the governance mechanisms are constraints, sensors, and gates. Other domains will supply different representations and different means of evidence and control.

That is Model-Based Agentic Engineering.

docs.title: What changes next
docs.text:
When commodity intelligence makes realization cheaper, the cost of the surrounding engineering work becomes more important. If a software factory can produce changes faster than engineers can specify consequential intent, evaluate evidence, or maintain control over the resulting system, then improving realization further does not remove those constraints. Engineering attention moves to them.

The probability analysis in Chapter 6 distinguishes adequate encoding from reliable realization. An agent can faithfully fulfill encoded obligations even when they omit or misstate what the system needs. Better agents can help engineers improve the encoding, but reliable fulfillment alone does not establish that it is right. This leaves two engineering problems: representing consequential intent adequately without spending more on representation than it is worth, and establishing that the resulting work is acceptable through independent evidence and evaluation. Modeling and Alignment address these problems from different directions.

Neither problem has a fixed solution. As agents improve, they can help engineers discover representations, maintain correspondences, construct controls, and evaluate evidence. The engineering environment can become more capable alongside the agents it governs. The relevant question is how to allocate work among the reasoner, the environment, and human judgment as their respective capabilities and costs change.

docs.title: How much specification, and of what kind?
docs.text:
This leaves two related questions open: how much consequential intent must engineers make explicit, and in what form? There may be different answers for realization and assurance. As agents become better at recovering familiar intent, engineers may need to say less to obtain a useful result. A prototype may be judged by the useful behavior it demonstrates; a production system must also provide evidence that its consequential obligations are satisfied. The latter requires suitable representations of consequential properties. The specification frontier therefore depends not only on what an agent can infer, but on what the engineer must be able to establish—and on which representations make that establishment economical.

Agents can also help construct and maintain those representations, analyze them, gather evidence, and build the controls that enforce selected obligations. This reduces the cost of the engineering machinery itself, potentially making richer representations and stronger assurance economical. The opportunity is not merely to realize systems more cheaply, but to improve the machinery through which engineers govern their realization.

docs.title: The Authority and Responsibility of the Engineer
docs.text:
I would not define the engineer by a permanent collection of tasks that only humans can perform. The boundary will move as capabilities improve. Engineering competence will change with it, as it has changed with earlier technologies. What persists is the need for informed control over consequential work: understanding what the engineering arrangement can establish, recognizing where its evidence is insufficient, and accepting responsibility for the decisions made under its authority.

That responsibility need not mean personally making every decision. Indeed, MAGE is an argument for moving suitable decisions and decision-making processes into engineered structures so that they can operate more reliably, consistently, and economically. The engineer's responsibility extends to the design and governance of those structures, including the judgment to revise them when their assumptions no longer hold.

The question from the Preface was how to grant autonomy safely. The answer is to engineer the conditions under which autonomy can be exercised, evaluated, and governed. As commodity intelligence grows more capable, those conditions may become richer and more automated. The responsibility for establishing them remains an engineering responsibility.

Commodity intelligence has not come to abolish engineering, but to demand it.

Back MatterAbout the Author

James C. Davis is an assistant professor of software engineering in the Elmore Family School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Purdue University. His work appears at venues such as ICSE and IEEE S&P and has been recognized with three ACM SIGSOFT Distinguished Paper Awards. He received the NSF CAREER award in 2026. docs.text:
Appendix A — MAGE Engineering HandbookA.1 Engineering Moves: A Field Reference

Choose the move by the recurring problem. A mechanism is one implementation of the move; Table A.1-1 shows choices made in DocAble rather than prerequisites for practicing MAGE.

Table A.1-1. Ten engineering moves, the problems that motivate them, and concrete realizations in DocAble.Recurring problemEngineering moveDocAble exampleDifferent consumers disagree about the same fact.Make one source authoritative. Assign the fact an owner and name its consumers.The component catalogue defines the zones used by repository accounting and agent audits.A copied declaration drifts from its source.Derive; do not copy. Compute the second representation where a reliable transformation exists.Deployment derives invocation-grant plans from service dependencies and runtime identity.A useful representation no longer describes its subject.Check correspondence. Compare declared facts with independently obtained evidence.A governance-graph check resolves modeled hooks against their configured events and implementing scripts.A collection of tests has no explicit account of what it must cover.Derive the obligation set. Enumerate required evidence from represented properties.Cross-service invariant declarations identify verification obligations and references to their checkers.A rule is checked where the necessary state is unavailable.Enforce where the property is legible. Place the decision and its consequence at a suitable boundary.The PDF applier resolves the target before deciding whether an artifact-demotion request is admissible.A protected operation remains available through ungoverned paths.Close the action surface. Offer supported operations through a controlled interface.External PDF editing uses typed operations; the applier can refuse a request before mutation.Relevant knowledge is discovered after the consequential choice.Deliver knowledge at the decision. Join the work’s scope to the representations it needs.Dispatch context extraction selects constraints associated with the brief’s target files.A result cannot be traced to the work that produced it.Carry cause with consequence. Preserve identities and attribution across transformations.PDF mutation records identify the responsible pass or editing session; applied results can be compared with proposed edits.The same operational judgment must be reconstructed repeatedly.Externalize recurring judgment. Record states, evidence, and sanctioned responses.Lifecycle descriptions and runbooks distinguish recovery work from ordinary completion and identify where judgment remains.Individually reasonable changes conflict when combined.Make dependencies queryable. Represent the relationships needed to analyze the interaction.The governance graph records firing events, resource use, and chosen resolutions among selected mechanisms.

The third move, checking correspondence, has two possible responses. If a descriptive representation is stale, repair it to match the implementation. If an authoritative obligation is violated, repair the implementation or reconsider the obligation through the appropriate engineering decision. A check that reports disagreement cannot decide which side ought to change merely because it found a difference.

The sixth move also has a scope. Closing the external PDF editing interface does not establish that every internal document mutation uses it. A useful control has a stated boundary and evidence that the relevant paths cross it. Extending that boundary is further engineering work, with its own compatibility and maintenance costs.

When choosing among these moves, ask what the next task will inherit. Sometimes it needs a clearer representation; sometimes a generator, a check, or a smaller set of permitted operations. Sometimes the right response is to leave a local decision local. The worked compositions that follow show how those choices can reinforce one another.

docs.title: A.3 Governance Conversion
docs.text:
Appendix A — MAGE Engineering HandbookA.3 Governance Conversion

Governance Conversion changes what later work inherits after an engineer understands a failure. Its product may be a representation, a test, a constraint, a gate, or a better operating procedure. The difficult step is deciding which part of the failure should become durable. A prompt to reflect can start that work, but it cannot establish that the resulting control is adequate or that it has been installed.

docs.title: A.3.1 Refusing Duplicate Work
docs.text:
In October 2026, DocAble repeatedly dispatched, or nearly dispatched, agents against engineering phases whose work had already landed. The recorded phase status lagged behind the artifacts. Four encounters in one session required an operator to inspect the repository and discover that the proposed task was redundant. Repeating that inspection was a poor use of another agent.

The investigation found that the system already had ways to record completed phases. The missing protection was more specific: phase identity did not travel through every landing path, and the automated warning arrived only during dispatch, after the brief had been composed. The engineering obligation became: refuse a new assignment when the reconciled phase record positively establishes that the cited phase is complete, while retaining a deliberate route for genuine rework.

The repair reused the phase model. Briefs and commits carry a phase identity, allowing the landing machinery to update the corresponding record. A gate in work-order composition resolves the brief’s cited project and phase, reads that record, and refuses to emit the brief on a positive completed-phase match. Dispatch repeats the relevant check. The gate prints the evidence and offers two ways forward: reopen the phase when more work is required, or supply an explicit override reason through the audit channel. Audit writing is best-effort; failure is reported rather than silently represented as a persisted record.

The positive-match boundary matters. An absent record or an unresolvable phase is not evidence that the work is complete, so it does not trigger this refusal. An earlier version also treated the existence of a phase document as completion evidence. That blocked legitimate multi-wave work and defeated reopening. The repair narrowed the gate to the reconciled phase state, leaving weaker Git evidence advisory. Tests exercise both the refusal and the reopened-phase case.

This is a complete conversion: a recurring failure prompted diagnosis, the diagnosis selected an obligation and representation, implementation placed a gate where the decision could be made, and subsequent briefs inherited that restriction. The engineer still decides whether a new task is worthwhile and whether an override is justified. The environment remembers the part that can be decided from the phase record.

A conversion ledger supplies supporting traceability. A failure-class identifier links the proposed intervention to the engineering phase that installs it; recorded phase transitions let the ledger derive that link’s status. This gives an engineer a route from the original incident to the responsible change. The mechanism’s behavior is established separately by its code, tests, and use.

Figure A.3-1 shows the completed-phase control inherited by subsequent work orders.

Refuse a duplicate assignment on positive completed-phase evidence A work order names its project and phase. Composition resolves that identity against reconciled phase state. A positive DONE match without a valid explicit override refuses the brief; otherwise composition continues subject to its other checks. Missing or unresolved state does not establish completion. Reopening changes the phase to queued; an explicit override permits one dispatch and attempts a best-effort audit write. Dispatch repeats the completed-phase check. WORK ORDER Project · phase RECONCILED PHASE STATE Landing + phase identity COMPLETED-PHASE CHECK Sidecar DONE; no valid explicit override yes otherwise REFUSE BRIEF Show completion evidence CONTINUE COMPOSITION Other checks still apply Reopen to queued, or override one dispatch; audit write is best-effort. Figure A.3-1. A work order is refused when its resolved phase is recorded as DONE, unless a valid explicit override is supplied. Missing or unresolved state does not establish completion. Reopening sets the phase to queued; an override permits one dispatch and attempts a best-effort audit write. Dispatch repeats the check.

docs.title: A.3.2 Governance Graph
docs.text:
Question and representation. Once several mechanisms participate in the same operation, the engineer needs to know how they interact. DocAble’s governance graph records selected process mechanisms, their firing events, resource requirements, enforcement characteristics, and implementation anchors. The core record includes these fields:

id: str
kind: MechanismKind
lifecycles: frozenset[Lifecycle]
firing_event: FiringEvent
requirements: frozenset[Requirement]
output_power: frozenset[OutputPower]
enforcement: Enforcement
anchor: MechanismAnchor

A requirement records whether a mechanism reads, writes, requires a property of, or constrains a named resource. An anchor identifies its configured command, lifecycle event, implementing script, and entry symbol. Conflict edges connect mechanism identities and record the shared resource, interaction type, and chosen resolution. These are implementation records; their categories of hook, mediator, or lint do not replace the book’s functional distinction among constraints, sensors, and gates.

Authority and consumers. The node census records existing mechanisms; interaction edges and their resolutions specify engineering choices. Queries compare firing events and resource paths to identify potential interference. A topological sort computes the declared order and rejects cycles. The proposed driver that would execute this computed order is a separate implementation step: a query returning an order does not itself schedule hooks. The graph also names soft mechanisms honestly. A reflection hook can inject a suggestion without blocking work.

Correspondence. The anchor check compares modeled hooks with the configured lifecycle events and implementing scripts. It can report a modeled command that no longer resolves, a hook missing from the model within the inspected event set, or a mismatched firing event. Its coverage is scoped; it is not a census of every possible control in the repository. Nor does finding the expected function name establish that the function still has the intended semantics.

Chapter 3’s hook-ordering example is one application. A declared order can prevent an inspection from consuming the opportunity needed for reflection, but the resource-consumption reason is richer than a conventional read/write conflict. The model need only record enough to support the required ordering; it need not simulate every token of context consumption. Enlarging the model becomes worthwhile when the additional detail changes an engineering decision.

docs.title: A.3.3 Accessibility Decision Policy
docs.text:
Question and representation. The same conversion process applies inside the product. When should a possibly decorative image be omitted from the accessible reading experience? A visual appearance alone is insufficient: an abstract shape can be furniture in one document and the subject of instruction in another. A vision-language model (VLM) can supply contextual evidence, but the product still needs a policy for acting on uncertainty.

DocAble represents that policy with a closed three-value vocabulary. These constants and the decision function come from DecorativeConfidenceBand; only the explicitly decorative result permits the internal decorative flag:

public const string ClearlyDecorative = "clearlyDecorative";
public const string Uncertain = "uncertain";
public const string Informational = "informational";

public static bool IsClearlyDecorative(string? decorativeConfidence) =>
    string.Equals(
        decorativeConfidence?.Trim(),
        ClearlyDecorative,
        StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

Authority and consumers. The VLM’s answer is an observation about the document, with the limitations of that inference. The mapping from answer to permitted action is an authored product decision. An uncertain, absent, or unrecognized answer does not become permission to suppress content. The shared vocabulary is consumed by description contracts and downstream code, so the conservative default need not be recreated independently by every caller.

This policy developed through a failure investigation. Evaluation found content-bearing images being treated as decorative, including instructional material. The response strengthened the presumption that content should receive a description unless the evidence clearly supported treating it as ornament, and added checks around consumers that could otherwise broaden the exception. The important change was not a new adjective in a prompt. It was an explicit decision rule and its propagation through the relevant interfaces.

Alignment and its limit. The typed PDF applier supplies a further boundary. An artifact-demotion request must name the source of its decorative verdict. The applier refuses certain structurally informative targets, including headings, formulas, and elements carrying authored alternative or replacement text. These refusals can prevent specific damaging actions even when the upstream judgment is wrong. They cannot determine every image’s instructional importance. Content with no such structural protection may still require semantic review.

The resulting composition therefore preserves several different responsibilities. The VLM interprets context, and the decision policy determines how uncertain evidence should affect action. The operation contract carries the proposal to the applier, which enforces selected restrictions. Subsequent evaluation looks for remaining harm. A failure can motivate a change at any of those points. Treating them separately makes it possible to repair the faulty part without claiming that one more check settles the entire accessibility problem.

docs.title: A.3.4 Composing Only What Is Needed
docs.text:
Start from the capability, not the mechanisms. “Every supported edit can be attributed to its producer” identifies a result; “add a logging service” has already selected an implementation. Enumerate the failures that would defeat the result, then identify the evidence or restriction needed for each. Missing identity, a bypassing mutation path, and a log that cannot be joined to an artifact are different failures.

Next establish the dependencies among those protections. A provenance reader cannot recover a record the writer never emitted; a completeness check needs a defined population of operations. Separate these necessary dependencies from useful enhancements. A dashboard can improve diagnosis without being part of the guarantee itself.

Finally, ask what the composition costs to build and carry, where it can still fail, and how its own correspondence will be checked. Once the required capability has adequate support, further mechanisms need a further purpose. Stop.

docs.title: A.4 Governed Delegation
docs.text:
Appendix A — MAGE Engineering HandbookA.4 Governed Delegation

Governed Delegation connects the knowledge needed to do work with the boundaries and evidence needed to accept it. DocAble provides two settings in which to inspect that connection: a reasoner repairing a document, and an agent changing the engineering environment. Their mechanisms differ, but both need a representation of the subject, a bounded assignment or action interface, and a way to distinguish a proposed result from an accepted one.

docs.title: A.4.1 Document Model and Typed Changeset
docs.text:
Question and representation. A repairer needs to inspect the document’s structure and propose a change without manipulating arbitrary format-library objects. The PDF model provides typed access to document elements. An editing operation records a supported change in that vocabulary: its kind, target, and payload. An ordered changeset collects those operations.

This excerpt shows the essential fields of a replacement-description operation. It is taken from EditOp.cs; optional fields are omitted.

public sealed class SetAltOp : EditOp
{
    public override string WireKind => "set-alt-text";
    public string StructId { get; init; } = "";
    public string BeforeAlt { get; init; } = "";
    public string AfterAlt { get; init; } = "";
    // Optional fields omitted.
}

The target is expressed in the document model’s terms, rather than as a byte offset. A request can be inspected before it is applied, compared with another proposal, or associated with the judgment that produced it. The before-value is useful evidence for comparison and reversal; its presence alone does not establish that every editing path rejects stale requests. That requires a separately configured comparison and refusal policy.

Authority and consumers. The document view describes the current artifact. The operation schema specifies which requests the interface can express. The proposed changeset records a producer’s intended intervention. The applied-result record reports what the applier accepted or refused. These are four related representations with different meanings. Keeping them distinct prevents a proposed edit from silently becoming a claim about the resulting document.

The wire vocabulary is shared with the browser editor, and schema-derived types help its clients agree about operation names and shapes. The PDF applier dispatches each supported operation to its handler, resolves targets against the document, and returns per-operation results. A failed operation can therefore be reported with its reason rather than silently counted as a completed repair.

Worked example: refusing a destructive proposal. Suppose a producer classifies an element as decorative and proposes mark-artifact. First the applier requires an attributable verdict source. It then resolves the target and checks structural evidence. A heading, a formula, or authored replacement text can cause the request to be refused before mutation. The producer receives the failure and can reconsider its proposal. A plausible explanation from the producer does not bypass these conditions.

The applier is not proving that the image is decorative. It is enforcing a smaller set of obligations over information it can inspect. The contextual classification remains a semantic judgment, and subsequent checks provide evidence about the result. This division allows a useful hard restriction even when the broader problem cannot be reduced to a predicate.

Figure A.4-1 shows the controlled editing path and the evidence its applier produces.

Supported typed edits cross a common controlled application boundary A document model supplies structure and semantics to edit producers: a structured pipeline, an agent, or a human editor. Supported proposals are encoded as typed changesets with kind, target, and payload. The controlled PDF applier resolves targets, checks selected restrictions, and applies or refuses each operation. Its outputs are an updated document and application evidence: per-operation results plus attribution for edits actually applied. This is the controlled editing path; some internal remediation paths still mutate documents directly. DOCUMENT MODEL Structure · semantics EDIT PRODUCERS Structured pipeline · agent · human editor Propose supported typed edits inspect TYPED CHANGESET Kind · target Payload CONTROLLED APPLIER Resolve · check Apply or refuse APPLICATION EVIDENCE Per-operation results Applied-edit attribution UPDATED DOCUMENT Controlled editing path; some internal mutations still bypass this interface. Figure A.4-1. Supported typed edits share a controlled application path. A pipeline, agent, or human editor can propose changes against the document model. The PDF applier checks selected restrictions and applies or refuses operations individually; results and applied-edit attribution describe what occurred. Some internal remediation still edits directly.

Correspondence and provenance. The external editing route and migrated internal passes can use the same operation vocabulary and controlled application machinery. Applied edits have attribution records, while per-operation results identify refusals and failures. The two records must not be conflated: the producer’s complete proposal may include changes that never occurred. A consumer reconstructing history must read evidence of application, not merely the proposed operation list.

DocAble also models the boundary of this architecture. Remediation-graph nodes distinguish read-only work, direct editing, and production of typed patches. A code-parity analysis compares declared posture with implementation behavior. Some internal operations still mutate directly, so a picture of the common editing interface must not imply that every document change passes through it. The graph’s migration account is useful precisely because it can name both the controlled path and its present limits.

The representation permits different producers to be compared without giving each one an independent writer. A structured pipeline, an agent, and a human editor may reason differently about the same document. Whether one strategy is sufficiently good or economical is an empirical question; Chapter 5 reports the measured comparisons. The architecture supplies a common place to inspect proposals and apply supported changes. It does not establish that the producers have equal competence.

docs.title: A.4.2 Work Orders and Context Delivery
docs.text:
Question and representation. An agent working in a large repository needs the knowledge relevant to its assignment. DocAble’s work order makes that assignment computable. Alongside the engineering objective, it declares target files, new files, the work’s genre and role, verification, acceptance criteria, and non-goals. The generator emits a Markdown document with fields that dispatch and checking tools can read.

These fields come from an actual November 2026 brief to add a standards-evidence check. Only line wrapping has changed; unrelated fields are omitted.

<!-- target-files:
  tools/lint/lint_all/registrations/batch_d.py,
  system-models/standards_universe.py -->
<!-- new-files-to-create:
  tools/lint/lint-standards-evidence-escape-admission.py -->
<!-- compute-class: lint-all-on-commit -->
<!-- brief-genre: lint -->

The two existing paths identify where the check must be registered and which model it consumes. The new-file declaration distinguishes a file that ought to exist from one the agent must create. The genre selects applicable authoring obligations. None of those fields specifies how to implement the check; the brief preserves freedom inside a consequential boundary.

Authority and consumers. The work order specifies the assigned scope and acceptance conditions. Its file list also keys a join to the environment’s knowledge. The component catalogue relates paths to architectural zones; constraint registries relate paths and genres to applicable obligations; the assembled brief presents the selected information to the agent. Dispatch validation checks such facts as a registered project, resolvable paths, and required instruction markers. These checks establish a usable assignment structure, while review judges whether its objective and proposed evidence are adequate.

Context reaches the agent in three ways:

  1. Standing knowledge selected during composition. An include-when table associates instruction snippets with conditions on the assignment. A brief that creates a lint receives the policy for introducing new checks in advisory mode. A brief that invokes a particular build tool receives its serialization instructions. Checks look for the required markers in the composed brief.
  1. File-specific constraints selected at dispatch. The extractor matches declared paths against engineering registries. For the November brief above, the assembled record contains 47 entries: 25 from the lint registry and the rest from banned-API rules, architectural invariants, code style, test requirements, and project context. Each entry identifies its scope and a source or corrective action. This was one selection for one declared scope, rather than a recommendation to give every agent a fixed quantity of context.
  1. Retrieval as the task develops. The agent can query components, service flows, designs, and operating runbooks when it needs another representation. When the actual file list differs from the plan, a later constraint-selection step can repeat the join for the expanded scope. The selected prose guides the agent; the applicable checks and permissions supply any enforcement.

The November brief had a concrete origin. A comparison of the standards project’s acceptance criteria with the implementation found that the exception data existed but the rule admitting those exceptions lacked its checker. The work order named that obligation, the files involved, and the verification commands. Model-based context selection then supplied the rules relevant to building the missing check. The fresh investigation captured this task during execution; earlier waves supplied the observed completion path. The example demonstrates how a represented obligation becomes an assignment without treating an in-progress task as an observed success.

The extractor’s usefulness depends on the representations it queries. It cannot recover an omitted design intention merely by matching paths. A no-match result should remain visible as a limit of the available knowledge, and an agent that changes scope needs to revisit the selection. This is also why local implementation details can remain in code: the work model needs to preserve scope and obligations, while repository inspection supplies details as they become relevant.

Figure A.4-2 connects brief validation and agent implementation to the evidence used at completion.

Model-guided delegation and two different checks A structured work order and maintained engineering models select a brief containing relevant knowledge and obligations. Brief validation precedes agent dispatch. The agent implements and commits. Completion review uses landed changes and independent checks to update work-order status; a completion message alone does not establish acceptance. WORK ORDER Role · target paths Verification · acceptance ENGINEERING MODELS Components · constraints Procedures select ASSEMBLED BRIEF Selected knowledge and obligations AGENT Implement Commit validate COMPLETION EVIDENCE Landed changes Independent checks Review and update status Figure A.4-2. A structured work order selects applicable engineering knowledge from maintained models. Brief validation precedes dispatch; the agent implements and commits. Completion review compares landed work and independent check evidence with the work order, then updates its status. An agent report alone does not establish completion.

docs.title: A.4.3 Completion and Recovery
docs.text:
A work order needs a corresponding account of completion. DocAble’s agent commits carry progress information, and a final validation marker distinguishes work prepared for integration from an interrupted sequence. Landing checks compare the committed changes with the shared repository. A completion message can prompt that inspection; it does not establish that the requested work arrived. Tests and review must still evaluate the acceptance conditions.

The distinction mattered after an orchestrator restart on 9 November 2026. Background agents’ completion notifications were lost, while their committed changes remained in Git worktrees. The operator inspected the branches, recovered and landed completed work, then released the affected slots. The session record and registry trace document that recovery. They support the practical claim that committed work can survive loss of the conversational channel, without requiring the agent to repeat its implementation.

The product has a related ownership problem on a different substrate. In the current whole-document worker path, a database compare-and-set changes a job from queued to remediating before the engine runs. A concurrent delivery that loses that claim returns without rerunning the engine. Finalization uploads the result before conditionally marking the job complete; if another terminal decision has already won, the completion path does not overwrite it. In the GEE, a pool-slot model records assignment and reset states, while the worktree and landing evidence establish what can safely be retained or released.

Table A.4-1 keeps the common engineering questions visible without imposing one recovery algorithm on both systems.

Table A.4-1. Document processing and agent dispatch preserve ownership and completion through different durable records and operating mechanisms.ConcernWhole-document processingAgent dispatchWork unitA document job with a database identity.An engineering brief assigned to a worktree.OwnershipA conditional database claim admits one consumer.A recorded slot assignment reserves the worktree before reset and handoff.Durable resultUploaded document and persisted terminal job state.Committed changes, then verified integration into the shared branch.LivenessJob progress and process telemetry, considered separately from terminal status.Registry, process, and repository observations; a stale signal prompts inspection.Failure responseThe engine records a failed terminal outcome; redelivery cannot reclaim a nonqueued job.Inspect existing commits, resume or recover work, and release the slot after safe integration or disposition.Completion evidenceUpload precedes the conditional completed-state update.Landing evidence plus the assignment’s verification and acceptance checks.

The state representations have distinct consumers. The runtime’s conditional database operations enforce ownership and terminal changes. The pool’s transition table constrains slot management, while its registry records which executor is assigned. Neither a reported idle process nor a stale heartbeat establishes that an agent’s work can be destroyed. DocAble’s operating procedure asks for further inspection and recovery rather than making that inference automatically.

The appropriate boundary is the durable result. Model the ownership and transitions that protect it, retain enough evidence to decide what happened, and leave the executor’s internal reasoning outside the lifecycle unless an engineering question requires it. A job’s output and an agent’s commits need different mechanisms; both need to outlive the conversation with the actor that produced them.

docs.title: A.2 Model Coherence
docs.text:
Appendix A — MAGE Engineering HandbookA.2 Model Coherence

Model Coherence keeps a useful representation connected to the system as both change. DocAble’s engineering environment expresses architectural models in typed Python modules: records declare entities, closed vocabularies distinguish their kinds, and collections declare relationships. Component records identify repository zones; service-flow records describe communication; deployment representations supply resource names and runtime identities. They remain separate because they answer different questions.

Agents can query these representations through a repository command interface; tools can import them directly. The component query locates the owner of a path, while the service-flow query exposes a caller’s dependencies. Tests and correspondence checks compare selected declarations with independently obtained facts. This supplies a modest modeling workbench using ordinary code and test tools, without requiring a second implementation of the product.

docs.title: A.2.1 Component and Zone Catalogue
docs.text:
Question and representation. The component model answers which parts of the system exist, which repository paths belong to each part, and which documentation and boundaries apply there. Its records distinguish leaf components, groups used for cross-component audits, and accounting categories. This distinction matters: a group can overlap several leaves without becoming another unit of source code to count.

The following declaration is an excerpt from system-models/components.py. It identifies the PDF model library and its repository location.

Component(
    name="pdf-model",
    focus_dirs=(RepoRelPath("backend/src/AdaTool.PdfModel"),),
    tags=frozenset({"model", "stamps"}),
    kind="leaf",
    boundary_kind="internal",
    display_name="Remediation: PdfModel",
    # Additional fields omitted.
),

Other fields support shared-directory partitions, exclusions, read-first documentation, deployment artifacts, and declared imports. These are consequential distinctions. Two components may share a directory while owning different files; a file exclusion and a directory exclusion are not interchangeable; documentation for a neighboring component may be useful background without being mandatory reading for this one.

Authority and consumers. Engineers choose the catalogue’s component boundaries and groupings as an authored classification of the codebase. Repository accounting uses its component boundaries, while agent audits use its leaf and group zones. Documentation pointers give consumers an entry into the knowledge associated with a zone.

Correspondence and Alignment. Checks can establish narrower facts about those decisions. Declared paths should exist; service deployment files should be represented; an import should respect a declared boundary where that boundary is enforced. A component’s existence in the catalogue does not itself constrain imports. The import analysis and its configured admission consequence do that work.

Consider adding a new service. Its source directory, deployment files, and service catalogue entry are different artifacts. Naming the component gives them a common identity. A service-integration check compares the component’s declared deployment paths with the repository and looks for service Dockerfiles that no service component claims. It can therefore expose a missing connection while the change is still being prepared. It cannot establish that the service’s decomposition is a good design. That question remains with the engineer.

docs.title: A.2.2 Inter-Service Calls and Deployment Identity
docs.text:
Question and representation. A caller knowing a service’s address does not imply that it may invoke that service. DocAble encountered this distinction when service URLs were wired but the corresponding invocation grants were absent. The resulting calls failed at the cloud authorization boundary before reaching application code.

The inter-service model represents a synchronous dependency as a typed edge. This actual edge connects the accessibility-quality service to the GenAI service:

SyncEdge(
    caller=ComponentName("accessibility-quality-service"),
    callee=ComponentName("genai-service"),
    callee_api=ApiEntityName("genai-service-complete"),
    callee_url_env=EnvVarName("ADA_TOOL_GENAI_SERVICE_URL"),
    auth=_SOA_IAM_AUTH,
    url_seam=UrlSeam.DOWNSTREAM_URL_DEPS,
    expected_status=_SOA_STATUS_BASELINE,
),

The referenced authentication contract records the transport, whether the token’s audience must be the callee URL, and whether an invocation grant is required. The service catalogue separately describes the API. Deployment configuration supplies the runtime identity and environment-specific service name. These representations have different purposes; a common service identity lets tools join them.

A worked join. Start with the declared caller–callee edge. Resolve the environment variable that supplies the callee’s URL. Resolve the caller’s runtime service account and the deployed callee’s name. The joined facts determine an invocation-grant plan: which principal needs which permission on which deployed service. The deployment tool then applies that plan. Several logical edges can require the same concrete binding, so the application step deduplicates by service account and callee.

This is a useful example of derived information. Neither the architectural edge alone nor the runtime identity alone contains the resulting grant. The join answers a deployment question without requiring one enormous model containing every architectural and operational fact. It also exposes a limit: DocAble’s inspected deployment configuration uses a shared runtime service account. Different logical callers can therefore collapse to the same cloud principal. The model must describe that actual authority arrangement rather than imply isolation that deployment does not provide.

Figure A.2-1 distinguishes the implemented grant path from its correspondence checks.

The implemented grant derivation and its separate correspondence checks The service-flow model is a verified mirror compared with the deployment dependency map by a parity check. The deployment dependency map and runtime identity feed the IAM grant plan; deployment applies those grants for Cloud IAM enforcement. In a separate lane, a name-set check compares declared deployment names with the observed fleet. That comparison is not verification of IAM bindings. SERVICE-FLOW MODEL Verified mirror RUNTIME IDENTITY Accounts · resources parity check DEPLOYMENT DEPENDENCY MAP Caller to callee IAM GRANT PLAN Principal · service APPLY GRANTS Per-grant result DECLARED DEPLOYMENTS Service names OBSERVED FLEET Service names name-set check Figure A.2-1. The deployment dependency map and runtime identity determine the IAM grant plan; deployment reports each grant’s application result. The service-flow model is checked for parity with the map. Declared/live service-name correspondence is a separate check, not verification of IAM bindings.

Correspondence and enforcement. The edge model currently acts as a verified mirror of the deployment dependency map. A test requires its projection to equal the live configuration; retirement of the independently maintained literal is a later step. A test that removes an edge from the model confirms that the comparison detects the disagreement. This is a useful brownfield sequence: establish correspondence first, move consumers to the representation, then retire the duplicate owner. Calling the new representation authoritative on its first day would skip the work that makes that transfer credible.

A separate parity check connects service edges to the API catalogue. The grant planner consumes the deployment map and runtime identity; cloud IAM enforces the resulting permissions once applied. A declared edge, a generated grant plan, an applied binding, and a successful authorized call are different evidence. The deployment tool retains individual grant failures rather than treating the existence of a plan as proof that every grant was installed.

The deployed fleet also needs correspondence. An August 2026 investigation found 49 deployed service names across production and staging, while the declared deployment-name set accounted for 28. Nothing had been reconciling the two populations. The resulting check compares the declared service-name set with a stored snapshot of the live fleet; deployment-time observation refreshes that snapshot. It was introduced in advisory mode while existing discrepancies were resolved, so the new control could expose drift without making every unrelated change inherit an immediate blockage.

These checks answer related but different questions. Name-set correspondence detects an undeclared or missing deployment; it does not inspect every IAM binding. The grant plan and its application results concern authorization. Keeping those responsibilities explicit gives the engineer a useful account of the deployment without pretending that one equality check establishes everything about it.

docs.title: A.2.3 Maintaining the Composition
docs.text:
The essential path is short: assign a fact an authoritative representation, give it a consumer, and connect it to the relevant implementation. Derive secondary artifacts when the transformation is dependable. Where two independently authored representations must coexist, compare the facts they claim in common and name who resolves disagreement.

This composition is worth maintaining when several tasks need the same knowledge or when disagreement would have a substantial consequence. It becomes less useful if the representation is too detailed to keep current, if no consumer uses it, or if its checks merely compare two copies derived from the same mistaken source. Local implementation details can remain outside the model. The component model leaves service calls to the service model; the service model leaves deployment identity to deployment configuration. Useful omission is part of the design.

docs.title: B.2 Brownfield Migration
docs.text:
Appendix B — Practicing MAGEB.2 Brownfield Migration

An existing system usually has fragments of the desired environment: documentation, tests, review rules, ownership records, deployment policy, runbooks, and expert knowledge. Begin by finding which of these the selected work already relies on. The problem is to make consequential knowledge and obligations dependable without first documenting or redesigning the whole system. §4.3 explains the recovery techniques; the procedure here supplies operating decisions and exit criteria.

Keep two dimensions of progress separate. Representation reach asks how much of the important system can be understood through trustworthy explicit models. Enforcement reach asks which important obligations are enforced by constraints or gates and which have only observations or advisory checks. A thinly modeled system may have strong local permissions and tests that block admission. A richly modeled system may report violations without preventing anything. Address the gap that matters to the selected work; neither dimension is a maturity score that must reach 100 percent.

docs.title: Audit, Synchronize, Govern, Extend
docs.text:
Apply the four stages in Table B.2-1 to one surface at a time. Their exit criteria describe what must become dependable before the next investment can rely on it. They are not dates in a rollout plan. A new discrepancy can send one obligation back to reconciliation while other parts of the environment continue to operate.

Table B.2-1. The brownfield migration path. Advance when the selected surface meets its exit criterion.StageWorkExit criterionAuditInventory claims, their subjects, and existing mechanisms; classify gaps.Important gaps are classified rather than merely counted.SynchronizeReconcile the representations that upcoming work will rely upon.Their intended correspondence is explicit and credible.GovernEnforce selected obligations where sufficient evidence is available.The selected obligations no longer depend primarily on someone remembering to inspect them.ExtendAdd capability where expected reuse or consequence justifies its cost.Each addition has a named consumer or engineering question and a reason to exist.

During Audit, trace a few consequential claims all the way to their subjects and consumers. A wiki may declare that only one service can call an external API; inspect the implementation, deployment policy, and any check that relies on that declaration. Record whether the claim describes current behavior or intended behavior. A disagreement does not tell you which side should change. Keep the audit advisory while those decisions remain unresolved; making a recovered mistake authoritative would make the system harder to repair.

Classify unlinked code before treating it as a modeling backlog. An orphan can have three explanations:

  • Missing representation. A consequential subsystem or relation has no useful account. Propose a representation around the question that work repeatedly needs to answer.
  • Missing anchor. The representation exists, but code, tests, or work records do not lead to it. Repair the link rather than creating a competing account.
  • Below the grain. The implementation is too fine-grained or generic to warrant a separate representation, such as a typed-ID alias or configuration loader. Record the exclusion where coverage reports need to distinguish it from a gap.

An orphan count without this triage rewards unnecessary modeling. Follow the important questions instead. If a model identifies a component, it need not enumerate every helper used to implement it. Conversely, a small piece of code may deserve explicit treatment if it determines a consequential permission or transition. Size alone does not decide the appropriate grain.

During Synchronize, repair high-value correspondence as ordinary work touches the relevant surface. Link the claim to the code and evidence that support it; provide the reverse route where engineers or agents need to discover the claim from an implementation location. Repair stale anchors and surface semantic disagreements for an engineering decision. When a machine can derive the needed view from the authoritative source, avoid maintaining a second handwritten version.

An existing configuration can remain authoritative while a recovered model earns trust as a verified mirror. In DocAble’s service-flow migration, tests required the model-derived dependency table to match the existing deployment table byte for byte; an injected discrepancy tested whether the check could detect drift. Transferring authority was a separate, planned step: migrate consumers to the model, then retire the duplicated table. This gives brownfield adoption a useful intermediate state. Check correspondence first, resolve disagreements, and move authority deliberately rather than treating a newly recovered representation as authoritative on its first day.

A wiki can remain the entry point. Tell agents how to locate and maintain its relevant pages, and have designs identify the pages their changes affect. Before accepting the work, compare those pages with the current repository rather than relying on the producer’s statement that they were updated. Automate comparisons only for the claims the comparison can actually decide. A mechanically correct link does not establish the truth of the sentence at its destination.

During Govern, choose which selected obligations should constrain an action or block a transition. Place enforcement at the earliest boundary with the necessary semantics and evidence. Some properties can be enforced directly by a type, permission, or local check; others depend on the representations just reconciled. Exercise the rejection path as well as a successful case, and examine whether an alternative route bypasses the mechanism. A check that emits the correct finding but permits the prohibited action has not completed this work.

Name the response to missing or stale evidence. Depending on the obligation, the environment may wait, reject the work, or require an explicit engineering decision. An override should record the affected obligation, the available evidence, the person accepting the exception, and its scope. A temporary exception should not silently become the policy for later changes.

During Extend, use observed friction and recurring failures to choose the next investment. Better retrieval may be enough; a new model, stronger evaluator, generator, or gate should answer a question that current machinery cannot settle economically. Record both its consumer and its maintenance obligation. The useful endpoint is a selected surface on which work can proceed with an adequate account of intent and acceptability, while the rest remains explicitly outside that claim.

docs.title: B.1 Getting Started
docs.text:
Appendix B — Practicing MAGEB.1 Getting Started

Choose a recurring unit of work that an agent can usefully perform and whose result you can inspect. A service change, a document transformation, or a deployment procedure is a more useful starting point than an organization-wide commitment to autonomy. Name the artifact being changed, the expected outcome, the point at which it can affect someone else, and the engineer responsible for accepting that consequence. A bounded first attempt makes both failure and improvement easier to interpret.

Before building machinery, watch how the work is done now. What must someone reconstruct from source, documents, or conversations? Which decisions recur? What must remain true while the implementation changes? Preserve the requirements and decisions that matter to acceptance, including qualitative obligations that still require judgment. Also identify choices that can safely remain open. A brief that specifies every implementation decision can consume the very engineering effort delegation was meant to save.

Inventory the knowledge and enforcement you already have. A schema may reject invalid data, and a permission may prevent a dangerous action. A test may expose a regression, while a review may settle an ambiguous case. Determine which of these actually affects whether work proceeds. An adequate existing mechanism needs a place in the workflow, not a replacement bearing a new name. Where the obligation is already enforced economically, additional system modeling may contribute little. Where people repeatedly recover the same architectural relation, a small representation may help before any new gate is needed.

docs.title: Use a Change as the First Model
docs.text:
A structured ticket can preserve desired behavior, rationale, acceptance criteria, affected concepts, constraints, related changes, and prior decisions. When it carries enough information to reason about one requested change, it functions as a purposeful change-scoped model. It should connect the change to longer-lived system knowledge rather than repeat that knowledge in a growing collection of tickets. For a defect, record the observed discrepancy and the intended correction; diagnosis may still be the difficult part of the work.

Give those connections a consumer. An agent may follow the ticket’s component reference to the relevant ownership model; a reviewer may follow an invariant to its tests; a completion audit may compare the requested behavior with the landed result. Add a field when someone or something will use it. Fields without a consumer become additional material to keep current. The first useful investment may be a reliable link between an existing ticket, an architectural decision, and its acceptance evidence.

The ticket’s lifetime matters. A ticket written in 2022 need not describe the product in 2026, but it can remain an accurate representation of the intent governing the 2022 change. Its persistence is useful history rather than a synchronization burden. A current architectural model makes a different claim and must be reconciled when the relevant system or intent changes. Mark that distinction before installing freshness checks: otherwise a well-intended audit can classify valid history as drift.

docs.title: Establish the Delegation Boundary
docs.text:
For the first trial, state what the agent may change, what evidence will support acceptance, and what should stop the work. Separate the producing agent’s completion report from the evidence used to evaluate it. Existing tests, analyses, measurements, and review procedures may already provide much of that evidence. When they do not settle a consequential question, name the remaining judgment and who must exercise it. Keep an escalation path for a mistaken premise, an unavailable dependency, or an obligation the environment cannot adequately evaluate.

Run a small number of comparable work units and retain the interventions they required. Distinguish time spent creating new intent from time spent reconstructing known facts, checking routine conditions, or recovering from a recurring failure. These observations tell you what the next investment should address. A repeated escalation can indicate an appropriate human judgment boundary; it does not automatically justify a new evaluator or permission.

Expand the scope or consequence of delegated work when the evidence supports doing so. Check that someone remains able to inspect the result, diagnose failures, and continue essential work when the preferred agent or service is unavailable. Review the boundary by engineering surface; a successful workflow does not establish that the rest of the product is equally governable. This keeps the adoption decision connected to demonstrated capability and its costs.

Then stop. Once the selected capability has adequate representations, evidence, and enforcement, further machinery needs a new reason to exist. Stop when additional representation costs more to maintain than the reasoning it saves. A useful first result can be modest: one dependency that stops being rediscovered, one recurring review decision made explicit, or one acceptance condition that no longer depends on memory.

docs.title: B.4 Measuring MAGE
docs.text:
Appendix B — Practicing MAGEB.4 Measuring MAGE

Read outcomes before diagnostics. The operating question is whether delegated work produces durable, trustworthy progress at a cost the environment can sustain. The five primary readings in Table B.4-1 keep that question visible. They are not a composite score: a gain in throughput does not cancel an unacceptable escape, and a large stock of models does not compensate for models that cannot answer their claimed questions.

Table B.4-1. Read outcomes and the condition of the environment together; use diagnostic counts to investigate changes in these readings.ReadingQuestionRecordDurable throughputHow much accepted work survives without reopening, rollback, or repeated repair?Accepted units, observation window, and later repair.Defect escapeWhat incorrect or policy-violating work crosses the boundary intended to catch it?The obligation, boundary, affected revision, and discovery.Human-attention burdenWhat attention does each durable unit require?Reconstruction, review, exceptions, recovery, and deliberate judgment.Representation healthCan relied-upon models still answer their claimed questions?Correspondence, relevant coverage, and unresolved drift.Engineering-capital returnDoes inherited structure repay its construction and carrying cost?Later uses, avoided work, maintenance, and retirement candidates.

Before changing the environment, record several comparable work units under the existing process. Preserve their acceptance criteria, completion evidence, human interventions, and subsequent repairs. Use the same unit and observation window after introducing a model or control. Where work differs materially in complexity or consequence, report those differences rather than attributing every change in throughput or attention to MAGE. A before-and-after comparison can suggest whether the investment helped; it does not by itself establish causation.

Agree on the unit, boundary, and observation window before interpreting a trend. A landed change, completed work order, and released capability are different units. Keep their denominators visible and distinguish changes in the workload from changes in the machinery. Retain the revisions and evidence behind consequential observations. A dashboard can help locate a change in behavior; it cannot supply a comparison that the underlying records do not support.

docs.title: Define the Five Readings
docs.text:
Durable throughput counts accepted work that remains useful after the initial completion claim. Choose a window appropriate to the work and follow reopenings, rollbacks, and repeated repairs within it. Report recent work whose durability is not yet observable separately from work that has survived the window. A later change in requirements is not necessarily evidence that the original work failed; repeated repair of the original obligation is. Commit count and immediate ticket closure omit this distinction. The desired result is more accepted capability without a proportional increase in intervention.

Defect escape concerns a particular obligation and boundary. Record what crossed, which mechanism was supposed to prevent it, and how it was eventually discovered. A failed test before admission demonstrates detection; the same defect found after the relevant boundary demonstrates an escape. Compare rates only when the governed obligations and opportunities for observation are sufficiently comparable. More reported defects may reflect better observation rather than worse production, and no reported defects may reflect weak observation. State the limits of the evidence instead of converting absence of reports into confidence.

Human-attention burden includes the work hidden behind an apparently autonomous result. Record repeated reconstruction, routine inspection, exception handling, recovery, and consequential judgment, using time where it is practical and intervention records where it is not. Relate the burden to durable output rather than generated output. Keep intentional engineering decisions visible: choosing new obligations or interpreting ambiguous evidence is different from explaining the same repository convention again. A reduction is valuable when the work has been made unnecessary or carried reliably by the environment, not merely when it stops being recorded.

Representation health depends on the claim each representation makes. A descriptive model must correspond to the system it describes; a normative model states intent the system must satisfy; a derived view depends on its source and transformation. Historical work records have the different lifetime described earlier. Examine drift findings, failed queries, missing consequential coverage, and the evidence used to reconcile them. Freshness means correspondence after relevant change, not simply a recent edit date. A synchronized filename and a valid link do not settle a disagreement about meaning.

Engineering-capital return asks what later work inherits and what that inheritance costs. Retain concrete examples: a dependency no longer reconstructed, a recurring failure prevented, a larger task made tractable, or knowledge available after its original author has left. Account for construction, execution, understanding, reconciliation, and maintenance. A model may repay its cost without preventing a defect, just as a control may justify itself through a consequential risk rather than frequent use. Reuse counts alone cannot establish either return. Review structures whose carrying cost has outlived their purpose, and retire them when appropriate.

docs.title: Use Diagnostics to Explain, Not to Score
docs.text:
Churn, model coverage, support ratio, control count, closure rate, and queue length can help explain a primary reading. Churn can reveal repeated repair or useful restructuring. Coverage can expose a consequential gap or merely code below the model’s grain. A support ratio describes the amount of surrounding engineering machinery relative to implementation; it does not establish that the machinery pays. More controls can indicate greater protection or accumulated interference. Inspect the underlying work before treating any direction as healthy. The empirical observations in Chapter 5 are evidence from particular settings, not operating targets.

Include the health of observation in the review. Did scheduled checks run? Which revisions did they inspect? Could a check fail without anyone seeing or acting on its result? Were exceptions closed through verified repair or only acknowledgment? An empty findings list is uninterpretable when the check never ran. Similarly, an uncalibrated visual indicator is status, not a quantitative measurement. Preserve enough of the observation process to distinguish a quiet system from a silent sensor.

Review the readings at a cadence suited to the work and after a consequential incident. Investigate the explanations before prescribing another model or gate. A rise in attention may be temporary investment in new capability; declining throughput may be the deliberate cost of exposing previously hidden defects. Decide whether to repair an existing structure, extend coverage, retire unnecessary machinery, or keep the current arrangement. Measurement earns its place through those decisions and through the evidence that later shows whether they helped.

docs.title: B.3 Operating a GEE
docs.text:
Appendix B — Practicing MAGEB.3 Operating a GEE

A GEE has to turn an engineering priority into bounded work, preserve the evidence needed to judge the result, and recover when the work stops short. DocAble’s November 2026 workflow provides one concrete arrangement. Its strategy, epic, design, and dispatch documents have different consumers; they can be combined in another organization without losing the distinctions. The important connections are from priority to authorized scope, from scope to obligations, and from the resulting work to acceptance evidence.

In DocAble, I record requirements for the next deployment alongside longer-term priorities, and the orchestrator maintains the strategy document from my instructions. An epic develops a selected effort into scope, rationale, risks, relevant models, and a Definition of Done. Its machine-parseable phase table exposes dependencies and required reasoning capability to the scheduler. If review changes those dependencies, the schedulable plan must change too. Selecting a priority authorizes planning; it does not establish that the proposed decomposition is sound.

The design develops the engineering argument. It identifies the motivating failure or requirement, considers alternatives, and explains the proposed components and interactions. Stable invariant identifiers connect obligations to tests or analyses, while uncovered obligations remain explicit. A dispatch brief then assigns one ready phase, with a role, scope, time budget, relevant source, verification work, and expected hand-back. DocAble’s brief linter can reject missing structure and selected dispatch errors. It cannot decide whether the engineering premise is right.

docs.title: From a Brief to Accepted Work
docs.text:
As an illustration, consider an assignment to improve PDF heading detection. Prepare the brief from the current repository, not from a remembered account of the component. Four kinds of information make it usable:

  • Intended change and preservation. Identify the heading behavior to improve, the existing behavior that must remain, and exclusions such as unrelated document mutations. Leave implementation choices open where they do not affect these obligations.
  • Engineering context. Point to current source, the representation the component operates through, and relevant invariants. Require the agent to query the models and checks associated with its refined target files before changing them.
  • Acceptance evidence. Specify evidence for the intended behavior, preservation obligations, and affected integration paths. Evaluate those properties independently of the implementation the agent happens to choose. Record unavailable evidence as an open question.
  • Budget and hand-back. State when to stop and what to preserve: commits, completed checks, partial results, unresolved questions, and unmet obligations. An honest partial result supports a decision about further work; an unsupported completion claim hides that decision.

The agent records its refined plan in the first commit and progress in later commit metadata. A sentinel check verifies selected prerequisites early: the expected worktree, branch, working directory, and registration marker. These checks can discover an unusable working environment before substantial effort is spent. They establish those prerequisites at that boundary; later integration still needs its own evidence. The companion epic, design-document, and dispatch-brief starters supply field structures that can be adapted to these consumers.

Completion review follows the work back into the repository. Check that the promised change exists, was integrated, and has evidence supporting closure. A complete sequence of commit markers helps locate unfinished work but cannot establish semantic correctness. If the work is incomplete, preserve what the next agent or engineer needs to resume it. Reconcile partial commits and current ownership before launching replacement work; otherwise recovery can create a second competing attempt while the first remains stranded.

docs.title: Keep the Checking Process Operational
docs.text:
The factory’s own controls need the same scrutiny. In November, I retained cheap synchronous checks at merge and moved expensive validation into a periodic sweep. An intermediate design launched that sweep after every merge, so bursts of completed work still caused bursts of expensive validation and overloaded the host. Background execution had changed who waited without removing the coupling that caused the overload. The replacement gave the sweep its own schedule and lock, inspected the main branch in a disposable worktree, and allowed one sweep at a time. Broader validation remained part of release.

A configured schedule is not evidence that a check runs. The November 3 investigation found the timer in the configuration manifest but not installed. Checks had been running through a debounced post-merge hook, masking the missing schedule. Installation and inspection of the live schedule corrected that gap. Another failure concerned closure: an alert was marked resolved while its lint still failed. Rechecking before closure, or reopening the alert when the next sweep finds the condition again, was identified as necessary follow-up work.

Distinguish detection, acknowledgment, and repair in the operating record. The observed sweep detected a blocking failure and emitted an alert. A different alert, concerning accumulated worktree branches, caused a hook to refuse an orchestrator operation until acknowledgment. Those observations did not demonstrate detection, blocked dispatch, and verified repair for the same failure. Acknowledgment permits a deliberate response to a known problem; it does not make the problem disappear. Record the revision each check examined so that evidence for an earlier snapshot cannot silently validate later changes.

docs.title: Make Recovery Improve Later Work
docs.text:
After recovery, ask what subsequent work should inherit. Was the problem missing knowledge, a stale representation, an implicit obligation, late evidence, or a mechanism that failed to act? The answer determines whether to improve a model, move a check, restrict an action, change the procedure, or retain deliberate human judgment. Record the obligation and intended consumer of the repair, then verify that the consumer actually uses it. This is the practical handoff from incident response to governance conversion.

The duplicate-dispatch incident in Appendix A illustrates this handoff. Its repair placed a completed-phase gate in work-order composition, so later assignments inherit the refusal automatically. The gate acts on recorded completion rather than inferring it from arbitrary repository changes; that boundary defines which recurrence the repair prevents.

Price that inheritance. A rare, inexpensive failure may not justify permanent machinery; a repeated reconstruction or recurring loss may justify it readily. Remove the superseded procedure or control when its replacement makes it unnecessary. Otherwise every repair adds another thing that later work must understand. The next run should inherit a better starting point, with the evidence needed to tell whether the repair worked.

docs.title: Appendix A — MAGE Engineering Handbook
docs.text:
Appendix A — MAGE Engineering HandbookAppendix A — MAGE Engineering Handbook

An engineer consulting a handbook usually has something to do. A rule keeps being forgotten; a representation has drifted; an agent has completed work that cannot yet be accepted. This appendix starts with a short reference to the engineering moves developed in the book, then shows how several moves work together in DocAble.

The three worked compositions answer different questions. Model Coherence connects representations to the implementation they describe or govern. Governance Conversion turns a failure into something later work inherits. Governed Delegation gives a reasoner useful freedom while preserving boundaries around its actions and the evidence needed to accept its work. The examples were selected because each shows a different way an explicit representation changes engineering work: supplying knowledge, deriving configuration, controlling an action, or preserving evidence. Their value depends on what consumes them and how their correspondence with the system is maintained.

Not every engineering decision belongs in a model. Local implementation details remain in code, operational procedures often remain in runbooks, and judgments that cannot be reliably mechanized remain with engineers. The aim is to preserve consequential distinctions at a useful level of abstraction. A model that duplicates every implementation detail has surrendered much of its purpose.

Where to Find the Models

Each example identifies an actual representation, its consumers, and the correspondence or enforcement machinery around it. The excerpts omit unrelated declarations. They are intended to show what the engineer made explicit, rather than provide a complete implementation to copy.

Table A-1.ModelEngineering questionWorked compositionComponent and zone catalogueWhich implementation belongs to a component, and which knowledge applies there?Model CoherenceInter-service call contractsDoes a declared call have consistent wiring and the required invocation permission?Model CoherenceGovernance graphWhich mechanisms can interfere, and does their recorded wiring still exist?Governance ConversionAccessibility decision policyHow should uncertain evidence affect whether an image is described?Governance ConversionDocument and changeset contractWhat can a reasoner inspect and propose, and which edits can the applier refuse?Governed DelegationWork order and completionWhich knowledge applies to this assignment, and what establishes that its work arrived?Governed Delegation

A representation’s authority must be stated separately from its syntax. An authored contract specifies an obligation; an extracted view records what the implementation currently does; a derived plan computes a consequence of other facts. All three can be useful. A correct derivation from a mistaken obligation remains mistaken, and a faithful description can expose a system that should change.

docs.title: Appendix B — Practicing MAGE
docs.text:
Appendix B — Practicing MAGEAppendix B — Practicing MAGE

A practical reference for beginning, operating, and evaluating a Governed Engineering Environment

Begin with one engineering surface: a recurring kind of change, an operational workflow, or a consequential obligation. This appendix follows that surface from the first investment through brownfield migration, delegated work, and measurement. Use the section that answers the decision in front of you. The MAGE Engineering Handbook supplies concrete models and compositions of mechanisms; the main chapters develop the method behind them.

The governing question is whether the environment makes future work more capable, trustworthy, or economical than it costs to maintain.
